title: Dolly Parton dead at 80
summary: Dolly Parton, country music legend, has died after months of battling unknown health issues. Her nephew announced the news in a video posted to her Instagram page.
story: Music icon Dolly Parton has passed away at the age of 80 due to health complications in Nashville, Tennessee.
Legendary country singer and songwriter Dolly Parton died. She was 80.
Parton died peacefully in Nashville, Tennessee on Tuesday, according to a press release obtained by Fox News Digital. Her representatives confirmed she faced a "brief battle with cancer."
"Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched," her team said in a statement.
DOLLY PARTON ADMITS HUSBAND CARL DEAN'S DEATH HAS BEEN 'BIG ADJUSTMENT' AFTER 60-YEAR ROMANCE
Dolly Parton has died. She was 80.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand. Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.
"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," the statement concluded.
Her nephew revealed the news in an Aug. 25 Instagram video. The news comes after Parton spent months battling an unknown health issue.

"My name is Brin Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he says in the video. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now."

"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens."

"I first went on the road with Dolly as a kid, getting a taste of the road life in the early 1980s. Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible. Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," Seaver added in the video message. "By her example, we believed that anything is possible. She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."
Parton had been battling a series of health issues.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," Seaver continued. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not. Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever. Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy; he farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because, after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."
"Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly — Aunt, Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you."

Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child, started writing songs at a young age and moved to Nashville after graduating high school to pursue music.

Her breakthrough came as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," where she became a fan favorite before forging a solo path that would establish her as one of country music’s most prolific and influential songwriters.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"I’ll always be a country musician because I’m a country girl," she told People in 1975. "My style is my soul and my feelings. I’ll tell the world in my songs what I wouldn’t have told my mother."

Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard."
DOLLY PARTON UNABLE TO WRITE NEW SONGS AFTER LOSING HUSBAND OF NEARLY 60 YEARS
The legendary country music star built her career on talent, charitable work and charisma.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

Parton made her feature film debut opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in 1980’s "9 to 5." Parton later appeared in films including "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," "Rhinestone," "Steel Magnolias" and "Joyful Noise."
Parton was also known for her decades-long marriage to Carl Dean, who largely stayed out of the public eye during their nearly 60 years together. Dean died in March 2025.
After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs.

"I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes."
"I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said.
Dolly Parton's husband, Carl Dean, died in Nashville in March 2025. He was 82. (Dolly Parton Instagram)

In November of that same year, the country music legend opened up about her impressive career spanning more than seven decades, got candid about the personal sacrifices she's made throughout the years and explained why she feels like she's "just getting started."

"You know, I have just been going so fast my whole life," Parton told People at the time. "And I just start thinking, ‘How in the world did I even have a life? How did I even get it done?’ I really realized when I was putting this book together just how much I had sacrificed in my life. I never had children, so at least I didn’t have a guilty feeling. I’m thankful that I got to see my dreams come true."

"People say, ‘Well, you’re going to be 80 years old.’ Well, so what? Look at all I’ve done in 80 years. I feel like I’m just getting started," said Parton. "I know that sounds stupid, but unless my health gives way, which right now I seem to be doing fine… I think there’s a lot to be said about age. If you allow yourself to get old, you will. I say, ‘I ain’t got time to get old!’ I ain’t got time to dwell on that. That’s not what I’m thinking about."
Parton canceled her Las Vegas residency in May due to ongoing health concerns.  (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki, File)
Parton has battled various health issues over the past couple of years.
In May, the country legend announced she was canceling her planned Las Vegas residency, which had already been postponed from 2025 to September 2026 because of health concerns.
Earlier this month, Parton missed a major Dollywood event per doctor's orders.
"I’m still in Nashville, and I’m sorry about that," Parton told the crowd during a video appearance at the event, according to video shared by the Knoxville News Sentinel.

"I’m supposed to be there in person, like we planned," she continued. "Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues. And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated."

"And I’m dehydrated," Parton, who appeared on-screen wearing fairy wings, told the crowd. "And, so, my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying, 'You ain’t traveling this week.’"
Parton was also known for her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library. (David Redfern/Redferns)
Parton had previously discussed problems involving kidney stones, saying her immune and digestive systems had gotten "out of whack" and were being treated.

Beyond her impressive career, Parton built a business empire centered in her home state of Tennessee. Dollywood became one of Tennessee’s most popular attractions, while her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library left an equally lasting mark.

The Imagination Library, which sends free books to children from birth until kindergarten, was inspired by Parton’s father, who never learned to read or write. The program grew into an international literacy initiative and distributed millions of books to families around the world.

"With heavy hearts, the Dollywood family mourns the passing of our beloved Dreamer-in-Chief, Dolly Parton. Everyone at Dollywood shares the sorrow of countless people around the world touched by Dolly’s warmth, wisdom and generous spirit," a representative from Dollywood said in a statement. "Dolly’s heartfelt wish was that Dollywood always remain a place of joy, hope and togetherness—a space where families and friends could honor her memory, not with silence, but with laughter, music and shared dreams.""Dolly’s enduring legacy extends beyond her music and generosity to her remarkable work ethic—an inspiration to people everywhere. In her spirit, Dollywood will be open Wednesday as Dolly wanted, always reminding everyone with her signature sparkle — 'the show must go on.' Together, we honor her by carrying forward her message of love, perseverance, and hope."
At Parton’s request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family.

title: Jennifer Garner says she 'panicked' about financial stability after divorce from Ben Affleck
summary: Jennifer Garner reveals she "panicked" about finances after her split from Ben Affleck, realizing she needed to become a serious earner for her kids.
story: Celebrity matchmaker Alessandra Conti told Fox News Digital that Garner and Affleck are incredible co-parents.
Jennifer Garner once "panicked" about her financial stability shortly after her marriage to Ben Affleck came to an end.

During an episode of the "Aspire with Emma Grede" podcast, Garner — who shares three children with Affleck — opened up about her past fear that she would no longer be able to financially support herself and her children post-divorce and explained how she pushed through.

"I panicked when I was first out of my marriage and realized I had taken such a step back in my work," said Garner. "Suddenly I realized I don't know how long I'll be able to work. This isn't a career that's like, 'Hey, you're 60, you're 55, you're 43, come on, let's pay you more than you've ever made.' You know what I mean? That's not been traditionally the role. I was suddenly like, 'Wait a minute, I have to take care of myself, I have to take care of these kids. So what is it going to be?'"

Jennifer Garner said she "panicked" after her divorce from Ben Affleck. (Getty Images)

"I can't leave these kids for six months at a time," she said. "I would love to. I love going on location, but it's not this time in my career."

Affleck and Garner met on the set of 2001's "Pearl Harbor," but didn't spark a romantic relationship until 2004, after starring alongside one another in the 2003 film "Daredevil." They married in 2005, but eventually called it quits in 2015.

"I was so lucky to be able to luxuriate and working some and being home and being a mom a lot of time," Garner said. "I was really grateful for that opportunity. I got to kind of have the best of both worlds, so I can't really look back and complain about any of it … it is what it is."

While balancing her work and professional life, Garner said she learned there is beauty in imperfection.

title: Prince William ‘blindsided’ by Harry, Meghan return as Kate fears new turmoil from royal feud: experts
summary: Prince William was reportedly "blindsided" by the Sussexes' U.K. return, with royal experts saying he and Princess Catherine are concerned about the fallout.
story: Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, discusses Prince Harry's expected UK return, his relationship with King Charles, and why a meeting with Prince William remains unlikely.
Prince William was reportedly "blindsided" by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s surprise decision to return to the U.K. with their children.

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that the Prince and Princess of Wales are "concerned" about the Duke and Duchess of Sussex returning for an extended period beginning this month. Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are set to begin school there in September, People magazine reported.
"Prince William was blindsided," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state, on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the brothers haven't spoken since 2022. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"He had found Harry’s recent eagerness to publicly signal that he wanted to spend more time in Britain unusual, but that is very different from anticipating a full return. William now has to navigate a situation he did not create, did not ask for and, given the state of their relationship, almost certainly would not have chosen."
A Kensington Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "We would never comment on private family matters."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, Duke of Rothsay and Prince George of Wales attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)

In a statement shared with The New York Times, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, speaks at Scotty's Summer Festival at Maxstoke Castle near Birmingham, central England, on July 11, 2026. (Heathcliff O'Malley/AFP via Getty Images)
The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California.
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that the Waleses are "feeling uneasy" about facing another chapter in the "endless Sussex soap opera."
WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

"It’s about broken trust," Chard explained. "Prince William is said to feel that Harry and Meghan have spent years attacking the institution, then monetizing their grievances through a very lucrative media operation. From his view, it’s an ongoing campaign for maximum impact and self-gain. He’s not going to fuel it, and he’s not going to endorse behavior he sees as damaging."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, arrive for a service at Crathie Kirk Church in Crathie, Aberdeenshire, on Aug. 23, 2026. (Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images)

William and Kate were seen arriving in Scotland on Thursday, where they’ll spend time with King Charles at Balmoral Castle. The royal family has spent summers at the Scottish estate since the reign of Queen Victoria, with family members traditionally hunting, fishing and horseback riding there.
The king learned about Harry and Meghan’s move three days before it was made public, according to reports.

King Charles III inspects the Balaklava Company, 5th Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland, at the gates of Balmoral as he takes up summer residence at the castle on Aug. 18, 2026. (PA Images via Getty Images)

"Prince William, along with Catherine, is currently at Balmoral Castle visiting the king," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "Harry and Meghan have, so far, not been invited to visit the king privately while on a holiday. This will not happen while William is there. I’ve been told he has no desire to connect on any level with his younger brother and simply has no time for [Meghan]."

A spokesperson for Archewell, which handles the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, told Fox News Digital: "We do not comment on the family’s private travel arrangements or meetings with the extended family."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, attend the David Foster Foundation 40th Anniversary Celebration on Aug. 7, 2026, in Victoria, British Columbia. (The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)

The Daily Mail reported that the king and his heir held a "Sussex Summit" following the announcement. A source told the outlet that the Prince and Princess of Wales "have no interest in engaging with anything Harry and Meghan do or say."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Balmoral Castle in Scotland. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"Things are projected to be tense at Balmoral," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "... Princess Catherine is particularly guarded given how deeply hurt she was by both of them. Both she and Prince William are very determined to maintain their own family stability and remain focused on duty with their royal roles paramount."
Several royal experts previously told Fox News Digital that William and Harry haven’t been on speaking terms since at least 2022.

From left: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, Prince William and Princess Catherine watch a Royal Air Force flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"My sources have described genuine concern within the Wales camp," Schofield said. "I don’t think Prince William and Princess Catherine are sitting at Balmoral panicking about Harry and Meghan returning, but they are understandably apprehensive about what their return could bring. The last several years have taught them that private family tensions have a habit of becoming very public."
King Charles III and Queen Camilla attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)

"The concern isn’t simply that Harry and Meghan will be geographically closer," Schofield continued. "It’s the unpredictability that comes with the Sussexes. There have been interviews, books, documentaries and very personal allegations about members of the royal family. … My sources tell me the Wales camp has not forgotten the hostility directed at them after some of Harry and Meghan’s previous public accusations."
Schofield said unnamed sources told her Kate is also unsettled by the news.

Meghan Markle told Oprah Winfrey in 2021 that Kate Middleton made her cry during a disagreement over flower girl dresses ahead of her wedding to Prince Harry. Meghan said Kate later apologized and brought her flowers and a note. (Chris Jackson/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"My sources tell me that Catherine does not want to revisit that chapter of her life," Schofield explained. "She has endured very personal allegations, an enormous amount of public scrutiny and a difficult few years. My understanding has always been that her priority is Prince William, their children and the future."

Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales attend the 2026 EE BAFTA Film Awards at The Royal Festival Hall on Feb. 22, 2026, in London. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)

"Meghan returning to Britain doesn’t mean Catherine suddenly has an obligation to reopen a relationship that has caused considerable hurt," she said. "Catherine can wish Harry and Meghan well without wanting them back inside her private life. ... The idea of resurrecting the ‘Fab Four’ is fantasy. Too much has happened, and too much has been lost."
The Sussexes are expected to live at a private, nonroyal residence outside London, The Associated Press reported. They won’t resume their royal duties, which they gave up in 2020.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen greeting members of the public at the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia on April 17, 2026, in Sydney, Australia. (Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

The couple’s return to the U.K. comes as the king continues treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer diagnosed in 2024. In 2025, Harry said he didn’t know "how much longer my father has" and expressed a desire for his children to get to know their grandfather.

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father, King Charles III, at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
Last month, the king met with Harry, Meghan and their children at Highgrove House.
Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl reported at the time that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware that the meeting was taking place."
Prince William, Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales are seen here at the DMMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026 in Windsor, England, on July 10, 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"The Sussexes played a blinder with the king welcoming them, having not told him last month of a plan they have had for ages as their children will soon be in school," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital.
The move is understood to have come together relatively quickly, as Harry and Meghan waited to learn whether their children had been accepted to the private school they applied to.

Highgrove House, the king's private residence, in Doughton, Gloucestershire. (Neil Bennett/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)

"Since the brothers haven’t spoken in years, the imminent arrival of the Sussexes places William and Catherine in a pressured and difficult situation," said Fitzwilliams. "William is reportedly furious. But what is essential is that the king accepts that the Waleses and their children are the future of the monarchy."
Schofield doesn’t believe reconciliation between the brothers is likely, at least anytime soon.

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the last time the brothers spoke was in 2022 during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral. (Dominic Lipinski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"Geography cannot repair a relationship where trust has been so badly damaged," she said. "Harry’s return could make that estrangement more obvious because people will inevitably ask why two brothers living in the same country still aren’t seeing one another. ... William and Catherine could suddenly find themselves under public pressure to perform a reconciliation that probably doesn’t exist behind closed doors."

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex sits in a car as she attends Queen Elizabeth's state funeral and burial in London on Sept. 19, 2022. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"... William may have reached the conclusion that distance is healthier than reconciliation, and he is entitled to make that decision," Schofield said. "The realistic goal at this stage probably isn’t friendship [with Harry]. I would argue it’s peaceful coexistence for the sake of their father. ... Harry and Meghan moving back to Britain creates proximity, not reconciliation. They can buy a house near London. They cannot buy back trust."

title: Kacey Musgraves divides fans with immigrant children’s plea, faces boycott calls to ‘shut up and sing’
summary: Kacey Musgraves asked fans to donate to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights during her tour opener, sparking a divided reaction on social media.
story: Mickey Guyton said she "loves" both Reese Witherspoon and Kacey Musgraves and enjoyed working with them on the show "My Kind of Country."
Kacey Musgraves is facing backlash after asking fans to donate to an immigrant children’s rights group as her birthday wish while kicking off her "Middle of Nowhere" tour.

On Friday, the country music star marked her 38th birthday on the opening night of her tour at the United Center in Chicago, Illinois. At one point, Musgraves paused her show and urged concertgoers to contribute to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights.

"It’s a wonderful organization, and they help give aid — legal aid — and money to children whose parents have been deported unfairly," Musgraves said. "It’s not a political thing. It’s just, these kids need help."

Kacey Musgraves sparked backlash on social media after asking fans to donate to an immigrant children’s rights group as her birthday wish during the opening night of her new tour. (Getty Images for Coachella)

She continued, "They have no guidance and no way to get through this thing without their homebase or their parents. So anyway, 50 cents, whatever the hell, I don't know, whatever you want to do but that would mean a lot to me."
KACEY MUSGRAVES FACES BOYCOTT CALLS AFTER ASKING FANS TO DONATE TO IMMIGRANT CHILDREN'S GROUP
"If you don't want to, that's totally fine too," Musgraves added.

The eight-time Grammy Award winner's appeal was immediately met with applause and cheers from the crowd in Chicago. However, Musgraves' request drew a divided response online, including criticism from conservative political commentators.
The country star said the Young Center supports children "whose parents have been deported unfairly." (Christopher Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)
"What is an unfair deportation?" Tomi Lahren, host of Outkick's "Tomi Lahren Is Fearless" podcast, wrote on X alongside a video of Musgraves' birthday request.
KENNY CHESNEY TELLS BILL MAHER THE KEY REASON HE REFUSES TO TELL HIS LISTENERS HOW TO VOTE

"Kacey Musgraves stopped her concert to ask the audience to donate money for legal aid to kids whose parents have been deported ‘unfairly.’ How about donating money the help kids who's parents have been killed by illegal immigrants! What happened to the country music industry?" conservative influencer Vince Langman commented.
"Another TRAITOROUS woman who wants nothing more than to see our country fall," an X user chimed in.
"Shut up and sing Kasey (sic)!! Why do musicians think they Can draw a line in the sand? You alienate 50% of your audience," another commented.
Some critics declared that they would no longer support Musgraves and called for a boycott of her music and concerts.
NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS
"You just earned yourself a big ol’ boycott, you traitor," one detractor wrote. "Illegal aliens and their kids don’t deserve our patronage and neither do you!"
"I’m deporting Musgraves from all my music playlists," another X user commented.
Critics slammed Musgraves' comments while her fans defended her. (Christopher Polk/Dick Clark Productions via Getty Images)
Other social media users argued that Musgraves should donate her own money rather than ask fans to contribute.

"Kacey Musgraves is worth $15 million. Yet she’s asking fans who already paid $150 to $350 for tickets to donate to support the children of illegal aliens," one social media user commented. "If she cares that much, she can fund it herself and let them live in one of her multi-million-dollar mansions."
MUSICIAN KENNY CHESNEY'S REFUSAL TO SPEAK OUT ON POLITICS SPARKS ARGUMENT ON 'THE VIEW'

"Everyone she is speaking too (sic) gave her their money when they bought tickets," another added. "She did not give the audience money. So now she has the money, shouldn't she donate to whatever cause she wants? She is actually on stage at a show that the audience had to pay to get admission to and now she is asking for more of their money. That's rude."
However, some of the "Dry Spell" singer's fans defended her on social media and praised her for speaking out on behalf of immigrant children.
POP STAR OLIVIA RODRIGO FELT 'ENRAGED' AFTER ICE USED HER HIT SONG, BRANDS AGENCY 'BARBARIC'
"Love this. 'It's not a political thing. It's just, these kids need help.' Exactly. More artists doing this please," one fan wrote on X.

"In all fairness, the kids didn’t do anything wrong," another wrote. "I don’t believe their parents were wrongfully deported, but I equally believe that their children, if retained in the United States by law, should be taken care of. We’re not f------ animals!"
"No boycott here!" an X user declared.

"Helping children caught in difficult circumstances is a worthy cause," one commenter argued. "At the same time, immigration enforcement and whether a deportation was lawful or justified are matters for the courts and policymakers not concert stages."
Fox News Digital has reached out to Musgraves' representatives for comment.
Musgraves stood by her support for the organization following the concert.  (Dan MacMedan/Getty Images)
Meanwhile, Musgraves stood by her remarks on social media, taking to her Instagram Story to upload a post that read, "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone."
The singer also reposted a message shared by the Young Center's Instagram page, in which the organization expressed its gratitude to her.
"Thank you," the nonprofit wrote. "We appreciate your support of our work and mission to see unaccompanied immigrant children safe, free, and with their families."

Based in Chicago, the Young Center describes its work as pairing volunteers with attorneys and social workers to advocate for unaccompanied and separated immigrant children in government custody. Its website lists family unity, release from custody, fair proceedings and children's best interests among its priorities.

The nonprofit reported serving 1,975 children from 53 countries in 2024 and opening 1,388 new cases. Its 2025 annual report said children's average detention time increased from 30 to 198 days and requests for assistance from detained parents quadrupled from 2024.

Friday’s appeal extended Musgraves’ support for the charity. In April, resale platform Depop announced that 20 pieces from her wardrobe, including clothing from music videos and tours, would be sold in capsule drops. Women's Wear Daily reported that all proceeds would benefit the Young Center.
In announcing the sale, Musgraves described the beneficiary without discussing immigration enforcement.
The eight-time Grammy Award winner wrote "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone." (Taylor Hill/Getty Images for ABA)
"I also adore the fact that the sales are supporting a really beautiful cause," Musgraves said.

Musgraves also invited three brothers, ages 18, 14 and 12, to open three Texas shows in May after their family was released from ICE custody. The mariachi performers' family said they entered through the now-defunct CBP One appointment system in 2023 and sought asylum after fleeing violence in Mexico, KSAT reported.

DHS said the family entered illegally and had been released into the country by the Biden administration. Responding to the family’s detention, DHS said federal law required custody while its immigration claims were heard.

"The law requires illegal aliens who show up at a port of entry without valid entry to be detained while all their claims are heard. You can look it up in the statute," a DHS spokesperson told KSAT. "Unlike the previous administration, the Trump administration is not going to ignore the rule of law."
Musgraves previously invited a trio of brothers to open three Texas shows in May after their family was released from ICE custody. (Joseph Okpako/WireImage)

Musgraves' latest remarks came as ICE enforcement reached record levels. Federal sources told Fox News Digital that agents made about 51,000 immigration arrests in July, topping the previous record of roughly 43,000 in June.

"Every day, the brave men and women of ICE are arresting and DEPORTING dangerous criminal illegal aliens, including gang members, from our country," DHS said.

title: Mariska Hargitay nearly left 'Law & Order SVU' over fear of being a 'one-trick pony'
summary: Mariska Hargitay revealed she once told Julianna Margulies she needed to leave "SVU," but her blunt response changed everything.
story: Dennis Quaid spoke out about receiving the 2026 Patriot Ally Award at the 2nd Annual Military & Veteran Entertainment Awards Gala.
Mariska Hargitay once considered leaving "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" after more than two decades as Olivia Benson because she worried the role had come to define her career.
In a new interview with Variety, the actress — who has starred as Benson since "SVU" premiered in 1999 — said she began questioning her future on the long-running NBC drama around its 25th season.
"I’ve got to leave the show too. I don’t want people to think I’m a one-trick pony," Hargitay recalled telling "ER" co-star Julianna Margulies.

"It's a very sort of interesting dichotomy," Hargitay added. "Because you think about a crime show, which normally should sort of upset your nervous system, actually can settle it down because of that."
"Law & Order's" success spawned seven spinoffs, including "Special Victims Unit," "Criminal Intent," "Trial by Jury," "LA," "UK," "True Crime" and "Organized Crime."

title: John Candy's family calls out Hollywood for weight criticism the actor endured throughout his career
summary: Jennifer Candy-Sullivan and Rosemary Candy slam Hollywood's weight criticism of John Candy, revealing how the late comedian handled it privately.
story: The legendary actor's wife and daughter told Fox News Digital the focus on his weight was "upsetting," but that he handled it well.
John Candy's family is calling out Hollywood for how their father was treated.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital at Televerse 26, the late actor's daughter, Jennifer Candy-Sullivan, and her mother, Rosemary Candy, slammed Hollywood for the way their father's weight was discussed during his fame.

"I think everyone who had some sort of difference was kind of put under a magnifying glass. So for him, it was his weight. And he kind of... he took it like a gentleman," Jennifer said. "And I think as his career went on, he was able to be more comfortable with himself and kind of vocalize and speak up for himself."

She went on to say that because of his career, people "thought he was the everyday guy and everyone loved him," so it would be okay to "pal around" and "joke around him," but that "in reality, it wasn't that okay. It was not cool."
John Candy's daughter and widow slammed Hollywood for the way they spoke about his weight during his fame. (Robin L Marshall/Getty Images; Steve Schapiro/Corbis via Getty Images)

Jennifer doesn't think the public or the media would be any less harsh on her father if his rise to fame occurred today, saying, "I think there would be a different type of kind of critique to him."

"I think if he tried losing weight, then it would be like, 'You're too skinny, you're no longer funny.' So I think Hollywood would find something," she said. "It would be... he doesn't... he would do something wrong. Ultimately, I think anyone in Hollywood does something wrong."
The two attended a special FYC presentation of the documentary about the comedian, "John Candy: I Like Me," as part of Televerse 26, the Television Academy festival.

title: Shelley Fabares, star of 'The Donna Reed Show' and 'Coach,' dead at 82
summary: Shelley Fabares starred on "The Donna Reed Show," hit No. 1 with "Johnny Angel" and earned two Emmy nods for "Coach" over a career spanning decades.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Shelley Fabares, the actress and singer who starred in "The Donna Reed Show" and earned two Emmy nominations for her role in "Coach," has died. She was 82.
Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles surrounded by her loved ones, her family confirmed in a statement to the Associated Press. Her cause of death was not disclosed.

"To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter, and comfort," her family wrote, according to the outlet. "She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued, and cared for."
'GOMER PYLE: USMC' STAR RONNIE SCHELL DEAD AT 94 AFTER DECADES-LONG CAREER

"We will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives," they added.
"The Donna Reed Show" star Shelley Fabares has died at the age of 82. (Mark Sullivan/WireImage; Harry Langdon/Getty Images)

Fabares became one of television's most recognizable young stars when she was cast as Mary Stone, the teenage daughter of the characters played by Donna Reed and Carl Betz, on "The Donna Reed Show" in 1958.
During her time on the hit family sitcom, Fabares unexpectedly launched a successful recording career after the show's producer, Tony Owen, decided to incorporate singing into the series.

The actress' debut single, "Johnny Angel," reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1962 and sold more than 1 million copies. She released several albums and scored additional hits with "Johnny Loves Me" and "The Things We Did Last Summer," though she later acknowledged that she never considered herself much of a singer.

Fabares left "The Donna Reed Show" as a regular cast member in 1963 but returned for guest appearances before the series ended in 1966. She remained close to Reed, whom she credited as a mentor who helped her navigate Hollywood as a young actress.

Donna Reed and Shelley Fabares are pictured with baseball player Don Drysdale of the Los Angeles Dodgers in an episode of "The Donna Reed Show." (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
At the height of her teen idol fame, Fabares transitioned to the big screen and starred opposite Elvis Presley in three movies: "Girl Happy" in 1965, "Spinout" in 1966 and "Clambake" in 1967.
She also appeared in the 1964 surf movie "Ride the Wild Surf," the 1966 musical comedy "Hold On!" with Herman’s Hermits and the 1968 Hank Williams Jr. film "A Time to Sing."

Born Michele Ann Marie Fabares on Jan. 19, 1944, in Santa Monica, California, she was the niece of actress Nanette Fabray. Fabares began modeling as a young child and made her television debut at age 10 on an episode of "Letter to Loretta."

Her early credits included appearances in "The Bad Seed," "Never Say Goodbye," "Jeanne Eagels" and "Marjorie Morningstar." She also appeared with Annette Funicello in the 1958 Disney serial "Annette."

After her initial success as a teen star, Fabares built a prolific television career that spanned several decades. In 1971, she portrayed Joy Piccolo, the wife of Chicago Bears running back Brian Piccolo, whom James Caan played, in the acclaimed television movie "Brian's Song," which also starred Billy Dee Williams.
Elvis Presley and Shelley Fabares starred in the 1967 film "Clambake." (Getty Images)

Fabares later held regular roles on "The Brian Keith Show," "The Practice" and "Forever Fernwood." From 1978 to 1984, she played Francine Webster, the professional rival of Bonnie Franklin’s Ann Romano, on "One Day at a Time."
She also made guest appearances on television shows, including "The Twilight Zone," "Mannix," "The Rockford Files," "The Love Boat," "Fantasy Island," "Mork & Mindy" and "Murder, She Wrote."
MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SAYS SHE AND VALERIE BERTINELLI DRANK WINE, DID COCAINE DURING SITCOM BREAKS

In 1989, Fabares found renewed success when she joined the ABC sitcom "Coach" as Christine Armstrong, the girlfriend and eventual wife of Hayden Fox, the college football coach played by Craig T. Nelson.

Fabares remained with the series throughout its nine-season run, appearing with Craig T. Nelson, Jerry Van Dyke and Bill Fagerbakke until the show ended in 1997. Her performance earned her two Emmy nominations for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series, in 1993 and 1994.
'MIRACLE ON THE HUDSON' HERO CAPTAIN 'SULLY' SULLENBERGER REVEALS ALZHEIMER'S DIAGNOSIS
Shelley Fabares starred as Christine Armstrong on "Coach" from 1989 to 1997. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Later in her career, Fabares lent her voice to Martha Kent in several animated Superman projects, including "Superman: The Animated Series," "Justice League" and the 2006 film "Superman: Brainiac Attacks."

Fabares became an advocate for Alzheimer's awareness after her mother, Elsa, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. She helped raise money for research, delivered speeches and testified before Congress about the disease. Her mother died in 1992.

In 1999, Fabares faced a serious health crisis when doctors discovered she had progressive liver failure related to autoimmune hepatitis. After spending nearly two years on a transplant waiting list, she had a liver transplant in October 2000.
Shelley Fabares remained married to "M*A*S*H" actor Mike Farrell for more than 40 years until her death. (Getty Images)

Fabares married record and film producer Lou Adler in 1964. The couple separated two years later, and their divorce was finalized in 1980.

title: Motown songwriter behind 'Money (That's What I Want)' and other hits dead at 87
summary: Janie Bradford Hobbs co-wrote "Money (That's What I Want)" with Berry Gordy and penned hits for Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and The Supremes.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Janie Bradford Hobbs, an early Motown songwriter who co-wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)" and penned songs recorded by Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and other music legends, has died after an extended illness at 87.
Bradford Hobbs died at a Los Angeles hospital, her family said Saturday.
Born in Charleston, Missouri, Bradford Hobbs later moved to Detroit, where neighbor and singer Jackie Wilson introduced her to Motown founder Berry Gordy in the late 1950s.
COMMODORES CO-FOUNDER AND FORMER BASSIST RONALD LAPREAD DEAD AT 75
Janie Bradford attends the Mary Wilson tribute at The GRAMMY Museum on March 4, 2022, in Los Angeles, California. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images)

She started working for Motown as a receptionist in 1958, but her role soon went well beyond answering phones. Like many employees in Motown’s early days, Bradford Hobbs became involved in making the music.
She and Gordy wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)," which Barrett Strong recorded in 1959. The song became one of Motown’s first hits and was later recorded by The Beatles.

Bradford Hobbs also wrote "Too Busy Thinking About My Baby." The Temptations recorded the song first, and Marvin Gaye later had a hit with it. She also wrote songs for Stevie Wonder, The Supremes, Martha & The Vandellas and others.
Janie Bradford, left, and George Clinton attend a ceremony honoring Clinton with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, Jan. 19, 2024, in Los Angeles. (Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP, File)
"Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown, and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family," Gordy said in a statement.
COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DON SCHLITZ, WHO WROTE KENNY ROGERS' HIT 'THE GAMBLER,' DEAD AT 73
Gordy described Bradford Hobbs as one of the people who believed in Motown before anyone knew what it would become.

"Janie was one of a special group I have always thought of as the original Motown family — the unsung heroes who believed in the dream before anyone knew what Motown would become," Gordy continued. "She was one of the people who helped make Motown what it became."
Janie Bradford attends The Paley Center For Media Hosts A Legendary Evening With Mary Wilson at The Paley Center for Media on Feb. 25, 2019 in Beverly Hills, California. (Leon Bennett/Getty Images)

Bradford Hobbs later became head of Writer Relations for Jobete, Motown’s publishing company. After leaving Motown, she founded the annual Heroes and Legends Awards, which honored figures in the music industry and awarded scholarships for about 30 years, according to her family.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She is survived by her husband, Wardean Hobbs; daughter, Nicole Hobbs; son, Lance Finney; and two grandsons. Funeral arrangements have not been completed.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Andrew feels ‘abandoned’ by royal family, rejects King Charles’ invitation over outcast fears: experts
summary: Former Prince Andrew reportedly feels "abandoned" by the royal family after rejecting King Charles III's invitation to Balmoral, fearing outcast treatment.
story: Andrew Lownie, author of "Entitled," argues Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor worsened his own crisis and believes new Epstein-related details could still emerge.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly feels "abandoned" by his family as his royal exile deepens.
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that friends are reportedly checking in regularly on the former Duke of York and "he's certainly not hiding away" from them.

"Rather than spending the summer at Balmoral hidden away with the rest of the family, Andrew seems to be opting for time abroad with friends," she said. "Allegedly, he feels abandoned by certain family members."
FORMER PRINCE ANDREW SPOTTED WITH BRUISE COVERING HALF HIS FACE AS MYSTERY INJURY SPARKS QUESTIONS

Former Prince Andrew is seen departing Westminster Abbey after the Coronation of King Charles III and Queen Camilla on May 06, 2023, in London, England. The former Duke of York vacated Royal Lodge on Feb. 2, 2026. (Karwai Tang/WireImage/Getty Images)
British royal expert Hilary Fordwich echoed Chard's sentiments, citing her sources.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, attend the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025, in London, England. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press via Getty Images)
"Andrew isn't important anymore," said Fordwich. "No one is very concerned about how he's feeling. However, it's important to ensure he doesn't cause any more damage to the monarchy."
WATCH: FORMER PRINCE ANDREW REMAINS IN DENIAL OVER EPSTEIN SCANDAL: AUTHOR
A friend of the ex-royal's told The Sun that "Andrew feels he's been abandoned" and "he feels like he is no longer part of the family."

"He was invited but has got no great desire to be at Balmoral as he has nothing to gain and would be treated as an outcast," the unnamed friend told the outlet. "What's the point, he feels, of going all the way there for a much-needed holiday and being treated as an elephant in the room?"
The former Prince Andrew is seen attending the traditional Easter Sunday Mattins Service at St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle on April 20, 2025, in Windsor, England. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Andrew stepped away from royal duties in 2019 following a widely criticized BBC "Newsnight" interview in which he attempted to explain his friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
A photo of Prince Andrew and Ghislaine Maxwell found in the Justice Department's release of Epstein files. (Department of Justice)

In 2022, he was stripped of his military titles and patronages by his mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, as he faced Epstein survivor Virginia Giuffre's sexual assault lawsuit against him. Andrew and Giuffre settled out of court for an undisclosed sum that year.
Giuffre died in April 2025.

Virginia Roberts holds a photo of herself at age 16, when she says Palm Beach multimillionaire Jeffrey Epstein began abusing her sexually. (Emily Michot/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

In October 2025, King Charles III stripped his younger brother's royal titles as Andrew faced renewed scrutiny over his ties to Epstein. The scrutiny intensified following the publication of Giuffre's posthumous memoir and the release of documents detailing Andrew's relationship with Epstein.

Then-Prince Andrew, Duke of York attends Katharine, Duchess of Kent's Requiem Mass service at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025 in London, England. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Buckingham Palace also served Andrew formal notice to surrender the lease on his longtime residence, Royal Lodge. His ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, was expected to make separate living arrangements.

On Feb. 19, Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office over an allegation that he shared confidential information with Epstein during his time as a U.K. trade envoy. He was released after being held for 11 hours in police custody. The investigation remains ongoing.
This undated photo shows Prince Andrew and Jeffrey Epstein at Ascot in the U.K. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Andrew has repeatedly denied wrongdoing in connection with Epstein and the allegations against him.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and Lord Peter Mandelson are seen wearing bathrobes seated alongside late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in an undated photograph released by the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., U.S., as part of a trove of documents from its investigations into Epstein. (U.S. Justice Department/Handout)
"Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor obviously is feeling the contempt and distancing from other senior members of the royal family," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital.

"So his mental health will become more prevalent. Some of his favorite activities, like riding and shooting, may have been curtailed. The ongoing police investigation is a continuous worry for him. And still, his soulmate and former wife is being distant."

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, younger brother of Britain’s King Charles, formerly known as Prince Andrew, leaves Aylsham Police Station in a vehicle on the day he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after the U.S. Justice Department released more records tied to the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in Aylsham, Britain. The arrest took place on Feb. 19, 2026, Andrew's birthday. (Phil Noble/Reuters)
"Andrew is confined to a lonely existence," Turner continued. "Allegedly, he watches a TV channel which shows planes landing as one of his new methods of relaxation."

Balmoral Castle in Scotland. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Andrew's friend told The Sun that the disgraced ex-duke rejected the king's invitation to Balmoral Castle because he feared he would be treated as an "outcast."

Every summer, the royal family gathers at Balmoral to spend time together privately. About 30 family members are expected to join the king for the traditional gathering this year. The Sun reported that the king is not believed to have seen Andrew this year, despite at times staying only a mile away from him.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is seen returning after leaving police custody, following his arrest on Feb. 19, 2026 in Sandringham, Norfolk. (Peter Nicholls/Getty Images)

"Why would Andrew reject an olive branch from his brother?" said Turner. "There's a mixture of anger at what happened to him, a disdain for Charles, which he may see as a weak man, and, no doubt, arrogance with his belief that he can do what he wants without punitive measures taken against him. Also add to the tension with Prince William. Andrew is boxed in."

King Charles III carries out an inspection of the Balaklava Company, 5th Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland, at the gates of Balmoral, as he takes up summer residence at the castle on Aug. 18, 2026. (Jane Barlow/PA Images via Getty Images)
"There will never be any public restoration for Andrew at all, not now with King Charles and certainly not when Prince William ascends to the throne," said Fordwich.

"If Andrew did decline an invitation from the king, it might just be Andrew’s classic self-concern that he’d feel too awkward knowing he wasn’t wanted by the extended family at large. The only family member, I believe, who had visited Andrew was Prince Edward."
Prince Edward is reportedly the only royal who has visited Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. (REUTERS/Peter Nicholls/Pool)
The Sun reported that Andrew’s ex-wife and their two daughters have "avoided" his new home, Marsh Farm, where he’s "lonely."

Even as Andrew becomes increasingly isolated from royal life, one royal privilege reportedly remains intact.

The Daily Mail reported that Andrew remains on a confidential government list of royal family members with funeral plans prepared in advance. The arrangements are known as "bridge plans," with plans for senior royals named after bridges in the U.K.

Prince William and his wife Catherine have been "deeply concerned" by the latest revelations linking Andrew to late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, Kensington Palace said on Feb. 9, 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
When Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022, "Operation London Bridge" went into action. The plan for her husband, Prince Philip, was known as "Operation Forth Bridge" when he died in 2021.
Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022. She was 96. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

The plans are kept confidential until the royal dies, People magazine reported. According to the Daily Mail, Andrew's funeral service is expected to be held at St. George's Chapel before he is laid to rest at the Royal Burial Ground at Frogmore in Windsor.

Retired Rear Admiral Chris Parry, who captained HMS Fearless, told the Daily Mail that he believes the Royal Navy would provide volunteers to serve as pallbearers at Andrew's funeral. Andrew served in the Royal Navy from 1979 to 2001.
Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly feels isolated from his family. (Karwai Tang/WireImage/Getty Images)
"... He had a Falklands medal, and you can't take that away from him, and he deserves the credit for that," said Parry. "... If somebody said to me, 'Would you do it?' I'd do it."

Jubilant Prince Andrew ashore with proud father Prince Philip after the carrier HMS Invincible sailed home from the Falklands to a tumultuous welcome at Portsmouth on Sept. 17, 1982. (Kent Gavin/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)
Spencer Kuvin, an attorney who represented nine of Epstein's victims, told the outlet that "taxpayers should not ever be funding a funeral for a private individual."
King Charles III reportedly hasn't seen Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor this year. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
"No public money should be used to benefit him during death," he said. "It’s an embarrassment to the Crown."

title: Hayden Panettiere's 'Guiding Light' co-star Beth Chamberlin says she believed actress would overcome troubles
summary: Beth Chamberlin recalls her special bond with Hayden Panettiere on "Guiding Light" and why she believed the actress would overcome her troubled times.
story: Beth Chamberlin details 'strong bond' with Hayden Panettiere

Hayden Panettiere’s former "Guiding Light" co-star Beth Chamberlin believed the actress would overcome the "troubled times" she faced and emerge as an even stronger performer before her sudden death at 36.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Chamberlin — who starred as Panettiere’s on-screen mom on the 90s soap opera — opened up about her "special bond" with the late child star and the resilience she saw in her through difficult times.

"When I would hear about some of the troubled times that she was going through, I would think to myself, ‘She’s gonna get through this, and watch out world,’" Chamberlin told Fox News Digital. "Because when she gets through this, you are going to see some work on screen. You’re going to see things like you’ve never seen. I know Viola Davis made a comment that she is waiting to see what Hayden was going to fully become. And I think that puts it best because I think, that's how I was feeling too."
HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEAD AT 36
Beth Chamberlin, who starred as Hayden Panettiere's mom in "Guiding Light," opened up about her "special bond" with the late actress. (Getty Images; Everett Collection)
The "Heroes" and "Nashville" star was found dead inside a Greenville, South Carolina residence on Aug. 16.

Panettiere’s on-and-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother, Zach, called 911 after finding the actress unresponsive, according to a police report obtained by Fox News Digital. Hickerson later gave authorities a bag containing medication Panettiere had allegedly been taking.
POLICE SHOW UP AT HOME LINKED TO HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S ON-AND-OFF BOYFRIEND DAYS AFTER HER SUDDEN DEATH
Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, publicly raised questions about Brian’s role in her daughter’s life and death.

"Although my daughter and I were estranged, it was not for lack of care or love," she said in a statement to Entertainment Tonight. "It was due to the involvement of a toxic individual who I believe led to her death."

"Hayden was a beautiful and talented young woman who unfortunately became involved with the wrong person, and although her family tried to extricate him from her life, we were unable to be successful."⁠
Hayden Panettiere died on Aug. 16. She was 36.  (Getty Images)

Preliminary autopsy results found no signs of trauma that contributed to Panettiere’s death, the Greenville County Coroner's Office confirmed to Fox News Digital. However, Panettiere's death remains under investigation.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE REMEMBERED BY VIOLA DAVIS, BETHANY JOY LENZ AND OTHER CELEBRITIES AFTER SUDDEN DEATH AT 36
Fox News has learned the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has also been contacted and is assisting with the investigation.
For Chamberlin, processing Panettiere’s death has been particularly difficult because she remembers her as the extraordinarily talented young girl she worked alongside on "Guiding Light."

"She truly was just an amazing, amazing child actor," Chamberlin said. "You’ve never seen anything like it, actually."

"Acting requires a lot of work to create an emotional arc. Now in a soap opera, too, you have to remember everything's done in one take. It's a multi-camera shoot ... So you've got to get it right. And she was able to do that. With multiple pages, day after day."
DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH

Panettiere entered show business extraordinarily young, appearing in commercials as a baby before landing a role on "One Life to Live" at about 4 years old. Panettiere’s major breakthrough came as Claire Bennet, the seemingly indestructible cheerleader at the center of NBC’s superhero drama "Heroes," which ran from 2006 to 2010. She followed that success with another defining television role, country singer Juliette Barnes on "Nashville" from 2012 to 2018. (Getty Images)
Chamberlin says that while she has often discouraged children pursuing a career in acting, she strongly believed Panettiere was a special exception.

"I know there's so many people that will say, 'Oh, you shouldn't put children in the business' And I get that. And anybody that knows me, knows that when people in my life that have asked me, how about putting my kid in the businesses? I always say, 'Don't do it.' I didn't put my own kid in a business. But I've always maintained that Hayden was the exception to that. Because Hayden looked like she was in her element when she was there."

title: Jill Wagner pitched Taylor Sheridan 'Lioness' after military husband revealed real-life program: What to know
summary: Jill Wagner pitched Taylor Sheridan the idea for "Lioness" after her husband David Lemanowicz, a U.S. Army major, introduced her to the program.
story: Laysla De Oliveira and Jill Wagner told Fox News Digital how the third season of Taylor Sheridan's hit series will be different from the rest.
Jill Wagner has been in the industry for decades and stars in Taylor Sheridan's hit show, "Lioness."
Even though she moved to California early in her career to pursue acting, she has returned to her country roots and lives on her Tennessee farm with her husband and two daughters.

With season three of "Lioness" premiering earlier this month, Fox News Digital is taking a look at everything to know about Wagner's personal life, her military connection, how her husband inspired her role in the series and more.
Jill Wagner pitched Taylor Sheridan's "Lioness" series. (John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images)
Wagner portrays Bobby, the tough, highly skilled leader of the Lioness program's Quick Reaction Force (QRF).
WHAT TAYLOR SHERIDAN'S BIGGEST STARS REALLY THINK ABOUT WORKING WITH THE 'YELLOWSTONE' CREATOR

Wagner not only stars in Sheridan's hit series, she was the one who pitched him the idea. She told Parade in 2024 that Sheridan crafted the role as Bobby specifically for Wagner, and she serves as an executive producer on the show.
Jill Wagner stars as Bobby on "Lioness." (Lauren "Lo" Smith/Paramount+)

"Taylor Sheridan was my old acting coach, and I had access to him," she began. "Taylor writes in such an honest and raw way. I didn’t want this show to become Barbies with guns. I wanted it to represent the women I knew and respected in the military, and he’s done that brilliantly."
Wagner went on to explain that in order for her to really bring Bobby to life, she had to sit down and speak with her lionessess.

"At first, I didn’t understand who Bobby was. I still find things about her even right before we do a take. I have met and talked to several real-life lionesses while researching the show," she said. "I took all those personalities and mashed them all together; thus, we have ‘Bobby.'"
Wagner and David Lemanowicz's love story
Wagner and Lemanowicz first met when they were teenagers, but reconnected in Afghanistan while Lemanowicz was serving in the Air Force and Wagner was meeting troops during a USO tour.
David Lemanowicz and Jill Wagner tied the knot in 2017. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)
"I hadn’t seen her in 17 years," Lemanowicz recalled during a 2016 Hallmark Home & Family episode.

"My boss told me to check out the event, and I look at the photo and said, ‘I think I know this girl.’ Lo and behold, I go to the chow event where she’s signing autographs, and I ask her if she’s from North Carolina. She says ‘yes.’ I say, ‘Little town outside of Greensboro?’ She says, ‘yes.’ I say, ‘Did you ever go to any North Carolina Monarchs hockey games?’ She says, ‘yes.’ I say, ‘Do you remember dating the goalie?'" he called.
ZOE SALDAÑA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'REALLY SEES WOMEN' AS LIONESS SEASON THREE HITS PARAMOUNT+
At the time, Wagner and Lemanowicz were both in relationships and didn't take their connection further. They met again, a year later, in Los Angeles and were both single.
Jill Wagner lives in Tennessee with her family. (Getty Images)

"The day I came back from filming ‘Christmas Cookies,’ my girlfriends wanted to take me out to dinner," Wagner said in the same episode. "We were leaving (in Los Angeles)... and then I hear, ‘Jill!’ and David had just walked in the restaurant I was walking out of, and boom!"
They tied the knot the following year in 2017.
Wagner’s husband has a military background

Wagner's husband is a former professional hockey player who later pursued a military career. According to People, he joined the military after his hockey career ended in 2008 and became a lieutenant in the U.S. Army Reserve.
The outlet noted he was promoted to U.S. Army major in 2020.
Jill Wagner and David Lemanowicz in 2018. (Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
During Wagner's Parade interview, she explained that Lemanowicz was the one who introduced her to the lioness program.

"My husband, David [Lemanowicz], was the one who told me about the Lioness program. From that moment on, I knew there was a story to tell. It took about five years, but I never gave up," she told the outlet in 2024.
Wagner comes from a military family
Wagner previously told Parade that she was raised in a military family.

"My grandfather, my uncle and my father were all Marines," she began. "My husband currently serves in the Army. I come from a very patriotic family, and I’ve always greatly respected the men and women who serve our country."
Jill Wagner as Bobby in "Lioness" season 3. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
She told the outlet that, given her background, she was intrigued to star in a show that portrayed women in the military in lead roles.

"I have not seen women in the military portrayed in lead roles like this. It is important to give these women the moment they deserve on screen while not taking any away from the men who also serve. They both deserve our respect for the sacrifices they make," Wagner said.
Wagner's "Lioness" character always has a toothpick in her mouth – which she told the outlet was homage to her father.
Wagner, Lemanowicz and their two daughters live on a Tennessee farm
Wagner left Los Angeles in 2016 after finding a farmhouse in Tennessee that she previously told People "looked like a scary haunted house" at first.

When they purchased the home, Lemanowicz and Wagner were engaged and were planning on having a family.
Jill Wagner and David Lemanowicz kissing at the "Lioness" season 2 premiere. (Variety via Getty Images)
"We wanted a family, and I saw my children running around in the front yard. I knew it could be fixed. And I wanted to be the one to restore this piece of history," she said.
'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER CHOSE TENNESSEE FARM LIFE TO RAISE HER FAMILY
Lemanowicz and Wagner share two daughters: Army Gray Lemanowicz, 6, and Daisy Roberta Lemanowicz, 5.
During an interview with Fox News Digital, Wagner explained that her decision to put roots down in Tennessee was an easy choice given her background.
Jill Wagner's husband introduced her to the real Lioness program that inspired the hit show. (Lauren Smith/Paramount+)
"We looked in and around North Carolina – couldn't find anything," she said, adding that she's from North Carolina.

"So, Tennessee – found a piece of property in Tennessee. I wanted to get married, and I wanted to have my babies in a place that I thought was magical and, since I was born and raised in the country, that was my idea of what was magical. So, we live there," Wagner said.

Wagner explained what a typical day looks like on her Tennessee farm.

"My typical day on the farm is I'm out on my front porch in the morning at 6:30, and then I go to my flowers, and then I listen to my husband complain about the tractor being broken and the fence falling down, and the barn roof flew off last night, and then we just repair everything that's been broken," she said.
"That is my typical day," Wagner added with a laugh.

title: Tom Hanks put 'Band of Brothers' stars in their place during boot camp 'mutiny,' Neal McDonough reveals
summary: Neal McDonough reveals how Tom Hanks arrived by helicopter to deliver a powerful speech that ended a cast mutiny during "Band of Brothers" boot camp.
story: "Band of Brothers" star Neal McDonough recalled how Tom Hanks unexpectedly arrived at boot camp and reminded the actors what they owed the real-life heroes of Easy Company.
"Band of Brothers" star Neal McDonough recalled how Tom Hanks put the show's cast in their place during the grueling boot camp that they underwent prior to filming.
McDonough, 60, co-starred in the hit 2001 HBO war drama miniseries, which was executive produced by Hanks, 70, and Steven Spielberg, 79.

"Band of Brothers" told the story of the real-life soldiers of Easy Company, part of the U.S. Army’s 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division, as they fought their way across Europe during World War II.
NEAL MCDONOUGH SAYS HOLLYWOOD LABELED HIM A ‘RELIGIOUS NUT,’ COST HIM HIS CAREER AND HOME

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, McDonough recalled how the actors rebelled during the production's intense boot camp before Hanks arrived by helicopter and delivered a powerful message that they "never forgot."
"About five days into boot camp, there was a mutiny," McDonough said on the red carpet at Televerse 26 in Los Angeles.
"Band of Brothers" star Neal McDonough recalled how Tom Hanks shut down a "mutiny" on the hit WWII drama's set. (Kate Green/Getty Images for The Walt Disney Company Limited; HBO via Getty Images)
"All of a sudden, my teeth are knocked out by a .30 cal and I broke my toe, and a slew of other guys was getting tortured," he continued.
"The American guys really loved it," he added with a laugh. "But, there was this mutiny going on. They were like, 'This isn't what we signed up for.'"
TOM HANKS JOKINGLY SWIPES MS NOW'S VIEWERSHIP WHILE APPEARING LIVE ON-AIR WITH REPORTER

"All of a sudden, this helicopter shows up in the middle of our Army base and out walks Tom Hanks with his beard down here and his ‘Cast Away’ hair," McDonough recalled, referencing Hanks' starring role in the survival drama "Cast Away."
WATCH: Tom Hanks arrived by helicopter to confront ‘Band of Brothers’ boot camp ‘mutiny,’ co-star says

"And he got us all attention, and he says, ‘Look, we all owe it to everyone in Easy Company, and everyone in World War II, to work our hardest because they gave their lives for our freedoms. The least we can do is work our tails off to tell the truth as hard as we can so we give honor to those men and women,'" McDonough remembered of Hanks.
McDonough told Fox News Digital that the two-time Oscar winner's words completely shifted the cast's mindset toward portraying "Band of Brothers'" real-life heroes.
"Telling you after that, we were all brainwashed," he said before clarifying, "I'm not sure brainwashed is the right word."
McDonough recalled how a powerful speech from Hanks completely changed the cast's outlook during their intense boot camp. (Getty Images)
STEVEN SPIELBERG ADMITS HE'S BEEN CONVERTED ON UFOS, SAYS HE BELIEVES THE BELIEVERS

"Where we all realized Tom was right," McDonough continued. "They lived, breathed, and died for what we have this day, freedom. None of us forgot about that, and as soon as the show came out, we realized Tom was right the whole time."

"He knew it was going to be a massive hit. Stephen knew it would be a big hit. We were just lughead actors who were doing our jobs. And then when it came out, and it was the hit that it became, and it is still 25 years later, it just boggles my mind how fortunate every single one of us were to be cast in the show."
ADRENALINE-PACKED PREVIEW RELEASED FOR UPCOMING D-DAY FILM 'PRESSURE,' FEATURES LOADED CAST

McDonough played 1st Lt. Lynn "Buck" Compton, a real-life platoon leader in Easy Company. Compton fought in major WWII campaigns, including D-Day and Operation Market Garden and was wounded during fighting in the Netherlands.
"Band of Brothers" told the story of the real-life war heroes of Easy Company.  (Getty Images)

"Band of Brothers" also starred Damian Lewis, Ron Livingston, Donnie Wahlberg, David Schwimmer, Michael Cudlitz and Scott Grimes, while future stars including Tom Hardy, Michael Fassbender and James McAvoy appeared in smaller roles.

The 10-part miniseries was based on historian Stephen E. Ambrose’s 1992 nonfiction book, "Band of Brothers" and was created by Hanks and Spielberg, who had previously collaborated on the acclaimed 1998 World War II film "Saving Private Ryan." Writer Erik Jendresen also helped lead the series adaptation.
Hanks also directed episode five, titled "Crossroads," and had a brief, uncredited cameo.
MATT DAMON WAS 'PUSHED TO THE LIMIT' WHILE FILMING 'THE ODYSSEY,' DETAILS GRUELING PHYSICAL DISCOMFORTS
"Band of Brothers," which premiered in September 2001, earned widespread critical acclaim and received multiple awards, including seven Emmys and a Golden Globe.

The series was extensively praised for its gritty realism and attention to historical detail. The boot camp that the actors underwent was specifically intended to help them move, behave and bond more convincingly as soldiers.
WATCH: Neal McDonough went to hospital as his ‘Band of Brothers’ character after brutal boot camp injury

While speaking with Fox News Digital, McDonough recalled how the "brutal" boot camp was led by Dale Dye, retired U.S. Marine Corps captain, Vietnam War veteran, actor and longtime Hollywood military technical advisor.
McDonough explained that the boot camp was more challenging for some actors than others.
"I'm a knucklehead. I love that kind of stuff. Those two weeks felt like three months for a lot of guys," he said. "And it was tough."
McDonough told Fox News Digital that Dale intentionally "allowed himself to be the common enemy" to the actors during the series' production.

"We all hated his guts, because he pushed us all to the brink," he recalled of Dye. "And it wasn't until about a quarter of the way through filming that we realized he was putting on an act so we could all gel together as a unit."

"There are a few men on this planet that I love like I love Dale Dye because he allowed himself to be that guy and 'Band of Brothers' would not be ‘Band of Brothers’ were not for him,'" McDonough added.
"Band of Brothers" military advisor and actor Dale Dye is pictured at the show's premiere in 2001. (WireImage)

In additional to serving as the senior military advisor for "Band of Brothers," Dye also played Col. Robert F. Sink, the real-life commander of the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, in the series. Dye is one of Hollywood’s leading military advisors and has previously worked on movies, including "Platoon" and "Saving Private Ryan," and TV shows, including "The Pacific" and "Masters of the Air."

Despite the cast's eventual gratitude for Dye's dedication and methods, the physically demanding boot camp took a toll on the actors. McDonough recalled that Dye even considered suspending the training after several actors suffered injuries. The "Minority Report" star remembered that he was hit in the mouth with a ".30 cal" shortly after.

"I heard him say, ‘If one more guy gets hurt, then I might shut this whole thing down.’ That afternoon, I got hit," McDonough said. "We're enveloping this one house. Guy comes out with a .30 cal, boom, smashes my teeth, blood all the way down here."
McDonough remembered that his co-star Shane Taylor, who played medic Eugene "Doc" Roe, became incredulous when he asked him for medical treatment after the injury.
"I said, ‘Doc, get over here, stitch me up,'" McDonough said.
McDonough recalled how he suffered a serious injury to his mouth during boot camp. (Getty Images)
McDonough recalled Taylor replying, "'I'm not a doctor, I'm an actor,'" to which he said he responded, "'I don't care, just stitch me up.'"

"So he stitches me up in front of everybody, and then two or three days later, it's so infected, that Dale's like, ‘You need to go to the hospital.’ And I knew he was sweating," McDonough said. "But at the time, I was just gung ho, because of what Tom said."
McDonough recalled that he went to the hospital, where he provided his character's name and information instead of his own.
"I knew it was socialized medicine, I knew. But I needed to have ‘Lynn Compton’ on that report, not ‘Neal McDonough,’" he said.
McDonough told Fox News Digital that the doctor who treated him was horrified when he saw his infected mouth.
"The doctor's like, 'Oh gosh, that's awful, this is terrible,'" he recalled. "So they shaved it all off, they cleaned it up, stitched me up."
WATCH: ‘Band of Brothers’ stars ‘hated’ boot camp leader before discovering it was all an act, Neal McDonough says

The "Yellowstone" alum told Fox News Digital that he visited Dye afterward. He remembered Dye becoming emotional when presented with McDonough's hospital paperwork, realizing how deeply the actor had committed to his portrayal of Compton.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I get back to the barracks at 4 o'clock in the morning, I knock on his door, he's sitting there waiting. I put it down there [and said] ‘Sir.’ And he looks at it, and he looked at me and tears welled up in Dale's eyes," McDonough said.

"And I knew that I did a right thing for Easy Company and the whole movie, and after that, we became like that," he continued. "But that was probably the most difficult moment of the boot camp for me."
"Band of Brothers" was executive produced by Tom Hanks and Steven Spielberg. (FilmMagic, Inc)

McDonough met the real Compton prior to filming the show and the two developed a friendship that lasted until the former soldier's death in 2012. He previously described Compton as "another father figure" in his life, and said he nicknamed his son Morgan "Little Buck" in Compton’s honor. McDonough also attended Compton’s 90th birthday celebration and later gave a eulogy at his funeral.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

While speaking with Fox News Digital, McDonough explained that "Band of Brothers" also had a special place in his heart because he met his longtime wife Ruvé Robertson while filming the show in the United Kingdom.
McDonough met his longtime wife Ruvé Robertson while filming the show in the United Kingdom. (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
McDonough and the South African model married in 2003 and share five children, Morgan, Catherine, London, Clover and James.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The greatest thing about ‘Band of Brothers’ other than getting to play Buck Compton and work for Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks, is I got to meet the love of my life, Ruvé, the very first night I got into town on St. Patrick's Day, 2000," he said. "Five kids later, 26 seasons later, I love her more today than I did yesterday and I love her tomorrow more than I did today."

The couple kept a locked room in their home where they created content. She said their kids believed it was simply an office for her corporate work.
