title: Deadly measles outbreak hits Northeast as state records first deaths in 35 years
summary: Two unvaccinated Lancaster County residents died from measles, marking Pennsylvania's first measles deaths in 35 years amid 393 confirmed cases.
story: Senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the critical link between low MMR vaccination rates and surging measles cases in states like Utah and South Carolina. He emphasizes the vaccine's safety and role as the only tool to prevent the highly contagious disease.
Pennsylvania confirmed two measles-related deaths on Tuesday, according to the state’s department of health.
This marks the first losses related to the highly contagious virus within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in 35 years.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed that both Lancaster County individuals were unvaccinated, noting that the best way to prevent measles infection is to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL
The MMR vaccine administered over two doses can boost a person’s immune system and provide 97% lifetime protection, according to health officials.
Two deaths have been confirmed in Pennsylvania related to measles. (iStock)
In a press release, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen shared her "deepest sympathies" with the "loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss."

"Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness," she said in the statement. "We want to ensure that every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles."
The state's DOH has confirmed 393 cases of measles in 28 counties so far in 2026.
The Pennsylvania DOH has confirmed 393 cases of measles in 28 counties so far in 2026. (iStock)
Measles is a highly contagious virus that can be fatal in one to three patients per 1,000 cases, data shows.
The virus can cause long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Nearly 20% of individuals who contract measles are hospitalized.

Measles spreads when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, spreading the virus through respiratory droplets. It can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the person leaves the area, experts caution.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Early measles symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A measles rash follows a few days later, starting on the head and spreading down to the rest of the body.
Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. Those who believe they were exposed to measles should contact a healthcare provider.
Early measles symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A measles rash follows a few days later, starting on the head and spreading down to the rest of the body. (iStock)
Dr. Jesse Goodman, former FDA chief scientist in Washington, D.C., spoke with Fox News Digital about the MMR vaccine, calling it "extremely safe and highly effective."

"The vaccine prevents millions of measles deaths worldwide annually, including hundreds that used to occur in the U.S.," he said. "There is no evidence that MMR vaccine causes any chronic illnesses, including autism."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Dr. Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, Maryland, agreed that Pennsylvania's 35-year streak without a measles-related death "wasn't luck."

"It was the vaccine working so completely that an entire generation of parents grew up never seeing what this virus does to a child’s lungs or brain," he told Fox News Digital. "That protection is increasingly not valued, and this is the predictable result when the population turns their back on a life-saving technology."

"The vaccine prevents millions of measles deaths worldwide annually, including hundreds that used to occur in the U.S.," a doctor told Fox News Digital. "There is no evidence that MMR vaccine causes any chronic illnesses, including autism." (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, previously emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles amid elevated case counts across the U.S.

"Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, stressing the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel.

"In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn’t about personal choice, it’s about community protection. We need to protect those who can’t have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Major brain changes that occur around age 50 could impact dementia risk
summary: Microglia decline after age 50 as inflammatory blood-derived immune cells infiltrate the hippocampus, potentially driving neuroinflammation and dementia.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen — psychiatrist, brain imaging specialist and founder of Amen Clinics in California — says this quick, 15-second method can help calm the body and mind.
The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50.

Researchers from the University of California, San Diego; New York Genome Center; and University of California, Irvine, found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia.

The study analyzed postmortem tissue from the hippocampus – the portion of the brain that is responsible for learning and memory – in 40 neurologically healthy adults, ranging from 20 to 95 years of age.
THE 'AGE' OF YOUR BLOOD COULD PREDICT DEMENTIA RISK, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

"The most striking change was that after about age 50, the brain’s resident immune cells, called microglia, appear to be increasingly replaced by immune cells that enter from the bloodstream," first author Nathan Zemke, Ph.D., principal investigator at the UC San Diego Center for Epigenomics, told Fox News Digital.
"Microglia normally protect the brain by clearing debris and responding to injury, but the incoming cells carry stronger inflammatory signals."

The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50. (iStock)
The researchers believe this shift may contribute to chronic inflammation linked to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s.

They also noted the deterioration of cells involved in maintaining the blood-brain barrier – the protective filter that helps keep harmful substances out of the brain – as well as widespread changes in DNA and gene activity.
'LONGEVITY GENE' MAY PROTECT THE BRAIN FROM ALZHEIMER'S BY BOOSTING DNA REPAIR, STUDY FINDS

One of the most exciting implications of the study, according to Zemke, is that the replacement immune cells originate in the blood, which means they are more accessible than cells already deep inside the brain.

"It may eventually be possible to modify blood-derived immune cells so that they are more protective and less inflammatory when in the brain," he said. "That could provide an entirely new way to approach Alzheimer’s and other neurological diseases without having to directly manipulate cells within the central nervous system."
Researchers found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia. (iStock)

Although these findings are still in early stages, Zemke said, gaining a better understanding of why this immune-cell replacement happens – and why it happens earlier in some people than others – could lead to new strategies for preserving brain health during aging.
The study’s chief limitation is that it studied human brain tissue collected postmortem from different individuals across the adult lifespan, the researchers noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"That allows us to identify strong age-related patterns, but it cannot directly show how the same person’s brain changes over decades or prove that a particular cellular change causes cognitive decline or Alzheimer’s disease," Zemke said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"We also do not yet know what triggers the influx of blood-derived immune cells into the brain. Determining whether changes in the blood-brain barrier, inflammation, genetics, lifestyle or other factors initiate this process will be an important next step."
The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone. (iStock)
The researcher emphasized, however, that he would not recommend that people make any specific medical or lifestyle changes based on this study alone.
"These findings are primarily about understanding the biology of brain aging and identifying new directions for prevention and treatment," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone.
"The next challenge is to understand what drives that variation and whether some of those factors can be modified," Zemke added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study also included a small sample of just 40 people and examined tissue only from the hippocampus, meaning the findings may not reflect immune changes throughout the entire brain.
The study, which was funded by the National Institutes of Health, was published in the journal Science.

title: Anti-aging supplements taken by millions may undermine cancer treatment, study warns
summary: Popular NAD+-boosting supplements like NMN and nicotinamide riboside may shield pancreatic cancer cells from chemotherapy, a new study warns.
story: Family medicine physician Dr. Jessica Gray details a new experimental pancreatic cancer vaccine showing promise in its first human trial. The vaccine, targeting the KRAS mutation, generated an immune response in 90% of high-risk patients. Dr. Gray discusses the 5-7 year timeline for public availability and emphasizes why pancreatic cancer is so deadly, highlighting advances in cancer treatments.
Over-the-counter anti-aging supplements taken by millions of Americans to boost energy and lessen the side effects of chemotherapy may actually impair cancer treatments, a new study suggests.

Researchers at the Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine found that popular vitamin B3 derivatives – including nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide (NAM) – could help cancer cells survive chemotherapy.
Those compounds are used by the body to produce NAD+, a molecule that helps cells generate energy and repair damage.
IV THERAPY AND SUPPLEMENTS UNDER SCRUTINY AS EXPERTS WARN OF POTENTIAL SIDE EFFECTS

The study, published in the journal Cancer Letters, examined how these supplements interact with treatments for pancreatic cancer, a particularly deadly form of the disease with a 13% five-year survival rate, according to the American Cancer Society.
Over-the-counter vitamin B3 derivatives, specifically NMN, NR and NAM, could help pancreatic cancer cells survive chemotherapy treatment, the study suggests. (iStock)

While boosting NAD+ levels through dietary supplements can offer health benefits to non-cancerous cells, pancreatic cancer cells may exploit the extra resources to repair damage caused by chemotherapy and avoid cell death, the researchers found.

In both laboratory settings and animal models, the supplements shielded cancer cells against three common chemotherapy drugs: oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. As a result, tumors survived chemotherapy doses that typically would prove fatal to them.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Our findings highlight a potentially concerning role for NAD+-boosting supplements in the context of active cancer, especially when used in conjunction with chemotherapy," said study lead Jordan Winter, a professor at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine and co-leader of the developmental therapeutics program at the Case Comprehensive Cancer Center, in the press release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Our discovery is a call to action for the medical community."

The study notes that these B3 derivatives are not considered dangerous for healthy individuals using them for general wellness. However, the risk becomes significant for patients currently undergoing active cancer therapy.
Boosting NAD+ levels provides extra energy to cancer cells, allowing them to repair DNA damage caused by chemotherapy. (iStock)
"This research is a critical reminder that ‘natural’ doesn’t always mean safe, especially in the complex biology of cancer treatment," Winter added.

In light of the findings, the research team recommends that oncology teams begin routinely screening patients for supplement use. They also called for more studies into how NAD+ precursors interact with cancer therapies.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Winter urged patients currently in treatment to consult their oncologists before taking any over-the-counter supplements.
Because the study relied on laboratory cell cultures and animal models, the findings may not directly translate to how human patients process these supplements during treatment, the team noted.

The findings indicate these supplements are not inherently dangerous for healthy individuals using them for general anti-aging or wellness, but pose serious risks when taken during active chemotherapy. (iStock)
Additionally, the research focused exclusively on pancreatic cancer, meaning the supplements may not have the same effect on chemotherapy for other cancer types or with different drug combinations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The study also only evaluated short-term cellular responses under controlled laboratory conditions and not human clinical trials, so it remains unclear how these supplements could affect cancer patients over time.
Fox News Digital reached out to multiple NAD+ supplement manufacturers for comment.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: 'Perfect' workout formula can take just 10 minutes a day, Hilaria Baldwin says
summary: Hilaria Baldwin shares her "perfect" workout trifecta of cardio, strength training and stretching, plus tips for building exercise consistency.
story: The yoga instructor reveals how she incorporates running, stretching and toning into her routine, while involving her children and modeling the importance of caring for physical health.
Being motivated to work out is one thing, but staying committed to a routine is what yields results, experts say.
In an interview with Fox News Digital, certified yoga and fitness instructor Hilaria Baldwin shared her tips for building an effective exercise routine – and sticking to it.

"One of the most important things about exercise is consistency," said the mother of seven. "For many of us, life gets in the way – we are parents, and we work and all the chaos comes in, so bite-sized movements are really important."
CHIEFS HEIRESS GRACIE HUNT REVEALS WHY SHE LIFTS HEAVY WEIGHTS — AND DOESN’T COUNT CALORIES
Baldwin revealed that her "perfect" workout routine trifecta always includes cardio, strength training and stretching, even if it’s just 10 minutes per day.

For lasting consistency, a fitness routine should fit naturally into one’s lifestyle and schedule, Baldwin said. She recommends setting aside kid-free, work-free blocks of time for movement and self-care.
Hilaria Baldwin joined Fox News Digital for an interview about her "perfect" daily workout routine. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)

Baldwin said she makes time for a daily run as her cardio, which she said helps "work out her lungs." She also incorporates stretching and strength training, which might include physically picking up her kids or toning with weights.
She has also started exercising with her children as a way to blend family time with physical activity.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
The instructor emphasized consistency without overcommitment, noting that doing too much, too soon can lead to burnout.

"If something's overwhelming, we're not going to do it," Baldwin said. "Ultimately, we are going to be creatures of habit … we are going do what we feel like needs to get done – but starting to think of a workout more like brushing our teeth is really important."
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a deep lunge position during a yoga practice. She says yoga is "amazing" for staying flexible with age. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)

"People are not moving their bodies enough, and then we get sick," she went on. "So, the question is, can we do a little bit to prevent that? And obviously not everything can be prevented, but we know that we should move our bodies most days."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Baldwin advised against "biting off more than you can chew." For example, instead of running three miles as a response to being frustrated about your fitness goals, try running for just 10 minutes – or run for just two minutes at a time and take walking breaks.
"Doing something is better than thinking about it and doing nothing," she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The fitness instructor also suggested making exercise a family commitment, helping to reinforce that movement and self-care are priorities.
"As moms, we [often] put ourselves last," she said. "Everybody says put your oxygen mask on first, but we don't do that."
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a side stretch during a yoga sequence. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"I think showing our children that we are human, and we are worth taking care of is really important – not just for our relationship with them, but how they will treat themselves when they're older."
When life gets busy, she said, it’s easy to make excuses for not working out. Baldwin admitted that on most days, especially in the summer heat, she has "zero interest" in going for a run.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"But I know that I'm not going to regret it," she said. "It’s just about creating the habit and saying, ‘Okay, I'm going to do this, and it's going to be 30 minutes, and I might hate it, but I’m going to be happy to do it.’"
Baldwin added, "Showing up is the hardest thing. Once you do it, and you create a commitment, it completely changes everything."
"Showing up is the hardest thing. Once you do it, and you create a commitment, it completely changes everything," said Hilaria Baldwin. (iStock)
'Love yourself'
Baldwin encouraged the public, especially women, to tap into how "special and unique each person’s body is."
"Start loving yourself and loving your body, no matter what outside opinions you feel like people are directing at you," she said. "Feel capable and feel strong and that you're worth investing in."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Baldwin shared that she herself has struggled "tremendously" with this in her own life. "That is one of the reasons that I show up – to tell my body, ‘I love you, you're worth it.’"

She continued, "Nobody has ever existed who is exactly like you, and no one will ever be exactly like you again. So please live every single day cherishing your body, your unique self, and let's have fun and move together."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Louisiana girl, 8, dies after contracting suspected brain-eating amoeba linked to lake swim
summary: Lillian Smart's family says the 8-year-old's brain injuries were too severe to survive after contracting Naegleria fowleri while swimming in a lake.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel warns beachgoers about the rise of Vibrio vulnificus, a deadly flesh-eating bacteria found in warm salt waters. Already nine cases reported in Florida and five deaths in Louisiana.

Lillian Smart, an 8-year-old girl who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba while swimming in a northern Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen.
Lillian died one day after celebrating her eighth birthday.

"The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from," the Smart family said in a statement posted Sunday morning on Facebook. "Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?"
MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000

The Louisiana Department of Health announced Wednesday that a state resident had been hospitalized after becoming infected with Naegleria fowleri, a microscopic amoeba that can cause a rare and often deadly brain infection.
Lillian Smart, center, is pictured with her parents. The 8-year-old died Saturday after her family said she contracted Naegleria fowleri. (Facebook/Love for Lillian Smart)

State health officials have not publicly identified Lillian as the patient referenced in the announcement. Her family, however, said on social media that she had been admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit at a Ruston hospital and identified Naegleria fowleri as the cause of her illness.
The health department said the infection in the case it announced was most likely acquired while the patient was swimming in Lake Claiborne shortly before becoming ill.
BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE
A representative for the Louisiana Department of Health did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Louisiana Department of Health records identify three previous deaths associated with Naegleria fowleri in the state since 2011.
Lillian Smart, 8, died Saturday after her family said she contracted Naegleria fowleri, a rare amoeba that can cause a deadly brain infection. (Facebook/Love for Lillian Smart)

Two happened in 2011. A 20-year-old man in St. Bernard Parish died after using tap water to rinse his sinuses, while a 51-year-old woman in DeSoto Parish died after using tap water for a similar purpose.

In 2013, a 4-year-old boy contracted the amoeba while visiting a home in St. Bernard Parish, where he had played on a slip-and-slide. State officials later reported that CDC testing detected Naegleria fowleri in the parish water system.
DEADLY BACTERIA FOUND IN WATERS NEAR LUXURY VACATION DESTINATION AHEAD OF SUMMER

Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, or PAM, an extremely rare brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain. People cannot become infected by swallowing contaminated water.
The amoeba is not found in saltwater or properly chlorinated swimming pools.
A birthday memory jar invited loved ones to share favorite memories and messages for Lillian Smart ahead of her eighth birthday. (Facebook/Love for Lillian Smart)

Symptoms typically begin with headache, fever, nausea and vomiting before progressing to a stiff neck, seizures and coma. Symptoms generally appear about five days after infection, and the disease can lead to death within about one to two weeks.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
About 97% of people who develop PAM die from the infection, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CDC reported two PAM cases nationwide last year. Of the 173 infections documented over roughly the past 90 years, nearly 91% occurred in July and August.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Popular erectile dysfunction drug linked to eye disease that can cause irreversible vision loss
summary: Tadalafil users were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma, a study found, raising new questions about long-term Cialis use and eye pressure risks.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen discusses emerging research showing saffron may be as effective as SSRIs in treating depression, and could also improve sexual function.
A drug used to treat erectile dysfunction and enlarged prostate symptoms may raise the risk of glaucoma, a serious eye condition that can cause gradual vision loss, according to new research.

An international team of researchers analyzed health records from nearly 74,000 men ages 40 and older with lower urinary tract symptoms to examine whether long-term tadalafil use was associated with a greater risk of glaucoma.

The study, published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, compared about 37,000 men prescribed tadalafil with a similar group who did not use phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, the drug class that includes Cialis.
Researchers followed the men for up to five years and looked for new cases of glaucoma and high pressure inside the eye, along with whether patients needed treatment for glaucoma.
VISION PROBLEM LEADS TO MAN'S STAGE 4 LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, NEW DRUG EXTENDS SURVIVAL
New research suggests tadalafil, the drug sold as Cialis for erectile dysfunction and enlarged prostate symptoms, may be linked to a higher risk of glaucoma. (iStock)
Men who used tadalafil were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma than those who did not use the drugs, according to the findings.
They were also 32% more likely to develop high pressure inside the eye and 33% more likely to develop primary open-angle glaucoma, the most common type of the disease.
Dr. Valerie Kattouf, an optometrist at the Illinois Eye Institute who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that glaucoma can be difficult to notice in its early stages.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Glaucoma is an eye condition that especially in its early stages often does not present with visual symptoms," Kattouf said.
As glaucoma progresses, people may gradually lose their side, or peripheral, vision, she said.
The study found that men who used tadalafil were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma than men who did not take the drug. (iStock)
"Clinical findings of glaucoma are best detected in a comprehensive vision evaluation," Kattouf added.

Kattouf said people with a family history of glaucoma, high pressure inside the eye or severe nearsightedness may face a higher risk. Those who take Cialis daily over a long period of time may also warrant closer monitoring, she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

People who regularly use the medication should have a comprehensive eye exam to establish a baseline for their eye health, according to Kattouf. Doctors can check pressure inside the eyes and perform other tests to look for changes that could signal glaucoma.
The researchers noted several limitations to the study.
People who take the medication regularly should get a thorough eye exam to establish a baseline for their eye health. (iStock)
The study was observational, meaning it found a link between tadalafil use and glaucoma but could not prove that the medication caused the condition.
Researchers also could not account for changes in medication use or other health conditions that developed over time.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The researchers stressed that the findings do not mean people should stop taking tadalafil. Instead, they said, patients who use the medication long term, particularly those with existing glaucoma risk factors, may benefit from regular eye monitoring.
Fox News Digital reached out to Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of Cialis, and the study’s researchers for comment.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Men face new pressure to stay ‘hot’ as they age — and it’s not just about living longer
summary: Plastic surgeon Dr. Krishna Vyas reveals why men no longer feel stigma around cosmetic procedures and shares the foundational steps for extending "hotspan."
story: The stigma around men seeking esthetic treatments is fading. For many, the goal isn’t to look younger, it’s to make their appearance feel more aligned with how youthful, confident and socially engaged they feel.
Maintaining healthy cholesterol and blood pressure, along with regular physical activity, are widely recommended components of healthy aging.

But as interest in longevity grows, some older adults are looking beyond extending their healthspan — the number of years lived free of disease — to prioritize looking, feeling and remaining physically attractive as they age.
Experts say the desire to maintain one’s appearance — the pursuit of "hotness" — can be psychological, shaped in part by a disconnect between how people feel and the changes they see in the mirror.
COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY
"It really isn't about age," Dr. Krishna Vyas, M.D., Ph.D., a plastic surgeon at Blechman Plastic Surgery on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan, told Fox News Digital.

"I think it's when you look in the mirror and you're like, 'I don't recognize myself. I don't recognize the way I feel. I don't identify with how my appearance isn't concordant with how I feel at that point.'"
The push for aesthetic interventions is often driven by psychological friction when a person's mental self-image no longer matches their physical appearance, experts say. (iStock)
Men now account for roughly 15% of all cosmetic procedures, according to data from the American Society of Plastic Surgeons.
Social barriers that may have previously prevented men from seeking aesthetic treatment have diminished in the last two decades, Vyas noted.

"In the past, there was a stigma ... men were once shamed or ashamed of seeking out things that improve their appearance, especially in aesthetics, but that barrier has fallen significantly," he said.
DO RED LIGHT THERAPY AND COLD PLUNGES REALLY WORK? A DOCTOR REVEALS THE TRUTH

The motivations driving men to pursue "looksmaxxing" — a social media term for enhanced efforts to improve physical appearance — range from maintaining a competitive edge in youth-centric workplaces to addressing subtle signs of aging, such as dark under-eye circles or loss of jawline definition, according to Vyas.
Treatments range from minimally invasive procedures like Botox and laser therapy, to surgical interventions like chest masculinization and liposuction.
Men now represent roughly 15% of cosmetic procedure patients, driven in part by workplace competitiveness and a decline in the historical stigma surrounding aesthetic treatments. (iStock)

"The misconception often is that minimally invasive treatments will fix things and have no side effects," Vyas cautioned, noting that improper or excessive non-surgical treatments can change the normal layers and contours of facial tissue.
5 steps to looking your best
Before jumping to aesthetic procedures as quick-fix substitutes for biological health, the surgeon recommends taking the following steps to improve physical appearance.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Complete abstinence from all forms of nicotine is essential to maintaining microvascular circulation and preventing premature skin breakdown, according to Vyas.
Experts warn that minimally invasive cosmetic treatments are not risk-free fixes and can distort underlying tissue if overused. (iStock)

Avoid over-hyped trends and multi-step routines, the experts recommended. Guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology point to two daily essentials: a morning broad-spectrum sunscreen to block photoaging UV rays, and a topical retinoid at night to stimulate cell turnover.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Maintaining a healthy weight can prevent the chronic, systemic inflammation that is linked to metabolic syndrome, which directly accelerates structural skin and tissue aging.
Aesthetic procedures cannot substitute for internal wellness, making things like daily sun protection and early hair loss intervention crucial first steps. (iStock)

Intervene early at the first sign of thinning. Evidence-based medical treatments, like FDA-approved finasteride and minoxidil, remain the primary standard for maintaining hair density before follicle loss becomes permanent.
"The real longevity drug is exercise — aerobic and non-aerobic strength training exercises," Vyas said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Someone who's looking for a hotspan or a healthspan, because they're so intimately related … I think they should focus on the basics to start ... the foundation is what's most important," the surgeon added.

title: Healthy athlete had no symptoms before mandatory heart screening revealed hidden defect
summary: Cameron Crider had no symptoms despite years of football and basketball, but a mandatory ECG screening revealed a congenital heart defect needing surgery.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'America's Newsroom' to discuss a dramatic increase in fatal heart attacks among people under the age of 55 and how to keep the heart healthy.
A high school student-athlete with a potentially life-threatening heart defect had no symptoms and only learned of his condition through a screening required by Florida law.

The state’s Second Chance Act went into effect July 1 ahead of the 2026-2027 school year and requires students in grades 9 through 12 to undergo at least one electrocardiogram (ECG) screening the first time they participate in or try out for interscholastic athletics, with certain exceptions, affiliate FOX 13 Tampa Bay reported.
An ECG, also called an EKG, is a simple, noninvasive test that measures the heart’s electrical signals and can help identify irregular rhythms or other signs of heart trouble.
ECG screenings can help detect signs of heart conditions that may otherwise go unnoticed in young athletes. (iStock)
DIABETES DRUG COULD SLASH RISK OF FATAL HEART CONDITION IN ONE GROUP, SCIENTISTS REVEAL

For Cameron Crider, a sophomore football and basketball player at Calvary Christian High School in Clearwater, which requires ECGs for all student athletes, the screening led doctors to discover an atrial septal defect (ASD), a congenital heart defect involving an opening in the wall between the heart’s two upper chambers.

If a significant ASD is left untreated, the extra blood flow can strain the heart and lungs over time and may lead to complications such as pulmonary hypertension (high blood pressure), heart failure and, in some cases, stroke.
"I’ve been playing [sports] my whole life and didn’t notice anything, so I was surprised because I haven’t felt anything," Cameron told FOX 13.

"[Cam was] going to a three-hour football practice and then a two-hour basketball practice back-to-back and never having fatigue or shortness of breath, or, you know, anything that you would think would be a warning sign," his mother, Laura Crider, told the station. "So, we were completely shocked."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Crider is scheduled for surgery to fix the ASD in October and is expected to be able to play sports again next season.
The mandatory ECG is "a gift from God that has been given to us, truly," Laura Crider said.

"We were able to find this out in a doctor’s office with an explanation and a clear plan that says we can help you, and so many of these other parents who are advocating for these screenings, they had to find out through a tragedy," she continued.

Up to 80% of young athletes who suffer sudden cardiac arrest (SCA), the leading cause of death during exercise, don’t have any warning symptoms prior to their arrest, Dr. Jonathan Drezner, director of the University of Washington Medicine Center for Sports Cardiology, told Fox News Digital.
Heart screenings are one tool doctors can use to assess athletes for conditions that could put them at risk. (iStock)
Because intense physical activity places additional stress on the heart, undetected heart conditions can become dangerous during sports, the American Heart Association (AHA) told Fox News Digital.

"Sudden cardiac arrest is not the only concern," the AHA said. "These conditions can also lead to other serious heart-related complications and may require monitoring, treatment or restrictions on athletic participation to keep students safe."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The AHA does not recommend mandatory ECG screenings for every student athlete.

"A heart assessment that includes a review of a student's personal and family history along with a physical examination is the best way to identify serious heart conditions that can lead to cardiac events in student athletes," the AHA said.

"If the comprehensive heart assessment raises concerns, health care professionals can order appropriate follow-up testing, such as an ECG, echocardiogram, heart monitor or other advanced imaging based on the suspected diagnosis."
A student-athlete’s heart evaluation may include a medical history, physical exam and, when appropriate, additional cardiac testing. (iStock)

The AHA and American College of Cardiology support what they say is an "evidence-based, layered approach to identify heart issues so they can be diagnosed, monitored and treated as early as possible."
According to Drezner, an ECG screening, when interpreted properly, is one of the best screening tools in medicine.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"An ECG greatly increases our ability to detect conditions associated with SCA in the young," he said.

"A standard sports physical by history and physical alone will miss 80-90% of kids with at-risk heart conditions. An ECG can suggest or detect about 80% of the conditions that put young persons at risk. It is not perfect, but it is far better than the standard sports physical."
Young athletes may appear healthy and perform normally even when an underlying heart condition is present. (iStock)

Though healthy athletes and young people can have a potentially lethal heart condition and not know it, Drezner said chest pain, passing out and a racing heart are symptoms that should not be ignored.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Make sure your child feels well when they exercise," he advised. "If you have a family history of genetic heart conditions or SCA, you should bring this up with your child’s doctor. And get your child a proper heart screen with an ECG."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Navy veterans reunite after 30 years for 'grueling' cross-country bike challenge honoring 9/11
summary: Two Navy veterans reunited after 30 years to bike from San Diego to Ground Zero, raising over $17,000 for Tunnel to Towers before 9/11's 25th anniversary.
story: Two Navy friends reunited after 30 years to bike from San Diego to New York, raising awareness for Tunnel to Towers and visiting fire stations along the way. Their journey became a moving tribute to service, sacrifice and unity.
Two Navy veterans recently reunited to complete a great expedition across America.
Jim Serger, 55, of Cincinnati, Ohio, and Cory Hardy, 51, of Ennis, Montana, hadn’t seen each other in 30 years since serving together overseas.
On July 14, the two friends embarked on a bike ride across the country, from California to New York City, in honor of the upcoming 25th anniversary of 9/11.
NEW JERSEY MAN WALKS ACROSS US TO RAISE NEARLY $100K FOR HOMELESS VETERANS: 'RESPECT AND REVERENCE'
After writing three books for the nonprofit Tunnel to Towers, Serger said he felt he needed to challenge himself "with something bigger."

"And why not wrangle in my old Navy buddy, who I hadn’t seen for 30 years, that I knew was a tremendous bicyclist," he told Fox News Digital. "Back in January, I said, ‘Would you like to go on this trip?’ And he said, ‘Absolutely, Jimmy, count me in.’"
Navy veterans Jim Serger (left) and Cory Hardy (right) set off to bike across the country, starting in San Diego July 14, 2026. (Jim Serger)
Hardy said he’s always viewed himself as "incredibly patriotic" because he’s been granted "so many opportunities" through the military to see the world and get an education.
"When Jim approached me about the idea of doing this, I was like, ‘Wow, this is awesome. This is something that I can do,’" Hardy shared.
"It's the 250th anniversary of our country and the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and I don't want to forget. And I want people to keep it at the forefront of their minds."
TUNNEL TO TOWERS 5K DRAWS 40,000 PEOPLE TO HONOR 9/11 FIRST RESPONDERS IN NYC
Serger trained for 10 months, logging 5,000 miles on an indoor trainer. When spring came, he hit the trails around Cincinnati.

A few months later, the duo began their journey in San Diego and headed east. They were met with 20 road closures, a fire and flooding in Colorado, two flat tires, three bike shop visits and lots of backroad maneuvering.
A map depicts Serger's and Hardy's bike route across America. (Jim Serger)

Serger and Hardy focused on staying hydrated, especially in the California and Arizona heat, with a collective three gallons of water each day, sometimes including electrolytes. They snacked on energy waffles, protein bars and "salt gummy bears" and ate lots of carbs at meals.
Hardy said he took 10-minute ice baths "every single day." Serger reported losing six pounds by the end of the mission, which he gained back by eating "good food" in New York.
AMERICA'S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK
While Hardy was already accustomed to the elevation after living in mountainous Montana, Serger said the altitude posed a physical challenge.
"It was grueling ... so hard," he told Fox News Digital. "Cory had to take the mountains in Colorado. I stayed on flat ground. That was our game plan."
Serger and Hardy stopped at 25 firehouses along the way, connecting with first responders and community members from big cities to small towns. (Jim Serger)

Serger and Hardy met up with some of their old Navy buddies along the way. One fellow veteran, an Arizona state trooper, drove from Phoenix to Flagstaff to meet them on the route. Others opened their homes for the pair to stay the night.
The friends stopped at about 25 firehouses to hand out Tunnel to Towers books and to introduce themselves.

"Sometimes we were there for an hour, sometimes we were there for four hours," Serger said. "Talking about Tunnel to Towers, where they were on 9/11 … how much they train … it was just very heartwarming."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Serger said he and Hardy both foster the "patriotic mentality" of "what we can do for others." Hardy serves on city council and Serger's wife cooks for the fire department every month. These types of efforts were reciprocated on their journey.
"Every fire station, EMS, police station, they're all involved in the communities. We got patches. We got hats. we got pins. We got T-shirts," Serger said.
Hardy added that, at every firehouse, everybody was there to help, "regardless of their state’s political affiliation."
Serger and Hardy receive a grand welcome at the FDNY Ten House in Lower Manhattan Aug. 2, 2026. (Jim Serger)
"They're just another American out there willing to put their life on the line to save people," he said. "I thought it was super awesome to get to meet firefighters from East Coast to West Coast.

"The closer we got to Shanksville and the Pentagon and New York, it became very emotional, because then people said, ‘My mom was there’ or ‘My aunt was there' ... and then a firefighter said, ‘Three of our brothers went up there.’
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The closer we got, we knew we had hit the epicenter of how people responded to those terrorist attacks, and it really hit home."
At the Pentagon, Serger and Hardy got a police escort from the Pentagon Police and Pentagon Fire Department before receiving a five-hour tour, including the 9/11 memorial.
Serger and Hardy received a police escort in Shanksville, Pa., where they spent time at the firehouse. (Jim Serger)
Clocking about 170 miles a day, the pair made it to Lower Manhattan in 20 days.
They were welcomed by the FDNY, Port Authority and NYPD Honor Guard at FDNY Ten House, across from Ground Zero and the 9/11 Memorial & Museum.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I started crying," Serger said. "My wife was there. She flew in. We had Sal Cassano, the [former] FDNY fire commissioner, there. Fire Station 10 had firemen, civilians were there. It was very, very moving."
Serger and Hardy’s cause has so far raised more than $17,000 for Tunnel to Towers.
(L-R) Jim Serger's wife, Gina, former New York City Fire Commissioner Sal Cassano, Jim Serger, Tunnel to Towers CEO Frank Siller and Cory Hardy. (Jim Serger)

In addition to raising funds for the organization, Serger said the expedition aims to generate continued awareness for those who sacrificed and risked their lives on 9/11 as the 25th anniversary approaches.
"We never forget 9/11," Serger said. "We never forget the sacrifice of our heroes, of our military, our first responders and gold star families," he said. "We never want 9/11 to fade away."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Serger described the bike ride as a "surreal" and emotional experience.

"It started off with, we're going to raise money for Tunnel to Towers, and I think our final [takeaway] was there's a lot of love and pride and patriotism in this country, from far west all the way to the east," he shared.
"Everybody welcomed us with open arms. That's all we talked about."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Hilaria Baldwin shares 5 simple stretches to do at work to prevent pain and stiffness
summary: Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates five desk chair stretches targeting tech neck, core engagement and hip flexors to combat the effects of sitting all day.
story: Fitness instructor Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a series of chair-based mobility drills, including shoulder squeezes and spinal rounding, encouraging workers to check their alignment and breathing during busy days.
Sitting all day at a desk is the norm for millions of American workers, but it can take a toll on the body.

As long hours spent in the same position can contribute to poor posture, stiffness and other physical issues, experts say regular movement and stretching can help prevent joint pain and muscle weakness.

"Many people sit every day for most of the day, and this can cause so many problems in the body," certified fitness and yoga instructor Hilaria Baldwin told Fox News Digital. "We've all heard of tech neck, carpal tunnel – most of that has to do with the alignment of our spine."
'OFFICE AIR' TREND HAS PEOPLE CONVINCED THE WORKPLACE IS AGING THEM: 'LESS FRESH'
Baldwin shared the following simple stretches that can be done in a desk chair, while cautioning people to "be the judge of what’s appropriate" for their workspace before trying the techniques.
No. 1: Posture-correcting elbow squeeze
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates an elbow and shoulder stretch for better posture. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
Sitting in a desk chair, bring the arms up into a "goal post" position, with the elbows in alignment with the shoulders.
Pull the core in, squeeze the shoulder blades together and pull the chin back. Imagine that the back of the head is pressing up against a wall.
JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS
Keeping the arms in position, start bringing both elbows in front, touching them together. Open again and squeeze. Repeat this about 10 times.
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates an elbow and shoulder stretch for better posture. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"This, for me, feels really good," Baldwin said. "Check in with your body during the day. I'm going to do maybe a few at 10 a.m. and then maybe again at 11:30. You can't do too many of these."
"You also develop an incredible back if you want to wear those backless dresses, but it also makes you feel better," she added.
No. 2: Posture-correcting shoulder squeeze
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates an elbow and shoulder stretch for better posture. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
From the previous position, take the arms down until the palms of the hands are facing the floor. Start to squeeze the shoulder and back muscles.
Bring the arms forward to cross over each other and stop once the elbows are aligned.
FITNESS INFLUENCER SAYS ONE SIMPLE HABIT CAN HELP ANYONE GET BACK IN SHAPE
As the arms cross, round the head down, bringing the forehead toward the elbows. Open the arms up and repeat about 10 times, practicing the set consistently throughout the day.
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates an elbow and shoulder stretch for better posture. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"As I'm rounding, I’m pulling the shoulder blades away from the spine as a bit of a hug, and then I open again and squeeze the shoulder blades together," Baldwin described.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's going to help remind you that you need to be sitting up with your shoulders back, chin back," she added.
No. 3: Spinal stretch
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a rounded spinal stretch position. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
Interlace the fingers behind the head and bring the elbows toward one another.
Slowly drop the chin to the chest, lightly pulling down through the spine.
In the opposite direction, open the elbows wide, arching the back and lifting the chin to the sky.
Hilaria Baldwin is shown in an open spinal stretch position. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"Focus on your breath here as well, especially if you have a stressful job," Baldwin said. "We stop breathing and that just puts tension in our body, so try to take deep breaths. Inhale, exhale."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If you're about to write that email that maybe you shouldn't write, maybe just tap into your breath, do a few of these."
No. 4: Core engagement
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a subtle exercise for ab engagement while seated. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
Although subtle, Baldwin calls this exercise "extremely important," as it focuses on engaging the core while seated.
Sit up straight and pull the belly button toward the spine, noticing if you can feel where the sit bones are pressing into the chair.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Rock back and forth, pulling in the belly button. Think about pulling in the "seatbelt muscle," in the lower gut area, maintaining proper posture.
"This is actually a really good ab exercise," Baldwin noted.
No. 5: Hip and calf stretching lunges
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a calf and hip stretch when taking a break from sitting. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
For those who are able to stand, Baldwin encourages employees to rise from their chair and "stretch a little bit," since sitting for long periods of time can "shorten the hip flexors."
"Anything where you can stretch it out is going be really great for you," she said. "I like to mix it with a calf stretch as well."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Stand up and step one foot out in front of the other in a slight lunge, bending the front knee. Open through the back of the leg and press the heel down.
Press forward and bring the hips to center, making sure to maintain the same posture practiced while sitting. Switch the legs and stretch on the other side.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Cancer vaccine prevents deadly melanoma from returning or spreading in landmark trial
summary: Merck and Moderna's mRNA cancer vaccine hit its Phase 3 trial endpoint, showing improved recurrence-free survival in melanoma patients after surgery.
story: Dr. Murad Alam, vice chair of dermatology at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, shares the significance of Merck and Moderna's 'very exciting' Phase 3 trial results for a personalized melanoma vaccine.
An experimental skin cancer vaccine significantly reduced the risk of melanoma returning or spreading in a late-stage clinical trial from Merck and Moderna.
The results mark the first positive Phase 3 trial of an mRNA-based personalized cancer therapy, according to the companies.

Known as INTerpath-001, the study evaluated 1,137 patients globally who had surgery to remove high-risk (Stage IIB through Stage IV) melanoma. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either Keytruda, plus the personalized vaccine, or Keytruda, plus placebo.
'TANMAXXING' TREND COULD COME AT A DANGEROUS COST, SKIN CANCER EXPERTS WARN
Patients who received the combination experienced significantly better "recurrence-free survival," meaning their cancer was less likely to return than in those who received Keytruda alone.
The combination also significantly improved "distant metastasis-free survival," a measure of how long patients remained alive without the cancer spreading to distant parts of the body.
An experimental skin cancer vaccine was able to prevent melanoma from returning or spreading in the latest clinical trial from Merck and Moderna. (Merck)

"These phase 3 findings represent a pivotal moment for the field of cancer research," Stéphane Bancel, CEO of Moderna, said in the press release. "For many years, the idea of creating an mRNA treatment designed specifically for an individual patient's cancer was aspirational. We are now helping turn that vision into a reality."
How the personalized vaccine works

Unlike traditional vaccines that protect against external viruses, the custom-tailored mRNA vaccine (intismeran autogene) is a therapeutic vaccine given after surgery to train the body to hunt leftover cancer cells.

After a patient undergoes surgery to remove a tumor, doctors sample both the cancerous tissue and healthy cells. Then, advanced algorithms analyze the tumor's genetic sequence to select up to 34 tumor-specific neoantigens to encode in the personalized treatment.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
Dr. Murad Alam, vice chair of dermatology at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, noted that not all melanomas are the same.

"They're slightly different in every patient, which is why traditional chemotherapies often stop working or don't work in a particular patient," he told Fox News Digital. "This is almost individualized immunotherapy, where you're finding specific issues in a particular patient."
Merck and Moderna said they plan to engage with regulatory authorities worldwide about potential regulatory filings for the treatment. (Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp.)
The individualized approach is designed to direct the immune system toward tumor-specific targets, Alam noted.

"It doesn't hit normal cells, and it hits the cancer cells very effectively because it's not just a generic vaccine. It's one that specifically knows the signs of your cancer and can find it," he said.
FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS
The goal of this particular vaccine, according to the doctor, is to extend the lives of people who "already have a bad case of the disease."

It is not intended to prevent melanoma in people who do not have the disease, even if they have a family history that may put them at greater risk, nor is it intended for those with a very small melanoma.
"This is designed for people where the melanoma has grown to the point where it's threatening not just the local area of the skin, but their whole lives," Alam said.
The role of AI
Alam also spoke about the role of artificial intelligence in determining which antigens to include in the vaccine so that it is most effective.

"These things are difficult, and, historically, [they] took a lot of time, and it just wouldn't be feasible to do this for every individual patient without the power of AI," he said. "And I'm sure that will become better and better in the future.
"This is designed for people where the melanoma has grown to the point where it's threatening not just the local area of the skin, but their whole lives."
"Here, AI is a tool that allows you in a reasonable amount of time, with a reasonable amount of resources ... to come up with a vaccine for that individual person."
What comes next

After the successful Phase 3 outcome, Merck and Moderna announced plans to engage with regulatory authorities worldwide, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, about potential regulatory filings.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Plans are in the works to test the vaccine technology against other hard-to-treat cancers, including lung, bladder and kidney cancers.

"I think the underlying concept of targeting a particular tumor with the specific markers on that tumor is generalizable, meaning you could do this with different kinds of skin cancer or different kinds of cancer in general," Alam agreed. "It's very exciting."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Although the companies said the results were significant and meaningful, the findings are still early and did not reveal how long patients remained cancer-free.
The Phase 3 announcement also did not establish whether the treatment ultimately helps patients live longer.

By tailoring treatment to the biology of each patient’s disease, this approach has the potential to establish a new paradigm in the adjuvant melanoma setting when given in combination with Keytruda, a standard-of-care immunotherapy. (iStock)
The recurrence-free survival results were also based on investigator assessments rather than an independent central review, the release noted.
The study only looked at people with specific stages of skin melanoma who had surgery and no prior drug treatments, so the results may not apply to other types or stages of cancer.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Merck said the treatments’ side effects were similar to those seen in earlier studies, with no new safety concerns identified.
Alam reiterated that the vaccine seems to have both a "tremendous benefit [and] good side effect profile."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"When you're getting very strong cancer medications, even when they work, the toll on the patient is often terrible," he said. "It alters their life during the course of treatment where there's tremendous suffering.

"The nice thing about this, because it's so targeted, it doesn't damage many of your normal cells ... so the side effects are really mild — a little fatigue, a little chills, some injection side pain."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Cancer doctor reveals 5 habits that may reduce disease risk and improve outcomes
summary: A breast surgical oncologist shares five everyday strategies to reduce cancer risk, including how GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic could play a role.
story: Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based breast surgical oncologist and author, emphasized that while no lifestyle choice can guarantee cancer prevention, healthy habits can help support the body and reduce certain risk factors.
Even as new data shows cancer’s continuing toll in the U.S., a surgical oncologist says some simple lifestyle measures could help lower the likelihood of developing the disease.
An estimated 2,114,850 new cancer cases will be diagnosed in the U.S. in 2026 — about 5,800 per day, according to the American Cancer Society.

Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based breast surgical oncologist and author of "Real Talk, Real Hope: Breast Cancer Your Way," emphasized that while no lifestyle choice can guarantee cancer prevention, healthy habits can help reduce certain risk factors.
LEADING ONCOLOGIST REVEALS 6 HABITS THAT COULD PROMOTE LONGEVITY AND REDUCE YOUR RISK OF CHRONIC ILLNESS
From maintaining a healthy weight to staying active, Rourke shared the following five everyday strategies that support the body and improve overall health.
To lower the risk of cancer and premature death, the American Cancer Society recommends a diet rich in vegetables, whole fruits, whole grains and legumes. (iStock)
No. 1: Maintain a healthy weight
Being obese or overweight is associated with an increased risk of at least 13 types of cancer, according to the National Cancer Institute.
Rourke estimates that excess body weight is likely the third-biggest risk factor for breast cancer, after female gender and aging.
OZEMPIC-STYLE DRUGS LINKED TO MAJOR SLOWDOWN IN CANCER SPREAD, NEW STUDY FINDS
Growing research suggests glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may be associated with a lower risk of cancer diagnoses and recurrence.
Rourke said one possible reason GLP-1s could prove beneficial for cancer risk is that the drugs promote weight loss and reduce chronic inflammation.
Growing research suggests glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may be associated with a lower risk of cancer diagnoses and recurrence. (iStock)

"We know that a lower BMI equals a better prognosis with breast cancer," she told Fox News Digital. "So if the secondary effect of taking a GLP-1 means that you’re going to lose weight, that’s a benefit, because we know you’re going to do better with breast cancer."
GLP-1 drugs are not yet approved to prevent cancer, and more research is needed to determine whether they independently reduce disease risk.
No. 2: Stay physically active and fit
The American Cancer Society states that physical activity is linked to a lower risk of several cancers.
The official guideline recommends 150–300 minutes of moderate activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity per week for adults.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

"I think people underestimate overall fitness," Rourke said. "We tend to think about it for heart health, but it’s not just heart health — it’s mental health and reducing your risk of having lots of chronic medical problems that span from one end to the other, in addition to other cancers."
Even if staying physically fit doesn’t keep cancer at bay, it may help improve outcomes if the disease develops, she noted.
The American Cancer Society states that physical activity is linked with a lower risk of several cancers. (iStock)
"One in eight women get breast cancer. So if it comes knocking, you want to be ready," she said.

"Women come to me and say, ‘I’ve done everything. I’ve exercised every day. I’ve eaten a healthy diet, and here I am sitting in your office.’ And I say, ‘Well, that healthy body is now ready for this fight.’"
"If you can bring a healthy body and a healthy mind to the disease, you are going to do better."
No. 3: Eat a balanced diet and limit processed foods

To lower the risk of cancer and premature death, the American Cancer Society recommends sticking to a diet rich in vegetables, whole fruits, whole grains and legumes, while limiting red/processed meats, sugary drinks and highly processed foods.
Rourke agrees with these guidelines, but noted that even people who follow healthy eating patterns can face cancer diagnoses.
CANCER SURVIVORS SAW MAJOR IMPROVEMENTS IN SLEEP AND WELL-BEING WITH ONE WEEKLY PRACTICE
"I have vegans sitting in my office. I have people who don’t eat any sugar in my office. They’re all getting breast cancer," she said.
"What I say is, [eat] a healthy, balanced diet, limited processed foods, as close to farm-to-table as you can get," the doctor advised. "Just healthy eating, reasonable portions … nothing in excess."
Even people who follow healthy eating patterns can face cancer diagnoses, the doctor noted. (iStock)
"If you practice that, that’s going to suit you for so many things in your future."
The doctor added that it’s not necessary to take an extreme approach to dietary choices: "Do you need to give up all sugar? No. Do you need to go to the extreme? No."
No. 4: Limit alcohol and avoid tobacco

Cigarette smoking is responsible for about 20% of all cancers and about 30% of cancer deaths in the U.S., according to the American Cancer Society. The habit can cause cancer in numerous parts of the body, and quitting can reduce cancer risk at any age, experts say.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Meanwhile, alcohol consumption has been linked to an estimated 5% of U.S. cancer cases and 4% of cancer deaths in 2019, according to the National Cancer Institute.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The U.S. surgeon general issued guidance last year following research that linked alcohol to at least seven types of cancer, naming it as the "third leading preventable cause of cancer" in the country, after tobacco and obesity.
Rourke advised that alcohol should only be consumed in moderation, although even light drinking has been shown to raise the risk of certain cancers.

The U.S. surgeon general issued guidance last year following research that linked alcohol to at least seven types of cancer, naming it as the "third leading preventable cause of cancer" in the country, after tobacco and obesity. (iStock)

"Too many Americans are living with an outdated assumption that some amount of alcohol is not only harmless, but also good for you," Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel previously told Fox News Digital. "Increasing evidence shows that isn't true."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Even though traditional advice has been up to one drink a day for women and two drinks per day for men, in fact, no amount of alcohol is healthy," he added.
No. 5: Keep up with screening and investigate concerning changes
Early detection programs have enabled doctors and patients to detect disease earlier than ever before, which increases survival rates, Rourke noted.
"I think now there’s more awareness," she said. "People know if they have someone in their family and what kind of cancer they had."
Early detection programs have enabled doctors and patients to detect disease earlier than ever before, which increases survival rates, the doctor noted. (iStock)
"I think people are much more educated in general, and that is promoting wellness, health, early detection and screening."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rourke also expressed concern about relying too heavily on artificial intelligence when investigating possible symptoms.

"If you are worried about something, call your primary care doctor [or] gynecologist," she advised. "If you feel like something’s wrong, follow through with it and get it checked out. Never ignore your inner voice."
