title: Surrogate, California couple clash in court as newborn fights for life after heart surgery
summary: Nausheen Gilkar told a Dallas court her newborn is suffering after open-heart surgery as the surrogate custody fight with McKenna West intensifies.
story: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton discusses a surrogate who gave birth in Texas to baby with a heart defect after the biological parents requested abortion on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

The critically ill newborn at the center of a bitter surrogate custody fight was placed back on a breathing tube after his condition worsened following open-heart surgery, according to newly filed court documents.
The baby is in critical condition and being closely watched at the hospital, intended parents Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed said in filings obtained by TMZ.

The couple said the child suffered possible complications after a Norwood procedure, an operation used to treat his severe heart defect, and had to be re-intubated after his condition declined overnight.
SURROGATE SAYS BABY 'RIPPED AWAY' 60 SECONDS AFTER BIRTH AS CUSTODY FIGHT ERUPTS AFTER ABORTION REFUSAL
McKenna West, center, walks with her legal team at a Dallas family court hearing in the legal fight over a critically ill newborn. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

In a Dallas courtroom Tuesday, Gilkar and Ahmed faced surrogate McKenna West as they fought over who should make medical decisions for the newborn. The clash has drawn national attention because West says she refused the California couple’s earlier request to terminate the pregnancy after the baby was diagnosed with a life-threatening heart condition.

Gilkar and Ahmed call the baby Rumi. West, an Alaska cardiac nurse, calls him Gabriel and is asking a Texas judge to give her sole conservatorship, which would put medical decision-making in her hands.
HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY
California couple Nausheen Gilkar, center, and Omar Ahmed, right, arrive for a hearing over custody and medical decision-making for their newborn son. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

Gilkar told the court the couple has been at their son’s bedside as he fights through treatment. She said that since surgery, he has struggled to breathe, choked on tubes and needed a blood transfusion, according to court reporting by The Associated Press.
"He’s our child," Gilkar said, according to the AP.
She accused West of trying to take him away. "She’s trying to take him from us," Gilkar said.
Gilkar described the newborn as "the love of our lives" and said, "He’s suffering a lot."
NEONATOLOGIST SOUNDS ALARM OVER MASSACHUSETTS ABORTION LAW ALLOWING PROCEDURES UP TO BIRTH: 'VERY DISTURBING'
McKenna West arrives at a Dallas court hearing over the custody dispute. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

The custody feud began after the baby was diagnosed at about 20 weeks with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, or HLHS. West says Gilkar and Ahmed then asked her to terminate the pregnancy. She refused and later traveled to Texas to give birth, Fox News Digital previously reported.

HLHS leaves one side of the heart underdeveloped and disrupts normal blood flow. Without treatment, the condition can be fatal within days or weeks, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
AMERICAN RED CROSS DECLARES NATIONAL BLOOD CRISIS AS TYPE O SUPPLY DROPS TO DANGEROUS LEVELS
McKenna West, left, appears with attorneys at Dallas family court amid a custody dispute with the intended parents of the baby she carried. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

Budner disputes key parts of West’s account and says the couple did agree to the baby’s treatment. He told Fox News Digital that doctors determined on Aug. 14 that the child was eligible for the Norwood procedure, the first of three open-heart surgeries generally used to treat HLHS.
Gilkar and Ahmed consented to the surgery, which was performed Aug. 17, he said. At the time, Budner described the baby’s condition as "critical and complex."
BOARD-CERTIFIED OBGYN WARNS NEW MASSACHUSETTS LATE-TERM ABORTION LAW EXPOSES MOTHERS TO DANGER
McKenna West arrives for a Dallas court hearing in the surrogate custody dispute. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

West’s lawyers have argued that the court should make sure the baby continues to receive life-saving care. West told the judge she would abandon her custody request if the court determines the intended parents are committed to that care, according to the AP.
Gilkar and Ahmed have asked the court to delay a hearing over the temporary restraining order that gave them custody while the legal fight continues, TMZ reported.
TWO FAMILIES SUE NORTH DAKOTA HOSPITAL ON ALLEGATIONS BABIES WERE SWITCHED AT BIRTH
The custody battle is only one part of the couple’s broader legal fight with West.

Before the baby was born, Gilkar and Ahmed filed counterclaims seeking more than $100,000, alleging West breached their surrogacy agreement and caused them emotional distress. The counterclaims, obtained by TMZ, said the couple paid West $60,000 during the pregnancy under an agreement that addressed termination. West has denied wrongdoing and asked the court to dismiss the claims.
DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

The dispute has only grown more personal since the baby’s Aug. 12 birth. West said in a New York Post opinion piece last week that she had only about a minute with the newborn, while his umbilical cord was still attached, before he was taken away. A court order has since barred her from seeing or holding the baby.
On Tuesday, the judge left that order in place and did not immediately decide the larger question of custody or conservatorship, according to the AP.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured an emergency court order before the birth directing that medically necessary care not be delayed or obstructed, Fox News Digital previously reported. Paxton’s office also notified two Dallas medical centers of their obligations to provide life-saving treatment.
The Associated Press and Fox News Digital's Jasmine Baehr contributed to this report.

title: Attempted drone incursion at Virginia prison leads to $324K contraband haul with meth, 17 cellphones
summary: A drone smuggling attempt at a Virginia prison led to a $324,000 contraband seizure including methamphetamine and 17 cellphones, officials said.
story: The Justice Department announced charges against 12 people for a sophisticated drone smuggling operation introducing dangerous contraband into federal prisons across multiple states. Former federal prosecutor Jim Trusty discuss the challenges of catching drones, which were used for 38 deliveries of drugs, cell phones and weapons to 10 facilities.

Virginia prison officials intercepted a package containing an estimated $324,000 worth of contraband, including a pound of suspected methamphetamine and more than a dozen cellphones, following an attempted drone incursion at a state prison, authorities said.
The Virginia Department of Corrections (VADOC) said corrections staff discovered the "suspicious package" at Sussex I State Prison at around 1:30 a.m. Monday.
Inside, officials said they found a one-pound bag of suspected methamphetamine, 17 cellphones with charging cables and 20 sheets of paper that appeared to be saturated with an unknown liquid.
FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH
Virginia prison officials intercepted a package containing an estimated $324,000 in contraband following an attempted drone incursion at Sussex I State Prison. (Virginia Department of Corrections)
The agency said it also seized multiple hex wrenches, three USB Wi-Fi adapters and two SIM cards.

Officials also discovered an unusual assortment of other items, including 30 disposable lighters, two cartons of cigarettes, one pound of loose-leaf tobacco, three packs of cigars, two bottles of professional-grade tattoo ink, two bottles of perfume and two bottles of glue.
WILD VIDEO SHOWS INMATES RIOTING INSIDE JAIL AFTER FRUSTRATIONS OVER ACCESS BOIL OVER

Virginia corrections officials intercepted a package containing a pound of suspected methamphetamine, 17 cellphones and other contraband with an estimated "prison value" of approximately $324,000. (Virginia Department of Corrections)
VADOC estimated the contraband had a combined value of roughly $324,000 inside the prison.
VADOC Director Joseph Walters said the seizure highlighted the sophisticated methods people may use in attempts to smuggle contraband into correctional facilities.
DIDDY SENT TO SOLITARY CONFINEMENT AFTER PRISON FIGHT WITH ANOTHER INMATE: MULTIPLE REPORTS

Virginia prison officials said an attempted drone incursion at Sussex I State Prison led to the discovery of a package containing approximately $324,000 worth of contraband. (Photo by Long Wei/VCG via Getty Images)

"This investigation is an important reminder that some people will use sophisticated methods in an attempt to smuggle drugs and other dangerous contraband into Virginia Department of Corrections facilities," Walters said in a statement.

"I thank our institutional staff at Sussex I State Prison for their vigilance and focus on ensuring the safety and security of our facility," he continued. "Our dedicated correctional staff and OLES members stand ready to intercept any dangerous contraband that individuals may attempt to introduce into correctional settings to ensure the safety and security of our dedicated corrections team members, of incarcerated individuals in our custody, of probationers, and of people in communities all across the Commonwealth of Virginia."
The incident remains under investigation by VADOC's Office of Law Enforcement Services (OLES).
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Anyone with information about attempted smuggling into a VADOC facility is asked to call OLES at 540-830-9280.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Former news anchor pleads guilty to stabbing mother to death on Halloween
summary: Angelynn Mock pleaded guilty to first-degree murder after allegedly believing her mother Anita Avers was the devil during the Halloween stabbing.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A former Missouri television news anchor has admitted to fatally stabbing her mother on Halloween last year after apparently believing she was the devil, authorities said last week.

Angelynn "Angie" Mock, 48, pleaded guilty to one count of first-degree murder in connection with the slaying of her mother, 80-year-old Anita Avers, on Oct. 31, 2025, the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office announced Friday.
Under the terms of the plea, Mock faces life in prison with eligibility for parole after 25 years.
FLORIDA MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING MOM AND BURNING BODY BECAUSE SHE ‘WANTED TO BE CREMATED’
Former St. Louis television news anchor Angelynn "Angie" Mock has been charged with first-degree murder following the fatal stabbing of her mother in Wichita, Kansas. (Angie Mock/Facebook)

Officers were called to the Wichita home Mock and Avers shared with Mock's stepfather around 7:50 a.m. on Oct. 31. When they arrived, Mock was found outside with cuts on her hands, according to the Wichita Police Department.
Avers was taken to a hospital with multiple stab wounds, and later died.
Mock made several statements indicating she believed her mother was the devil, according to a probable cause affidavit. She allegedly told authorities that she killed her mother to "save herself."
Mock's stepfather told KAKE-TV that she had been diagnosed with mental illness and suffered from delusions and depression.
FORMER TV ANCHOR ACCUSED OF KILLING HER MOTHER RULED INCOMPETENT, MURDER CASE PUT ON HOLD
Angelynn "Angie" Mock has pleaded guilty to first-degree murder for the Halloween 2025 stabbing death of her mother. (Angie Mock/Facebook | Sedgwick County Jail)
She previously worked as a news anchor and reporter for Fox 2 in St. Louis from 2011 to 2015, according to her LinkedIn profile.
Prior to that, she worked as a morning anchor from 2007 to 2011 at KOKH-TV in Oklahoma City, the profile states. Mock held other reporting stints in Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska.
Angelynn "Angie" Mock seen after being arrested and booked into the Sedgwick County Jail on suspicion of first-degree murder. (Sedgwick County Jail)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She is scheduled to be sentenced on Oct. 5.
Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Helicopter rescue crew caught on camera saving 2 climbers trapped along popular California beach cliff
summary: Video shows a CHP helicopter crew hovering above a Big Sur ravine to hoist two climbers stranded 600 feet below the roadway at Hurricane Point.
story: California Highway Patrol video shows a helicopter rescue technician being lowered to two climbers stranded far below the roadway near Hurricane Point before lifting them to safety one at a time. (Credit: CHP - Coastal Division Air Operations)
Two climbers in California stranded on a steep Big Sur cliffside Saturday found themselves 600 feet below the roadway with a California Highway Patrol (CHP) helicopter crew their only way out.
Video released by the CHP shows the H-70 helicopter hovering above a steep ravine near Hurricane Point as a rescue technician is lowered on a cable to reach the trapped pair.
Big Sur Fire requested help from CHP’s Paso Robles Air Unit at about 6:24 p.m., according to the agency.
NOVICE CLIMBER SURVIVES 1,500-FOOT DROP ON CALIFORNIA'S MOUNT SHASTA AFTER HELICOPTER RESCUE DELAYED BY CLOUDS
A CHP helicopter rescue technician prepares for a high-risk hoist during the Big Sur cliffside rescue alongthe California coast. (CHP - Coastal Division Air Operations)

The terrain was so steep that the technician could not safely disconnect from the hoist hook after reaching the first climber. Instead, he secured the climber in a Pelican rescue harness and the two were lifted together to rescue personnel waiting at a staging area.
The helicopter then returned to the ravine and carried out the same technical maneuver to bring the second climber to safety.
RESCUERS FREE CLIMBER TRAPPED BENEATH 16,000-POUND BOULDER ON OREGON'S MOUNT HOOD IN COMPLEX OPERATION
A California Highway Patrol helicopter rescue technician works to secure a stranded climber during a technical hoist operation near Hurricane Point. (CHP - Coastal Division Air Operations)
CHP did not release the climbers’ names or explain how they became stranded.
Social media users praised the CHP air crew and the rescue teams involved after video of the operation was posted online.
"Incredible rescue!! Well done guys!!" one commenter wrote. Another called it an "amazing job by all involved," while another added, "Just incredible, you guys, thanks for what you do!"
Both climbers survived the ordeal, authorities said.
HIKER AIRLIFTED AFTER TERRIFYING RATTLESNAKE BITE ON REMOTE TRAIL AS INCIDENTS SURGE IN AREA
CHP helicopter lifts a climber and rescue technician above the Big Sur coastline during a hoist rescue. (CHP - Coastal Division Air Operations)

"These high-risk, low-frequency rescues are exactly what CHP Air Operations personnel continuously train for," the agency said. "There is no room for error when operating in steep terrain, under hoist, and in challenging environmental conditions."
The cliffside rescue followed two separate Aug. 9 rescue missions for the same H-70 crew.
MISSING GRAND CANYON HIKER, 83, RESCUED AFTER GETTING SEPARATED FROM COMPANION
A CHP air crew hoists a stranded climber to safety during a rescue near Hurricane Point in Big Sur, Calif. (CHP - Coastal Division Air Operations)
The air unit first hoisted an injured 13-year-old hiker from Pinnacles National Park, working with a Paso Robles Fire Department helicopter rescue technician, CHP said.
Later that day, the crew pulled a person who suffered severe injuries in a fall from a waterfall in Big Sur Gorge to safety.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

H-70 then responded to another call in the remote Los Padres National Forest, where a hunter suffering from heat exhaustion and dehydration was brought aboard using a hover step-on maneuver and flown to waiting medics in King City.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Globetrotting sailor nabbed in Canada over alleged child sex crimes aboard sailboat: FBI
summary: Donald Steven Lang, 62, was arrested in Canada after the FBI warned the alleged child predator could be sailing across the Pacific to evade authorities.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
An alleged child predator accused of exploiting a child aboard his sailboat was arrested in Canada, after the FBI warned he could be sailing across the Pacific Ocean to evade authorities.
Donald Steven Lang, 62, was taken into custody over the weekend at the request of the United States, federal authorities said Tuesday, ending a far-reaching search for the globe-trotting sailor.
Lang, a dual U.S. and Canadian citizen, was indicted Aug. 20 in Hawaii on one count of sexual exploitation of children.
'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE CAPTURED ON SAILBOAT OFF NJ COAST AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN
FBI photograph of Lang, who was arrested in Canada in connection with a federal child sexual exploitation case in Hawaii. (FBI)
Prosecutors allege he exploited a minor between September and December 2024 aboard his 55-foot sailboat, Ishi.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) said Lang was known to sail around the world and frequently harbored in Hawaii. But the FBI’s search for him extended far beyond the islands.

The bureau warned Lang, who was last seen on board Ishi in Hawaii in January 2025, could have been sailing between Hawaii and Fiji or Mexico, headed toward Papua New Guinea, or possibly Indonesia. He had ties or connections in Hawaii, Idaho, Washington state, California, Fiji, the Marquesas Islands, Mexico and Canada, the FBI said.

Federal prosecutors allege that Lang attempted to and knowingly used, persuaded, induced, enticed or coerced a minor to engage in sexually explicit conduct for the purpose of producing visual depictions.
The indictment identifies his sailboat as a 55-foot, 1985 Taylor Hatfield oceangoing sailing vessel.
Prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of the boat, digital devices and storage media, including a Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra phone, should Lang be convicted.
'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' EX-COP FUGITIVE RETURNED AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN TO FACE MURDER, CHILD SEX CHARGES
Donald Steven Lang was arrested in Canada after a search tied to child sexual exploitation allegations in Hawaii and an Idaho case, authorities said. (FBI)
Lang was already wanted in Idaho in a separate child sex abuse case, authorities said.

Kootenai County prosecutors charged Lang in April 2025 with three counts of lewd conduct towards a minor under 16 and one count of sexual battery of a minor in connection with allegations that he sexually assaulted a minor between 2003 and 2007.
MORE THAN 300 ARRESTED IN SPRAWLING CALIFORNIA CRACKDOWN ON CHILD EXPLOITATION CRIMES
Donald Steven Lang is pictured in an FBI photograph. (FBI)

"Protecting children from sexual predators is a priority of the highest order," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said. "We will continue to pursue this alleged offender and work with our law enforcement partners to return him to the United States to face trial for the crimes he is charged with committing."
FBI Criminal Assistant Director Heith Janke said Lang had been accused by multiple victims of sexually abusing minors.
FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN
Donald Steven Lang is pictured at the helm of a sailboat in an FBI photograph. (FBI)
"The FBI remains committed to identifying, investigating, and bringing offenders to justice who prey on some of the most vulnerable members of our communities," Janke said.
The FBI had offered a reward of up to $5,000 for information leading to Lang’s arrest and warned he should be considered an escape risk.
ALLEGED IRISH CARTEL BOSS ARRESTED IN COVERT OPERATION ON ORGANIZED CRIME CHARGES AFTER YEARS-LONG MANHUNT

Lang’s apprehension came through cooperation between the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police’s Pacific Region, authorities said. The RCMP’s Tofinoofino General Duty, Island District GIS, Nanaimo Detachment and Island District ERT assisted in the arrest, while the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs helped secure it.

If convicted in the Hawaii case, Lang faces a mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison and up to 30 years behind bars. He could also face a fine of up to $250,000 and supervised release of between five years and life.

title: Mamdani launches fast-track housing-court push, says landlords unable to comply ‘should not be a landlord’
summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced New York City's Unified Court System will fast-track emergency housing court cases involving vacate orders and violations.
story: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday announced the Unified Court System, a fast-tracking system for emergency housing court cases in New York to protect tenant safety. Under the new initiative, judges will expedite egregious cases of landlord negligence and require parties to return to court within five days.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Tuesday the debut of the city's new Unified Court System, a mechanism to fast-track emergency cases in New York City Housing Court.

"I am proud to announce that the Unified Court System will now fast-track emergency housing court cases where the health, safety and well-being of New Yorkers is at risk," Mamdani said during a Tuesday news conference.
The new system will reduce the time tenants face to have emergency hearings on potential negligence from landlords, Mamdani explained.

"This fast track will accelerate the cases that are both the most egregious and the most complex. Cases where at least one third of units in a building are subject to an open vacate order. Where families have been forced from their homes. Cases where at least one third of the units have an open and immediately hazardous violation for essential services," he announced.
MANHATTAN BUILDING STABILIZED, SOME EVACUATIONS LIFTED AFTER COLLAPSE FEARED
Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks at a press conference in Manhattan Housing Court in New York City. (Michael Brochstein/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

In cases of "persistent and extreme negligence" where tenants request entirely new building management, judges will require parties to return to court "within five days after service is completed," Mamdani announced.
NYC RENT BOARD DISSENTER WARNS MAMDANI-BACKED FREEZE COULD HURT AFFORDABLE HOUSING OVER TIME: 'SLOW BURN'

When asked how his office would differentiate between a landlord who was persistently negligent and one who simply couldn't afford to keep up with the costs of building management, Mamdani did not hold back.
"We're talking about cases where a third of the building is facing some kind of a serious violation. Cases where we have elevators broken down," he started.
MAMDANI RIPPED OVER 'FREAK SHOW' NEWS CONFERENCE WHERE EVICTION WAS DECLARED A FORM OF 'VIOLENCE'

"When it comes to the law, everyone has to follow it. And for far too long that has somehow not been understood when it comes to housing in our city. If a landlord is not able to follow the law, then they should not be a landlord of that property," he replied.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a press conference in Manhattan Housing Court in New York City on Aug. 25, 2026. (Michael Brochstein/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
When asked about how to enforce any violators who might not appear to Housing Court after the five-day window, Mamdani said, "There is still a lot of work to follow through on."
Fox News Digital contacted the mayor's office for further comment.

title: NYC mom survives neck-slash attack on hiking trip in Arizona: 'I can’t die like this'
summary: Ring camera footage captures New York City mother Alexis Rowan fighting for her life after a stranger slashed her neck on an Arizona birthday hike.
story: Footage shows 27-year-old hiker Alexis Rowan’s struggle to escape a neck-slashing attacker, followed by the accused arrest and helicopter transfer into federal custody.

A birthday hiking trip of a lifetime wound up being a death-defying fight for her life for a New York City mother of two, leaving her neck slashed, her hand stabbed, as well as physical and emotional scars that left 13 stitches and a nightmare that will never be forgotten.

Alexis Rowan, 27, survived the northern Arizona mountain-hike attack only because of screams that were heard by a woman in a nearby home, forcing the suspect to flee, harrowing doorbell camera footage showed.

"I was like, oh my God, my neck: I can't die like this, this is not the way," Alexis Rowan told WABC after returning to New York City after last week's ordeal on a tourist mountain hike in Arizona. "I have my kids to go home to."
NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING'

Ring camera footage captures a hiker, 27, in the Arizona mountains fighting for her life from the ground below a neck-slashing attacker, who only flees with a nearby woman comes out of the door after hearing her harrowing screams for help. (FOX 10 Phoenix)
Graphic photos shared by the New York Post showed the deep slash left on her neck and the 10 stitches that closed it, along with three more from being stabbed in the hand.
She never wants "to look at another mountain again," she told the Post, while the lasting scar will remind her of the horror with every look in the mirror.

On the Wednesday, Aug. 19, hike at the Havasupai Indian Reservation – just one day after her 27th birthday – Alexis was left briefly behind a friend when the suspect approached. The suspect, identified as Taylor Nardo Paya, 29, is a Havasupai tribe member with a rap sheet that included a guilty plea to assault, according to FOX 10 Phoenix.
GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL
Ring camera footage showed Arizona mountain hiker Alexis Rowan, 27, fighting her attacker who had just slashed her neck with a knife as she bleeds profusely. (FOX 10 Phoenix/Ring)

"It was the first person that I've seen in the village, and I said, 'Hey, excuse me, is that the gift shop?'" Rowan told WABC in one of the few interviews she granted. Fox News Digital reached out to her and her mother for an interview, but they have yet to respond.
"I kept walking, I went to go in and that's when he just came up from behind," she continued, "and as soon as I felt my neck, I'm like, 'Oh my God, I'm going to die.'"

Footage showed Rowan fighting for her life as she was dragged by the hair from the ground – with her screams finally bringing a woman to open the door and causing the suspect to flee. The video obtained by Fox News Digital did not have the sound of the screams, but they were key to the suspect fleeing, according to reports.
REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF COLLEGE STUDENT’S MURDER WAS KNOWN ‘THREAT’ AFTER PRIOR ARREST: VICTIM’S MOM

Federal police usher the neck-slashing suspect off after arresting him using the pings to the cellphone he reportedly stole from Alexis Rowan, 27, video from local authorities showed. (FOX 10 Phoenix)

"I'm just so grateful for the woman that opened the door that heard her screams; it's something you can never unhear," Tricia Rowan, Alexis' mother, told WABC of the "angel sent from heaven" woman who opened the door to help.

"She's a fighter. She fought to make sure she's coming home to her babies, and she's my baby. So I'm so glad she made it," Tricia Rowan said. "He picked the wrong one. My daughter is a fighter, she is a warrior. She wasn’t going to take it."
SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS
Federal police usher the neck-slashing suspect off to the helicopter, video from local authorities showed. (FOX 10 Phoenix)
Alexis Rowan told the Post she was "mentally aware" of the "danger" after her initial interaction with Paya.

"My gut instinct was like, ‘This is not OK. I’m not OK,’" she said, adding that the "next person may not be as strong, may not be prepared mentally that someone is going to attack them or able to put them in danger."
Reservation police located Paya the following day by pinging Rowan’s phone, which prosecutors say he allegedly stole after it fell from one of her backpacks.
WOMAN ALLEGEDLY CHOKED SUBWAY RIDER, YELLED ANTISEMITIC REMARKS IN ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO: POLICE

Alexis Rowan, 27, is holding her slashed and bloodied neck as she walks up to the home of the woman that came out of the house to scare off her attacker, saving her life, Ring camera footage showed. (FOX 10 Phoenix/Ring)

He was arrested and later taken into federal custody because the alleged attack occurred on tribal land, according to reports. Video obtained by Fox News Digital showed Paya being cuffed and taken away on a golf cart by federal police before another video showed him in an orange jumpsuit being perp-walked to a helicopter.

Paya faces a federal assault with a deadly weapon charge, according to FOX 10. Court records show Paya pleaded guilty in 2016 to robbing and assaulting another woman in a 2015 attack, for which he received a five-year prison sentence and was ordered to undergo sex offender treatment and counseling.
The victim's mother wants to see the perpetrator locked up indefinitely.
"People are evil," she told the Post, calling him "a threat to society" and someone "you cannot rehabilitate."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"There is no place on earth that they belong," she added, "other than behind bars like an animal in a cage because they’re predators and they prey on innocent victims."

title: Mystery trio in headlamps and overalls emerges from Manhattan manhole, prompting NYPD probe
summary: The NYPD is reviewing surveillance video after three people in overalls and headlamps were caught emerging from a Manhattan manhole near Penn Station.
story: The NYPD is investigating the Aug. 18 incident, with detectives saying they believe migrants sometimes go into the sewers to look for valuables. (Ricardy Fabre via Storyful)
The New York Police Department is investigating after video showing three people in overalls and headlamps emerging from a Manhattan manhole went viral on social media.
The NYPD confirmed to Fox News Digital that the incident occurred on Aug. 18 at 4:19 a.m. on the southeast corner of 32nd Street and Seventh Avenue, which is near Penn Station.
No arrests have been made in this case, but police said they are reviewing surveillance video.
NYPD detectives told WABC that they believe many of the people who have been caught on camera doing this are migrants searching for valuables in the sewers.
WOMAN DIES AFTER PLUNGING INTO UNCOVERED MANHOLE OUTSIDE LUXURY STORES
A video posted to social media captured three individuals exiting a manhole on Aug. 18, 2026, near Penn Station. This is the first person to climb out onto the sidewalk. (Ricardy Fabre via Storyful)
Detectives said a scavenger culture exists in nations like Venezuela.
City officials have said that sneaking into manholes is both illegal and "extremely dangerous."
Another individual seen exiting the manhole on Aug. 18. The NYPD is investigating this incident. (Ricardy Fabre via Storyful)
NYPD INVESTIGATING AFTER SURVEILLANCE VIDEO CAPTURES GROUP ENTERING SEWERS THROUGH MANHOLES

"DEP has inspected the sewers at the location, and our infrastructure is safe. DEP works closely with our public safety partners to help ensure the safety and security of critical infrastructure throughout New York City," the city's Department of Environmental Protection said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

The statement continued: "Entering the sewer system is both illegal and extremely dangerous. Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks, and confined spaces. For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole, or outfall."
A construction worker stands near an open manhole during street maintenance works in New York City, in October 2025. (Stefan Panaitescu/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
New York City's sewer system is made up of an elaborate network of more than 7,400 miles of wastewater and stormwater pipes, parts of which date back to the 1800s.
In June, The Associated Press reported on three separate instances of people exiting manholes in Queens and the Williamsburg and Gravesend neighborhoods of Brooklyn.
Many of them were wearing headlamps and were carrying shovels or other tools when they were caught on video.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Former TOPGUN pilot analyzes Marine Corps pilot's eerie calm after emergency F-18 ejection
summary: Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew Buckley explains the violent forces of ejection and why Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon appeared so calm after his F-18 crash.
story: Matthew "Whiz" Buckley, who flew combat missions in Iraq, told Fox News Digital what goes through a fighter pilot’s mind when ejecting from an aircraft traveling hundreds of miles per hour.

Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew "Whiz" Buckley told Fox News Digital that the recent crash of a Marine Corps F-18 in Washington state — and the pilot's split-second decision to eject — highlights both the violence of the maneuver and how the ensuing shock can leave an aviator feeling eerily calm.

On June 13, 2026, Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon emerged from a wooded area with a bloodied face and walked down the road toward a Yakima County sheriff’s deputy, whose bodycam captured the pilot appearing remarkably composed.
"I'm a little frazzled," was about as close as Simon came to expressing fear after his F-18 Hornet crashed into the forest and sparked a small wildfire near Rimrock Lake.

Buckley, who flew F-18 Hornets during his 15-year career in the U.S. Navy, said Simon was likely experiencing a combination of shock, an adrenaline letdown and the effects of training that teaches pilots to compartmentalize under pressure.
EIGHT BELIEVED DEAD AFTER B-52 CRASHES SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF FROM EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE

Marine Maj. Simon Jackson holds a Yakima County Sheriff’s deputy's cellphone after calling his superiors to flatly tell them "Pilot ejected; pilot safe" and casually, "Hey buddy, Maj. Simon, I just crashed." (Yakima County Sheriff’s Office bodycam footage)
"If anything's going wrong, we focus on the task. Everything else goes away," Buckley told Fox News Digital. "That was the most violent thing that ever happened to that Marine in his entire life."
Buckley served as a pilot in the Navy from 1991 to 2006 and said he was fortunate never to have ejected from an aircraft. The experience can have a devastating toll on the human body.
"Some folks don't go back to flying status. I mean, you can lose a couple inches in height. Your spine compresses. Some people get shorter," Buckley said.

A meta-analysis of more than a dozen studies looking at 1,710 military aircrew ejections found a pooled mortality rate of 10.5%, while 29.8% suffered major injuries. The studies were published between 1971 and 2019.
A photo of Matthew "Whiz" Buckley in the cockpit of an F-18 Hornet. Buckley flew as a pilot in the U.S. Navy from 1991 to 2006. (Courtesy of Matthew Buckley)
ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE

"When you pull that handle, you have two choices: die or maybe live. And I said 'maybe live' because it's incredibly violent. I think the average ejection seat is like 10 to 20 G's of force," Buckley added. "Most folks don't even remember the ejection. They remember pulling the handle and then waking up in their parachute."

Buckley said the pilot's body positioning before the ejection is extremely important in preventing potentially life-threatening injuries. For example, if their arm is extended away from their body, the sudden wind blast could cause it to be "ripped out of the socket."
There's also a phenomenon called "seat slap," which occurs if the pilot does not have their legs flush with the seat prior to ejecting.

"If you look at an ejection seat in a fighter jet, it's rock hard. We're not sitting on a cushion," he said. "If your legs aren't flat on the seat, it could break both of your legs and now you bleed out and die."
A military photograph of an F-18 Hornet that was being piloted by Maj. Jackson Simon at Naval Air Station Key West, Florida, on June 5, 2024. (U.S. Marine Corps)
US NAVY IDENTIFIES SAILOR LOST IN ARABIAN SEA AFTER HELICOPTER'S EMERGENCY WATER LANDING
In some instances, pilots who find themselves in trouble have time to slow their aircraft and perform a controlled ejection, which can reduce the forces involved, Buckley said.
Based on video of the crash, Simon’s plane was traveling at a high rate of speed before it struck the trees and exploded, likely leaving little opportunity for a controlled ejection.
Simon had been performing low-flying maneuvers while spectators on the ground watched, according to KIRO 7. After that, his plane reportedly clipped some power lines, which led to it going down.
The Marine Corps has not publicly confirmed that Simon’s F-18 struck power lines before the crash and has said the cause of the mishap remains under investigation.
UNITED AIRLINES JET FLEW TOO LOW AND TOO SLOW BEFORE STRIKING LIGHT POLE AND TRUCK NEAR NEWARK AIRPORT: NTSB
According to Buckley, this "clearly" wasn't supposed to happen.

"We have minimum altitude restrictions. And there ain't no 500-foot trees, right? So I don't know what they were doing. It doesn't sound like from his initial statement that there was anything wrong with the airplane. So that's usually not a good sign," Buckley said.
Buckley then speculated about what may have been going through Simon’s mind before the crash.

"It looked like a beautiful day. People out on a lake. 'Hey, there's some people down there on the lake. Why don't we go show them what their tax money is [for]? You know, America.' I hope it wasn't something like that," he said.
A photo of Matthew Buckley on the floor of the Chicago Board of Trade. (Courtesy of Matthew Buckley)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the third Marine Aircraft Wing, the West Coast-based Marine aviation unit to which Simon’s aircraft was assigned.

Buckley said Simon will likely go before a review board that will evaluate his actions surrounding the crash. At the conclusion of the process, the board can recommend what should happen to an aviator’s flight status.
If he's found to be at fault, Simon could lose his "wings" or he could be allowed to continue flying, just under what Buckley described as "double secret probation."
"I don't know what the board's gonna do, but it'll come out. It should because...this is a $60 to $65 million Hornet. We deserve to know what happened," he added.

title: Georgia sheriff seizes 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana shipped from California
summary: A 1,800-pound black market marijuana shipment from Sacramento, California, was intercepted in Georgia, reportedly bound for Atlanta and Orlando.
story: Daily marijuana use in America is rising, prompting family physician Dr. Jessica Gray to address common safety myths. She notes that cannabis being plant-based does not make it inherently safe. Gray also cites a JAMA Internal Medicine review showing insufficient evidence that cannabis effectively treats anxiety or insomnia, warning that accessing marijuana has become easier than finding mental health counseling.
A massive shipment of 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana from California was intercepted in Georgia on Tuesday, with authorities saying the drugs were destined for Atlanta and Orlando.

The shipment originated in Sacramento, where recreational marijuana is legal, according to the Butts County Sheriff’s Office. Sheriff Gary Long said about half of the marijuana was bound for Atlanta, while the rest was headed to Orlando.
The sheriff’s office did not say where or how the shipment was intercepted, whether anyone was arrested or whether charges were filed.
NY TIMES WALKS BACK STANCE ON MARIJUANA LEGALIZATION, ADMITS LOOSENING OF POLICIES HAS MADE COUNTRY WORSE OFF
The shipment, which originated in Sacramento, California, was intercepted in Butts County, Georgia, authorities said. (Facebook/Butts County Sheriff's Office)
Long used the seizure to make his case that legalizing marijuana does not eliminate illegal sales.
"But here is the reality: the black market isn't going away," Long said in a press release announcing the seizure.
Marijuana laws vary among the three states connected to the shipment. California allows recreational marijuana, while Georgia and Florida allow marijuana only for certain medical uses.
"The illegal marijuana trade does not stop at the state line," Long said.
Authorities seized about 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana. (Facebook/Butts County Sheriff's Office)

Long said Mexican drug-trafficking organizations and other criminal groups continue to move large amounts of marijuana across state lines. The sheriff’s office did not say the shipment seized Tuesday was connected to a cartel or any other criminal organization.
The sheriff also argued that illegal sellers can undercut licensed marijuana businesses because they don't pay taxes or licensing fees or have to follow testing and other regulatory requirements.
"As long as there is demand and money to be made, illegal dealers will continue to operate," Long said.
AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING
Long urged Georgia lawmakers to look closely at what has happened in states that have legalized marijuana before making changes to Georgia's laws.
Butts County Sheriff Gary Long said about half of the marijuana was bound for Atlanta, while the rest was headed to Orlando. (Facebook/Butts County Sheriff's Office)

He pointed to California, which has changed its cannabis tax and regulatory system while continuing to fight illegal marijuana sales. He also cited past ballot initiatives filed in Colorado seeking to repeal constitutional provisions that legalized recreational marijuana, though those efforts did not reverse legalization.

"That should be a warning to Georgia," Long said. "We should learn from the experiences of states that have already gone down this road instead of repeating the same mistakes and then spending years trying to fix them."

Long said his statement was not meant to settle the question of whether marijuana should be legal. Instead, he argued that lawmakers need to consider how illegal sales and trafficking would fit into any changes to Georgia law.

"Georgia, let's get it right the first time," Long said.

title: Jury convicts Kevin Salazar in execution-style killing of LA Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer
summary: Kevin Salazar was convicted of murdering Los Angeles County Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer in a 2023 drive-by ambush near his Palmdale station.
story: Brad Gage, who represents the family of Los Angeles Sheriff's Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer, says the guilty verdict against Kevin Salazar provides some solace — but the suspect's motives remain unclear.
A California man has been convicted in the drive-by ambush of a Los Angeles deputy shot and killed at a red light just steps from the sheriff's Palmdale station in 2023.
Jurors found Kevin Salazar, 32, guilty of the murder of Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer Monday after a week-long trial.

"It’s very helpful that the justice system prevail, that you have a conviction that is a benefit to the family," Brad Gage, the Los Angeles attorney representing Clinkunbroomer's family, told Fox News Digital. "That gives some solace. That gives some comfort."
MURDERED LOS ANGELES SHERIFF'S DEPUTY'S FAMILY SLAPS COUNTY WITH $20M WRONGFUL DEATH LAWSUIT

Attorney Bradley Gage, middle, and Kim Clinkunbroomer, left, and Mike Clinkunbroomer, the parents of late Los Angeles Sheriff's Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer, pictured left, announce the precursor of a lawsuit against the Sheriff's Department at a news conference in Los Angeles on Nov. 28, 2023. Around 6 p.m. on Sept. 16, 2023, Clinkunbroomer pulled up to a red light down the street from the sheriff's station in Palmdale. He was driving his marked car and wearing his uniform. As he waited for the light to turn green, another car pulled up alongside him – and a man inside shot him in the head.

Authorities said Salazar had followed Clinkunbroomer from the Palmdale Sheriff's Station to the intersection less than a block away before opening fire with a .22 revolver. He sped off, and Clinkunbroomer was pronounced dead at a hospital.
Authorities found Salazar at his family's home in Palmdale two days later and arrested him on murder charges after a standoff, part of which was caught on video.

"When a parent loses a child, there’s no name for it," Gage said. "It’s so painful, it’s so traumatic, it is so devastating that it is beyond words."

Jurors deliberated for just 2 1/2 hours before finding Salazar guilty of first-degree murder as well as the special circumstance allegations of murder of a peace officer, lying in wait and firing from a vehicle, according to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office.
Despite the conviction, a motive remains unclear, according to the family's attorney.
Los Angeles County Sheriff's Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer was shot Sept. 16, 2023. (Los Angeles Sheriff's Department)
"As far as we know, there was no reason," Gage told Fox News Digital. "It was just execution of a police officer."
The court will move on Wednesday to a sanity-deciding phase for Salazar, to determine whether he goes to prison or is confined in a state mental hospital after he raised an insanity defense.

title: Air Force officer who died in Alaska plane crash remembered as 'positive leader'
summary: The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah Borsich, 23, as a victim of the deadly Alaska charter plane crash that killed all eight on board near Cape Newenham.
story: A plane that crashed at a remote military site in western Alaska, killing all eight people on board, was making its second runway approach in heavy fog when it lost contact, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, told a virtual news conference.

A 23-year-old Air Force officer killed alongside seven others in a charter plane crash in remote western Alaska last week is being remembered as a "positive leader" who served with "professionalism, compassion and purpose."

The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah R. Borsich on Monday as one of the victims of the Aug. 20 crash near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, about 450 miles west-southwest of Anchorage. Borsich was a project programmer with the 611th Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson.

"Lt. Borsich was a positive leader who brought tremendous energy and enthusiasm to our command," Col. Timothy Meerstein, commander of the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center, said in a statement.
TWO US ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS EMPLOYEES AMONG 8 KILLED IN ALASKA CHARTER PLANE CRASH
The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah R. Borsich on Monday as one of the victims of the Aug. 20 crash near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport. (Facebook/ Leah Borsich)

"She led with professionalism, compassion and purpose, and her presence strengthened the bonds between the people around her," Meerstein said. "She made a lasting impact on our team, and we are grateful for her service and commitment to our nation."
The Cessna 441 was carrying two pilots and six passengers when it crashed west of Cape Newenham at about 12:15 p.m. Thursday. All eight people aboard were killed.

The charter plane had taken off from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport and was headed to Cape Newenham when it crashed during its second approach to the gravel runway in heavy fog, according to federal officials.

The pilots could not see the runway and were flying by instruments, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, said Friday. They aborted their first landing attempt because of poor visibility before crashing on the second approach.

An observation system near the airport reported fog and visibility of about 10 miles shortly before the crash. About 15 minutes later, visibility had fallen to less than a quarter-mile, according to the National Weather Service.
Search teams later found fragmented wreckage from the twin-engine plane, also known as a Cessna Conquest.
NTSB investigators document the accident site Aug. 23, 2026, of the Cessna 441 airplane that crashed near Cape Newenham, Alaska, on Aug. 20, 2026. (NTSB via AP)
The Air Force said an Army member, contractors and crew members with Anchorage-based airplane charter company Security Aviation were also among those killed.

"We also mourn the loss of our Army and contractor teammates and extend our deepest appreciation to the Security Aviation aircrew, whose professionalism and dedication are vital to our mission," Meerstein said. "Their service and sacrifice will not be forgotten."
Security Aviation, which operated the flight, said it was "heartbroken" by the crash.

"Our hearts go out to the families, friends and loved ones of those who were lost," the company said in a statement posted to Facebook. "We extend our deepest condolences to them and to everyone affected by this devastating tragedy."

Security Aviation thanked the military, Alaska Rescue Coordination Center and search-and-recovery teams that responded after the crash. The company said it is cooperating with the investigation and would not speculate about the cause.
"Our focus at this time is on those who are grieving and on supporting our employees and others affected by this tremendous loss," the company said.

In addition to the pilots, those aboard included two U.S. Army Corps of Engineers employees and four contractors. Two of the contractors worked for Calista Brice, which provides construction, engineering, logistics and other services in remote areas.
ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE

The Army Corps said its employees were part of a "project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force." Officials have not said what work the group was traveling to perform.

Cape Newenham is part of a network of remote radar sites that monitors aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders. The site, built in the 1950s as part of an early-warning network against a potential Soviet attack, now monitors the skies off Alaska’s coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China.
Borsich’s name was released after her family had been notified. The Alaska State Troopers will release the names of the victims who were not affiliated with the Department of War, the Air Force said.
Two U.S. Army Corps of Engineers employees were among the eight who were killed this week when a charter plane crashed in southwestern Alaska, the military confirmed Friday. (AP Photo/Andrew Harnik)

Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, who leads Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, previously described those aboard as "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment."
"This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said after the crash.

The criminal trial of a former Libyan intelligence official charged in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 was postponed by a federal judge Monday after defense attorneys said they received new evidence over the weekend from prosecutors.

The judge granted Al-Marimi’s lawyers the delay and scheduled a status hearing on Sept. 1.

Al-Marimi is charged with making the bomb that downed the Pan Am flight, killing all 259 passengers and crew members. The plane came down over the small town of Lockerbie, Scotland, where it destroyed an entire city block and killed 11 people on the ground.

Citizens of 21 countries were among the victims, including 190 Americans and 43 people from the United Kingdom. Among those aboard were 35 Syracuse University students returning home from a semester abroad.

Weipz said the families of the victims had already been packing to head to Washington for the trial.
