title: Melting Swiss glacier reveals remains of two Belgian mountaineers missing since 1992
summary: DNA testing confirmed remains found on a Swiss Alps glacier belong to two Belgian mountaineers who vanished in the Weissmies region in 1992.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A melting glacier in the Swiss Alps revealed the remains of two Belgian mountaineers who vanished more than three decades ago, authorities said Wednesday.
A hiker spotted the remains on the Trift Glacier on July 26 after melting ice exposed them, according to police in Switzerland’s Valais canton.
Authorities recovered the remains and sent them to a forensic medicine institute at a hospital in Sion for identification.
REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY
A view of the Trift suspension bridge at the Trift Glacier in Valais, Switzerland, on Jan. 2, 2018. (BlueRed/REDA/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
DNA testing showed they belonged to two Belgian men who disappeared in the Weissmies region in 1992, police said. The men were 39 and 41 when they went missing.
Valais police have kept records of missing-person cases dating to 1925. Many involve people who disappeared in the mountains or in bodies of water.
The glacial ice avalanche of the Trift Glacier above the village in Saas-Grund, Valais, Switzerland, Sunday, Sept. 10, 2017. (Dominic Steinmann/Keystone via AP, File)
WOMAN FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE ID’D AFTER 44 YEARS AS MILLIONAIRE TIED TO ESTATE MURDER PLOT
As glaciers retreat, remains hidden beneath the ice for decades can emerge, police said.
Similar discoveries have been made in Switzerland in recent years. In 2023, DNA testing identified a body found on a glacier near the Matterhorn as a German mountaineer who disappeared in 1986.
Regional police shared an image of Trift Glacier near Saas-Grund, Valais, Switzerland. (Valais Cantonal Police)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Switzerland’s glaciers have been melting at an increasing rate, a trend some scientists have linked to rising global temperatures.

title: Christian Zionists take on anti-Israel ‘propaganda’ from biblical heartland
summary: The Israel Guys inaugurated a major visitor center in Har Bracha on the West Bank, inviting Christians in Israel to see Judea and Samaria's biblical heartland firsthand.
story: CEO of The Israel Guys Joshua Waller urges Christians to ignore the propaganda and see Israel for themselves as his group opens a new visitor center in the biblical heartland.

A major visitors center in the West Bank town of Har Bracha in Samaria was inaugurated last month by The Israel Guys, a Christian Zionist organization that has spent nearly two decades bringing more than 5,000 volunteers from 35 countries to help develop the Land of Israel.

Joshua Waller, CEO of The Israel Guys, originally established as HaYovel, said the organization’s mission is to bring people to see for themselves how the biblical heartland is flourishing, despite what he says are media narratives portraying the area as beset by conflict.

"We live here, we see the people who live here, and then we tell everyone what is actually happening. Our role is to expand that and bring thousands of internationals to come and see for themselves," he told Fox News Digital.
US AMBASSADOR HUCKABEE SLAMS EXTREME GROUP OF ISRAELI SETTLERS FOR SEIZING PALESTINIAN HOMES ON WEST BANK
Joshua Waller of the Israel Guys at work on the West Bank. (The Israel Guys)

"You may love the Jewish people but be unsure how to deal with the propaganda, specifically the term ‘settler violence.’ Jews in Judea and Samaria have been branded as a radical group that would probably be dangerous to encounter. Well, come to the visitor center, and you will see the exact opposite," he said.
"You will see that it is a fake narrative built by the international community … it is a straight-up war against the Jewish [people]," he added.

The organization’s volunteer programs include the Heartland Experience, a 10-day trip to Israel combining touring, volunteer work and interaction with local residents; the Grape Harvest trip, a two-week program held in late summer and early fall that focuses on helping farmers with the harvest; and the Men’s Pruning trip, a two-week program in early spring focused on pruning vineyards.
Other programs include Zion Ops, a four-week program for young adults ages 18 to 30, and Day Visits, which offer two-hour visits to Har Bracha.
ISRAEL LAUNCHES 'BIBLICAL HIGHWAY' AMID CAMPAIGN TO ERASE JEWISH HISTORY
Volunteers working in vineyards on the West Bank are part of the Israel Guys' program that brings volunteers to Israel. (The Israel Guys)

In 2004, Tommy Waller, Joshua Waller’s father, traveled to Israel for the first time, where he met Nir Lavi, founder of Har Bracha Winery. Lavi shared his plan to fulfill the vision of the Prophet Jeremiah: "You shall again plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; the planters shall plant and eat them as ordinary food" (Jeremiah 31:5).
Waller Sr. asked how he could help.

In 2007, after moving with his wife, Sherri, and their 11 children from Tennessee to Har Bracha, Waller Sr. established HaYovel, a U.S. nonprofit that provides Christian volunteers with an opportunity to work the land alongside Israeli farmers.

In 2013, the organization sought to counter anti-Israel rhetoric by launching The Joshua & Caleb Report TV show, its first dedicated pro-Israel media project, which in 2018 transitioned into a weekly podcast. Five years ago, the organization rebranded as The Israel Guys and stepped up its advocacy efforts.
CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM
"HaYovel" volunteers from its international program work in the vineyards of Shiloh in Samaria help to pick grapes on the West Bank. (Hillel Maeir/TPS-IL)

The Israel Guys currently counts more than 20 team members and, since its founding, has helped develop some 120 farms. Volunteers who come to Judea and Samaria work alongside local farmers, planting trees, erecting fences, harvesting crops and assisting with infrastructure projects.

In the aftermath of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, massacre of 1,200 Israelis, The Israel Guys launched Operation Ittai and raised $3.85 million to provide tactical supplies to communities in the area and strengthen their defenses against possible terrorist attacks.
Anti-Israel activists protest outside the United Nations headquarters in New York on April 7, 2025. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
The group went viral at the time after bringing American cowboys to Israel to help farmers whose workers had been called up as reservists.
Addressing media coverage of recent incidents involving Christians in Israel, Waller said the narrative that they are no longer welcome in the country is false.
AMBASSADOR GEORGE DEEK: THE CHRISTIAN ISRAEL YOU ARE NOT BEING SHOWN
Josh Waller works the field in the West Bank, also known by its biblical names Judea and Samaria. (The Israel Guys)

"People put a lot of money into trying to make it seem as though Christians would somehow be better off living in Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, Jordan or other Arab countries surrounding Israel. Factually, that is completely wrong," he told Fox News Digital.

"I know Christians living in those places, and I even know Christians living in areas under the control of the Palestinian Authority, and they suffer immensely. The fact is that Israel is the safest place for Christians in the entire Middle East. It is the only place where the Christian population is growing," he added.
Volunteers, Waller explained, have come from a wide range of Christian denominations, including Catholics, Protestants, Evangelicals, Mormons, Amish and Mennonites.
The new center will include programs to support Israeli farmers, lectures on Israel and Zionism and be a place for communal meals. (The Israel Guys)
He emphasized that Israel is a partner for peace and urged nations to align themselves with biblical values, which he said could pave the way for "some incredible days ahead."

If antisemitism leads to efforts to destroy Israel, he added, "that’s not an option," saying Israel would have to fight that war while The Israel Guys would continue to "help on the information side."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The Bible says that this land that was desolate will become like the Garden of Eden. We are literally seeing it happen. It’s beautiful to see volunteers participate in the fulfillment of that prophecy and witness the ancient words of the Bible come back to life," Waller said.
Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: Dolly Parton through the years, in photos: From ‘9 to 5’ secretary to ‘Hannah Montana’ godmother
summary: Until she died Tuesday at age 80, Dolly Parton was the beloved Queen of Country music.
story: Dolly Parton craved the camera.

And until she died Tuesday at age 80, the Queen of Country’s life unspooled in photograph after photograph, turning the poor little girl with the angelic voice from eastern Tennessee into one of America’s most beloved — and recognizable — figures.
It was country singer Porter Wagoner who first introduced Parton to a wider audience when he invited her in 1967 to appear on his hit TV show.
By 1974, Parton was out on her own, and her signature public image — the blond wigs, the cleavage-baring outfits that showed off her hourglass figure — was cast in stone.

Soon Hollywood beckoned, and Parton took it by storm, winning a Grammy for her single “Here You Come Again” and appearing in a string of hit movies that eventually earned her a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1984.

Bubbly and witty, Parton was also a must-book guest on the small screen: She made more than 400 television appearances, performing on variety shows hosted by the likes of Cher and Mac Davis, and charming late-night and daytime hosts ranging from Johnny Carson and his successor, Jay Leno, to Oprah Winfrey and Conan O’Brien.
Parton also hosted not one, but two TV variety shows, both called “Dolly,” which millions of Americans tuned in to watch.

And in 1989, she even took a turn at hosting “Saturday Night Live,” where, during the opening monologue, the running gag was her cracking jokes while the cameraman was unable to focus on anything but her bosom.
Her duets with performers ranging from Elton John and Kenny Rogers to Miley Cyrus spanned the generational divide; she became the rarest of performers — one whose fan base expanded as she grew older.
With the acclaim came the awards, the invitations to give commencement speeches, the honorary degrees, the chance to perform before thousands of fans at big-time sports events.

But there was a part of Parton’s life she mostly kept hidden from America’s prying eyes, the part she is said to have cherished most — her nearly 59-year marriage to her husband, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025.
Dean almost never appeared in public with his famous wife and, as a result, there were very few photos of them together available to the public.
And they were fine with that.

“I’ve kept [my marriage] very personal and sacred and I try to keep my husband out of the business,” she said in an interview. “That’s not what he chose to do, he just happened to love me and I love him enough to not expose him to it.”

title: The second Dan Sullivan makes the general election in Alaska’s Senate race
summary: NBC News projects that GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Republican Dan J. Sullivan will face off in the general election alongside former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
story: Former teacher Dan J. Sullivan will join Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola on the general election ballot in Alaska’s Senate race, NBC News projects.

Republicans have criticized the other Sullivan’s candidacy as a potential ploy to confuse voters in a key battleground race, which he has denied. Alaska’s election system might also blunt the impact of any confusion. The top four candidates, regardless of party, advance from Alaska’s all-party primary to a ranked-choice general election, meaning voters could rank both Sullivans.
But some voters end up ranking only one candidate, which could matter in a close race — and Alaska’s Senate race could be one of the closest in the country this year.

Democrats have targeted Alaska as an opportunity to flip a seat since well before the same-name saga consumed the race, even though President Donald Trump carried the state by double digits in each of the last three presidential elections.

Peltola, a former state legislator and city council member, became the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress when she won a statewide special election in 2022 and then a full term months later. Peltola lost her seat after one term by 3 percentage points, running well ahead of Vice President Kamala Harris at the top of the Democratic ticket in 2024.
Sullivan was first elected to the Senate in 2014, defeating a Democratic incumbent, and re-elected in 2020. A former Marine, he has touted his work for veterans and the state’s fishing industry.

His campaign and Republican allies have criticized the other Sullivan as a potential Democratic plant, noting that he only recently registered as a Republican and got help with his campaign launch from a Democratic consultant.

State and federal prosecutors are investigating whether his candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. The federal investigation is moving forward, with a law enforcement official telling NBC News that a grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to the Dan J. Sullivan campaign.

The candidate told The New York Times that he registered as a Republican because his previous political party, the Alaska Independence Party, no longer exists. He declined to detail his involvement with the Democratic consultant because of the ongoing investigation.

title: Trump-backed Mike Mazzei wins the GOP nomination in the Oklahoma governor’s race
summary: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei has secured the Republican nomination for governor in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump’s preferred candidate.
story: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei has secured the Republican nomination for governor in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump’s preferred candidate.
Mazzei narrowly defeated state Attorney General Gentner Drummond by about 2,000 votes in the GOP primary runoff.

The initial June primary was also tight. Drummond finished in first place by just more than 1,000 votes over Mazzei. Since no candidate in the crowded field secured a majority, the race went to a runoff.

In the weeks leading up to the runoff, Drummond outraised and outspent Mazzei, with his campaign reporting last week that he brought in $2.3 million between the mid-June primary and Tuesday’s runoff. Mazzei, in the same time period, raised $816,000.
Both candidates have also loaned their campaigns significant sums: $11 million for Mazzei and $3 million for Drummond.
Trump first endorsed Mazzei in May in the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt and continued to reiterate his support for the former state lawmaker.

In a post on Truth Social last week, Trump praised Mazzei and criticized Drummond, writing, “Drummond is not the right guy. He’s got a bad attitude, and he doesn’t stand for the Values of Oklahoma, which must VOTE FOR ‘MIKE MAZZEI FOR GOVERNOR,’ on Tuesday, August 25th.”
Drummond also drew the president’s ire for suing to block the construction of the largest aluminum smelter in the country in Inola, Oklahoma, citing environmental and public health concerns.

“He wants to dethrone a magnificent, Job producing, desperately needed, and brand new, Aluminum Plant that will be one of the best projects ever conceived or built, not only in the Great State of Oklahoma, but in the United States, itself,” Trump wrote in the Truth Social post earlier this month.
Mazzei, on the other hand, supports construction of the plant.
This week, Drummond also broke with the president on his decision last week to waive tariffs on some beef imports in an attempt to lower beef prices in the U.S.

“I think Oklahoma and I are supportive of President Trump and many of his policies. I do think the majority of Oklahomans would agree that the tariffs are too far, that importing cheap beef only injures Oklahoma’s cattlemen, ranchers and farmers,” Drummond told NewsNation, echoing the concerns of GOP lawmakers in the House and Senate from states with large cattle-ranching communities.

While Trump’s endorsement remains the most coveted in GOP politics, he has had some stumbles, particularly in governor’s races. Five gubernatorial candidates he has backed this year failed to win their primaries.

With his victory Tuesday, Mazzei is the heavy favorite to win November’s general election, given the state’s deeply Republican voter base. He’ll face Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in the general election.

title: Democratic socialists notch another win in the Oklahoma Senate primary runoff
summary: Nurse N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas has won the Democratic Senate nomination in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, defeating an older, more moderate opponent.
story: Nurse N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas has won the Democratic Senate primary runoff in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, securing another win for the party’s democratic socialist wing.

Thomas, a 31-year-old member of the Chickasaw Nation, defeated attorney and minister Jim Priest, 70, in the contest, despite being drastically outspent. The two advanced to a runoff after neither clinched a majority of the vote in the initial June primary.

Thomas will face GOP Rep. Kevin Hern, who will be heavily favored this fall to win the open seat to replace former Sen. Markwayne Mullin, now the secretary of homeland security. Oklahoma is a solidly Republican state that President Donald Trump won by 34 points in 2024.

Thomas’ primary victory comes as progressive candidates have made inroads across the country this year. Democratic socialists have won a handful of high-profile primaries in recent weeks, including in Florida’s Senate race and a key House battleground in Michigan.

Thomas is “a self-proclaimed democratic socialist,” she told NBC News in an interview Tuesday morning, though she said she is “not yet” a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. She described democratic socialists as “the next generation” that is “looking to change the system.”

Thomas said that she does not support every plank of the DSA platform. A military spouse, Thomas said she does not support defunding the Defense Department. She did voice support for a slew of progressive policies, including Medicare for All, universal childcare and parental leave, and “making sure that everyone pays their fair share.” Thomas said she also favors abolishing the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.
“The system right now doesn’t work for us and it never has,” said Thomas, noting her pitch to voters is focused on healthcare, as rural areas in the state are struggling with access to quality care.

Asked if she considered herself a capitalist or a socialist, Thomas said, “Capitalism is what’s destroying our country right now,” but she later described capitalism as “inevitable,” saying she supports the concept of people owning their own businesses and property.
Thomas said fellow democratic socialists were finding success in some primaries this year as voters are clamoring for change and “people-first” and “family-first” policies.
“I’m just ready for change and I think everyone else is as well,” she said.
Like some other progressive candidates who have prevailed in primaries this year, Thomas was outspent in the primary by a more moderate opponent.

Priest’s campaign has spent $315,000 so far, while Thomas’ campaign has spent $57,000, according to campaign finance reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. She is also starting the general election at a massive financial disadvantage: Thomas had just $456 in her campaign account as of Aug. 5, while Hern’s campaign had $2.6 million on hand as of June 30.

title: Trump administration says it might demolish the Kennedy Center if court blocks renovations
summary: Justice Department attorneys called the Kennedy Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the Nation’s Capital.”
story: The Trump administration is, for the first time, threatening the demolition of the Kennedy Center if the arts institution isn’t allowed to follow its plans for the site, including adding President Donald Trump’s name to the front of the building.

“Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers wrote in a court filing on Monday.
The filing notes that any potential outdoor amphitheater would “fail to adequately honor” President John F. Kennedy, “but would be simpler and more economical to build, operate, and maintain.”
The DOJ attorneys called the Kennedy Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the Nation’s Capital.”

They said the center’s board, which was handpicked by self-appointed chairman Trump, “recognizes that President Trump’s efforts and prestige provide the sole hope for the Center’s financial survival, and structural renewal.”

“The Board also underscores, and the undisputed evidence demonstrates, that without the prominent recognition of The Trump Administration, and President Trump’s efforts, the donors will not contribute, and the Center will continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral. The Trump Administration, and President Donald J. Trump, should, therefore, be given the respect and dignity of acknowledgement,” the filing says.

It notes that Trump “obtained $258 million in funding from Congress for capital restoration, and has marshalled a new donor base to finance an endowment for the Center,” but does not say what has happened to that money.

The filing makes a dramatic twist in the monthslong saga to renovate the historic arts institution, which has faced multiple legal challenges and criticism from Democrats, musicians and members of the Kennedy family.
Add to Google
Add to Google

This language is a shift from what Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca has used in recent months to describe what the board has said are necessary renovations. Floca has said the renovations would include a “total replacement of stage lifts and rigging systems” and wide-ranging electrical work and leak prevention that could be completed within two years if the facility was shut down during the renovations.

He said in a court filing earlier this year that the “exterior of the Center’s main building will not be materially affected” and “the planned construction, renovation, and renewal efforts will not tear down the Center to its structural steel.”

A spokesperson for the center said Tuesday that the language in the filing “describes a hypothetical scenario of what could happen if the center’s desperately needed renovation is blocked by partisan interests.”
A center official had previously said the facility would not be gutted.

“You’re not going to be able to stand in Georgetown and look over the river and see through the building,” the official told reporters during a tour of the facility in April. “That’s not what’s going to happen.”
Mayers’ filing Monday suggested only Trump and his people could save the arts institution.

The administration has “committed an enormous amount of time and energy in planning for the forthcoming renovation and restoration of this building, a task which President Trump, given his unrivaled expertise and experience in real estate and construction, and prominence as President, is uniquely qualified to accomplish,” Mayers wrote Monday in opposition to a motion from Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, to block the administration from closing the center completely.

“Even Beatty should prefer a healthy, restored Center to a decaying hulk that is doomed to inevitable destruction or collapse. The Court should allow the Board and President Trump to bring the Center back to a level of greatness far higher than it has ever had before. This would be the fitting tribute that President Kennedy so well deserves.”
Beatty has claimed the closure decision was rushed and that board members weren’t presented with enough information about various scenarios before having to vote on it.
The congresswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the DOJ filing.

She is challenging the Trump-appointed board’s renewed bid to add Trump’s name to the front of the building. A judge found the board’s earlier bid to do so was unlawful and compelled it to remove the president’s name from the building, which is supposed to be a “living memorial” to the slain president.

Trump is appealing and the board voted this month to add his name back to the building in a slightly different way- going from the since-stricken “The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts” to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”
There is a hearing scheduled on the planned name change and closure in D.C. on Thursday afternoon. The judge said in his earlier decision that only Congress has the power to rename the site.

title: Immigrant dad of USS Lincoln sailor is released from ICE detention
summary: Joshua Aviles posted a family statement on Facebook saying his father, Luis Manuel Aviles, “has been released back to our family.”
story: The immigrant father of a sailor who is on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln is back with his family Tuesday after being detained by immigration authorities over the weekend.

The family confirmed the release of Luis Manuel Aviles in a statement posted on social media by his son Joshua Aviles, a Navy handling airman. Joshua Aviles has been deployed on the aircraft carrier for nine months, which is considered a U.S. military record for uninterrupted time at sea.

“Luis has been released back to our family. We are grateful for all of the support for both Luis and Josh throughout this situation. At this moment, our family is taking time to be together. While we await the return of our proud Navy sailor, we kindly ask for your understanding and respect,” the statement reads.
The Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to multiple requests for comment about the release of Luis Manuel Aviles.
USS Abraham Lincoln to return home amid condition concerns

DHS confirmed over the weekend that Border Patrol arrested Luis Manuel Aviles on Saturday during a traffic stop in Key West, Florida, where the family lives. The agency said he entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and was being held in ICE custody.

Originally from Nicaragua, Luis Manuel Aviles, 47, has been living in the U.S. for 20 years. He’s mostly worked as a handyman for hotels in Key West, according to his youngest son, Luis Aviles, and stepdaughter, Katty Delgado.

In an interview with Noticias Telemundo on Sunday, Luis Aviles said his father “never hid, he always did things the right way,” adding that he was working toward getting legal status and had complied with his paperwork and visits to ICE’s offices.

Delgado told NBC News on Saturday that her stepfather had a work permit, a Social Security card, a driver’s license and an active asylum case. Joshua Aviles, along with another family member, had filed immigration petitions requesting he remain in the country legally, according to the family.

Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS said in an email Sunday, “Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.”
“Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the email reads.

On the same weekend in which Luis Manuel Aviles was detained, the Key West Immigrant Support Network had been alerting immigrant communities in the area of an uptick in “immigration activity” following the detentions of three people Thursday afternoon.

“We saw this surge of officers we didn’t recognize. We saw cars that we didn’t recognize,” said Heather Slivko-Bathurst, the director of the nonprofit immigrant rights organization. “All of a sudden, boom! It was 28 people detained in 72 hours.”
After months of quiet immigration detentions, Slivko-Bathurst told NBC News, immigrant communities in Key West “saw this resurgence of almost like an operative type.”

DHS and Customs and Border Protection did not respond to questions about their enforcement operations in Key West in recent weeks. They said in an email that “ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day,” and cited the cases of several convicted criminals who were arrested in Florida.

Slivko-Bathurst said the presence of Border Patrol in the area seemed particularly heightened Saturday morning, prompting the Key West Immigrant Support Network to share a post on Facebook at 9 a.m. saying, “If there is ever a day to be as careful as possible, it is today.”

Later that morning, Luis Manuel Aviles was arrested by Border Patrol while running errands. He was among at least seven people immigration authorities detained in Key West on Saturday, according to Slivko-Bathurst.

Her organization verified the immigration detentions of 28 people this week, and it has been in contact with the families of most of them, she said. Most of the detainees “have work authorizations and have been following the legal process to be in this country,” according to the group.
The organization has also decried how its small Florida town has become “targeted on a huge level compared to our population size.”

It’s estimated that nearly a quarter of the roughly 25,000 people who live in Key West are foreign-born residents, many of whom work in the hospitality and tourism industries, as well as in landscaping, construction and contract work, Slivko-Bathurst said.

“Essentially, it boils down to the fact that we have a very large immigrant population, documented and undocumented,” Slivko-Bathurst added. “There is just this constant fear among everybody, because there’s not a single person in Key West — it’s a two-by-four island — that doesn’t know somebody who is an immigrant, whatever status they may have.”
The detention of Luis Manuel Aviles gained national attention after his son, Joshua Aviles, posted about it Saturday on Facebook while on board the USS Abraham Lincoln.

“I just got a call that my dad was taken by ICE. If you know my dad, you know he is a hardworking, humble man who is always willing to help anyone if he can,” the post reads. “We have done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting.”

The post continues: “This is heartbreaking for me. I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal. My dad’s only ‘crime’ was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life.”
The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln had officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more.

title: CIA director flies unannounced to Moscow to hold talks, source says
summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to holds talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
story: WASHINGTON — CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to hold unspecified talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
The person declined to say whom Ratcliffe was meeting with or what the focus of the talks was. The CIA declined to comment.

It’s Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Moscow as CIA director. He made headlines with a visit to Venezuela in January to meet with interim President Delcy Rodríguez about two weeks after the U.S. military seized President Nicolás Maduro in a raid in Caracas.

He also traveled to Cuba in May to meet with government leaders. He was the highest-ranking Trump administration official to visit the island, which is under severe economic pressure after the U.S. tightened sanctions.
News of Ratcliffe’s travel came as mystery swirled around a U.S. military transport aircraft that landed in Moscow, according to tracking data.
It was not known who was on board the plane and why it was in Moscow. When asked, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have information about the aircraft.
Neither U.S. military officials, the White House, the U.S. Embassy in Moscow nor the Russian Embassy in Washington immediately responded to questions about the flight’s mission.
Two planes, a C-130 cargo plane and a C-40, landed in Riga, the capital of Latvia, as part of the same mission, according to a U.S. official. The C-130 then went on to Russia, the official said.
Data from FlightRadar24 tracking site showed a plane approached Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow just after 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET) after taking off from Riga two hours earlier.

It had departed from the U.S. Air Force’s Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Sunday just before 5 p.m. ET, the data showed. That plane had apparently left Moscow on Tuesday afternoon, according to flight radar data.
CBS News and Axios first reported on the CIA chief’s unannounced visit.

CIA directors sometimes act as envoys for presidents in high-stakes talks with adversaries. Former President Joe Biden turned to then-CIA Director William Burns to relay stern warnings to Russia before and after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

title: Man seen in Philadelphia wearing creepy, Chucky-style mask is arrested in Las Vegas, authorities say
summary: An arrest warrant was issued in Philadelphia after a masked man chased a jogger there and said, “Are you ready to die?” Authorities say he wanted to boost his social media views.
story: A man alleged to have been seen in Philadelphia wearing a creepy, Chucky-style mask and harassing people there last week was arrested in Las Vegas, authorities in the desert city said Tuesday.
Zymire Hughes was arrested by members of the U.S. Marshals Service Violent Offender Task Force, the service said in a statement.

Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner said last week that the warrant is based on allegations of felony and misdemeanor assault after a masked man chased a jogger, asked, “Do you want to die?” and caused her to suffer injuries as she fled early last Wednesday in Center City.
He said that more charges were possible and that they would be outlined after the suspect was arrested.
Booking information from the Clark County Detention Center in Nevada shows Hughes in custody with no bail, with a hearing before a judge scheduled for Thursday morning.

It’s not clear whether he has legal counsel. Public defender’s offices in Clark County, Nevada, and Philadelphia did not immediately respond to requests for comment after regular business hours late Tuesday.

Police allege Hughes approached more than a dozen people in Center City before he fled after his interaction with the jogger. Police said he fled again after regional transit police in a train station contacted him and told him to remove his mask.

Authorities followed a trail via security cameras in the city that led to an apartment building where, they say, Hughes lives. Three people identified the masked suspect as Hughes, police said at a news conference last week.

The mask resembles the killer doll from the “Child’s Play” horror movie franchise. Police believe the masked man may have behaved in this manner before, and they asked any other possible victims to come forward.
A few days after the Center City incidents, Philadelphia Police Capt. Jason Smith said, police were tipped off that the suspect was alleged to have packed his bags and left the apartment.
Krasner said Hughes is on probation for an unspecified crime in nearby Montgomery County.
Smith said the suspect has two TikTok accounts and one Instagram account. He wore the mask to draw people to his online presence, Krasner said.
“We’re not having it in this city,” Krasner said of the antics. “We are not tolerating it.”

title: The second Dan Sullivan makes the general election in Alaska’s Senate race
summary: NBC News projects that GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Republican Dan J. Sullivan will face off in the general election alongside former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
story: Former teacher Dan J. Sullivan will join Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola on the general election ballot in Alaska’s Senate race, NBC News projects.

Republicans have criticized the other Sullivan’s candidacy as a potential ploy to confuse voters in a key battleground race, which he has denied. Alaska’s election system might also blunt the impact of any confusion. The top four candidates, regardless of party, advance from Alaska’s all-party primary to a ranked-choice general election, meaning voters could rank both Sullivans.
But some voters end up ranking only one candidate, which could matter in a close race — and Alaska’s Senate race could be one of the closest in the country this year.

Democrats have targeted Alaska as an opportunity to flip a seat since well before the same-name saga consumed the race, even though President Donald Trump carried the state by double digits in each of the last three presidential elections.

Peltola, a former state legislator and city council member, became the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress when she won a statewide special election in 2022 and then a full term months later. Peltola lost her seat after one term by 3 percentage points, running well ahead of Vice President Kamala Harris at the top of the Democratic ticket in 2024.

The federal investigation is moving forward, with a law enforcement official telling NBC News that a grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to the Dan J. Sullivan campaign.

The candidate told The New York Times that he registered as a Republican because his previous political party, the Alaska Independence Party, no longer exists. He declined to detail his involvement with the Democratic consultant because of the ongoing investigation.

title: Judge strikes down Texas ban on drag shows, tells people offended by them ‘just don’t go’
summary: The federal judge, who cited Dolly Parton in his ruling, found that the state law violated the First Amendment.
story: A federal judge in Texas struck down a 2023 state law Tuesday that sought to restrict drag shows, ruling it was unconstitutional.

U.S. District Judge David Hittner, a Reagan appointee, said the measure, known as Texas Senate Bill 12, improperly restricted speech, violating the First Amendment of the Constitution. The ruling prevents state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for the Senate, from enforcing the law and denies his motion for a new trial.
In the ruling, Hittner also had advice for “those who find such activities as described in this case offensive.”
“The solution is relatively simple ... just don’t go,” he wrote.
Paxton’s office did not immediately reply to a request for comment Tuesday night.

The state law would fine business owners who were found to be in violation up to $10,000 for hosting events, while performers could be charged with a Class A misdemeanor, which could result in up to one year of jail time.

The statute, which has been the source of a yearslong legal battle, has made its way to Hittner’s courtroom before. Hittner first deemed it unconstitutional and a violation of the First Amendment in 2023, but the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals returned it to him in November, lifting a pause on the law and giving him specific instructions about how to reassess it.
It went back into effect last year following the appeals court ruling.
Texas is among a handful of states that have passed legislation to restrict drag shows.
Hittner struck down the law Tuesday after having followed the framework the higher court asked him to follow.

In his ruling, Hittner mentioned Dolly Parton, whose death was announced Tuesday, and criticized the law’s definition of banning performances that “[appeal] to the prurient interest,” citing people who would chastise Parton “as a voluptuous sex symbol because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure.”
“There are ‘erotic’ elements in countless popular performances that could be subject to both civil and criminal penalties under S.B. 12,” he wrote.
One of the plaintiffs in the case, a drag queen who performs under the name Brigitte Bandit, impersonates Parton in her performances.

Bandit celebrated the ruling on social media Tuesday, posting a screenshot of the decision and captioning it, “Drag is free speech, b----.” She announced she would also perform as Parton, who gave her a rhinestone guitar as a gift in 2023, at an Austin bar Saturday in her honor.

Hittner added that the law was so overly broad as to lead even activities such as “cheerleading, dancing, live theater, and other common public occurrences” to be treated as civil or criminal violations. He also said that the law was vague on its face and that it failed “to give a reasonable person notice of what is prohibited.”

title: Trump-backed Mike Mazzei wins the GOP nomination in the Oklahoma governor’s race
summary: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei has secured the Republican nomination for governor in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump’s preferred candidate.
story: Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei has secured the Republican nomination for governor in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump’s preferred candidate.
Mazzei narrowly defeated state Attorney General Gentner Drummond by about 2,000 votes in the GOP primary runoff.

The initial June primary was also tight. Drummond finished in first place by just more than 1,000 votes over Mazzei. Since no candidate in the crowded field secured a majority, the race went to a runoff.

In the weeks leading up to the runoff, Drummond outraised and outspent Mazzei, with his campaign reporting last week that he brought in $2.3 million between the mid-June primary and Tuesday’s runoff. Mazzei, in the same time period, raised $816,000.
Both candidates have also loaned their campaigns significant sums: $11 million for Mazzei and $3 million for Drummond.
Trump first endorsed Mazzei in May in the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt and continued to reiterate his support for the former state lawmaker.

In a post on Truth Social last week, Trump praised Mazzei and criticized Drummond, writing, “Drummond is not the right guy. He’s got a bad attitude, and he doesn’t stand for the Values of Oklahoma, which must VOTE FOR ‘MIKE MAZZEI FOR GOVERNOR,’ on Tuesday, August 25th.”
Drummond also drew the president’s ire for suing to block the construction of the largest aluminum smelter in the country in Inola, Oklahoma, citing environmental and public health concerns.

“He wants to dethrone a magnificent, Job producing, desperately needed, and brand new, Aluminum Plant that will be one of the best projects ever conceived or built, not only in the Great State of Oklahoma, but in the United States, itself,” Trump wrote in the Truth Social post earlier this month.
Mazzei, on the other hand, supports construction of the plant.
This week, Drummond also broke with the president on his decision last week to waive tariffs on some beef imports in an attempt to lower beef prices in the U.S.

“I think Oklahoma and I are supportive of President Trump and many of his policies. I do think the majority of Oklahomans would agree that the tariffs are too far, that importing cheap beef only injures Oklahoma’s cattlemen, ranchers and farmers,” Drummond told NewsNation, echoing the concerns of GOP lawmakers in the House and Senate from states with large cattle-ranching communities.

While Trump’s endorsement remains the most coveted in GOP politics, he has had some stumbles, particularly in governor’s races. Five gubernatorial candidates he has backed this year failed to win their primaries.

With his victory Tuesday, Mazzei is the heavy favorite to win November’s general election, given the state’s deeply Republican voter base. He’ll face Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in the general election.

title: Man arrested after guillotine is found in pickup truck near Capitol
summary: Capitol Police said investigators were looking into why the 35-year-old suspect from California was in Washington.
story: U.S. Capitol Police on Tuesday arrested a man who they say was carrying a guillotine in the bed of a pickup truck.
Philan-Tam-Duy Le of Julian, California, was arrested on suspicion of “carrying a dangerous weapon” and being in possession of the guillotine, Capitol Police said in a news release.
Police said Le, 35, drove to Washington from California.
“USCP investigators are going through the suspect’s background to learn more about why he came to Washington,” police said in their news release.
Le’s truck was spotted near the Capitol and the Supreme Court, where officers say it was illegally parked.
Congress is in recess, meaning lawmakers are in their home districts, not in Washington.
An Instagram account that appeared to belong to Le included a Story on Tuesday afternoon featuring a video of a man with the guillotine outside FBI headquarters in Washington.
“Outside the FBI building, just eating some cheese pizza,” the man says in the video. The post included the caption “Guillotine adventures” and said, “Capital hill next.”
Capitol Police often make arrests beyond the Capitol grounds, and those incidents are not necessarily politically motivated.

title: Sen. Darline Graham wins the Republican Senate primary runoff in South Carolina
summary: NBC News projects that Graham, who was backed by Trump, defeated Rep. Ralph Norman to replace her late brother on the November ballot.
story: Sen. Darline Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s Republican primary runoff, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump, who recruited, endorsed and campaigned for her following her brother Lindsey Graham’s death six weeks ago.
With nearly all of the vote tallied, Graham was leading Norman roughly 52% to 48%.
At her election night party in Columbia, Graham paid tribute to her late brother and credited Trump for getting her across the finish line.
“I continue to miss Lindsey every day, and there is still a big hole in my heart. But I know he’s looking down right now, very proud of everyone in this room,” she told her supporters.

“Mr. president, Lindsey truly loved you and viewed you as one of his closest friends. I appreciate that bond and appreciate all that you’ve done for our country,” Graham continued. “Our victory would not have been possible without you, and we are truly grateful. South Carolina is truly Trump country.”
An hour north in Rock Hill, Norman said he had not prepared a concession speech and lamented Trump’s involvement, though he said he accepted the results and planned to call Graham.
Add to Google
Add to Google

“I really hate it for the state. I don’t hate it for me. ... I hate it for the state. But the public of South Carolina made the decision,” Norman told his supporters. As for Trump’s involvement, Norman said, “He has that right. That’s his prerogative,” adding that “his policies are good.”
But Norman added, “I never understood why he got in this race. ... But it is, it is what it is, and I’ll accept it.”

Trump had gone all in for Graham, who decided to run for a full six-year term after she was appointed to the seat by Gov. Henry McMaster. The president held an in-person rally for her Friday in Myrtle Beach and a tele-rally Monday evening, and his allied super PAC made a late $830,000 push to boost her.

During the Friday rally, Trump recounted how he asked her to run “because everyone loves her, everyone respects her.” He also said he’s supporting her to “honor Lindsey,” who had been one of his closest allies in Washington.
“She only knows how to put America first,” Trump told the crowd. “You vote for her, you’re going to be very proud of that vote.”

Graham, 62, will now face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the November general election, and is the heavy favorite in the deep-red state where her brother served in the Senate and House for more than 30 years.

To beat Norman, who’s spent nearly a decade in Congress, Graham had to overcome GOP attacks of nepotism and inexperience. She had never held or run for elected office before, though she did lead a 130-person state agency that helped blind people. In the initial primary earlier this month, Graham finished first with 33% of the vote, short of the 50% needed to avoid a runoff.

And the final week of the truncated, two-week runoff campaign was dominated by Graham’s blunder at a debate with Norman where she replied that she was “not that informed on national security” when asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea were important national security priorities.
“National security is not my thing,” she said.
It was a particularly notable moment given that her senator brother had served more than three decades in the Air Force and was one of the leading voices on national security on Capitol Hill.
Darline Graham said that she would be more focused as a senator on domestic policy issues, such as affordability.

“Her brother was very much about the world. … That’s good, that’s fine. But she’s more about affordability,” Trump said about the Graham siblings, who have both talked about their humble beginnings being raised in a single room next to their family’s bar and pool hall.

In the closing days of the campaign, she touted herself as someone who would continue her brother’s legacy and also be a reliable vote for Trump. In one ad, she noted she was the lead sponsor of a tough Russia sanctions bill that was renamed for her brother, and she highlighted her vote to confirm Todd Blanche, Trump’s nominee for attorney general.

Graham’s victory caps a tumultuous six-week stretch in South Carolina Republican politics. Fresh from a trip to Ukraine, Lindsey Graham died the night of July 11 from what doctors preliminarily said was a tear in the aorta due to the hardening of the arteries.

Three days later, Darline Graham was sworn in to serve out the rest of his term. Despite her appointment and Trump’s endorsement, the primary to replace her brother attracted a crowded field of candidates, including Norman, Rep. Russell Fry, former Gov. Mark Sanford and wealthy self-funding businessman Mark Lynch.
Norman first irritated Trump when he became the only House Republican to endorse former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley over Trump in the 2024 presidential primary race.

Since then, he’s been a constant thorn in Trump’s side. Last year, Norman, a member of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, clashed with Trump and GOP leaders by initially opposing the president’s landmark tax-and-spending cuts package, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” But he eventually voted yes after successfully negotiating to speed up work requirements for Medicaid recipients and the elimination of Biden-era wind and solar tax credits.
The runoff was a rare race that divided conservatives.

While Darline Graham had Trump, McMaster and Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., in her corner, Norman secured endorsements from former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, who now lives in the state; Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., his onetime rival for governor; former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, who had run in the special Senate primary race; and former Sen. Jim DeMint, R-S.C., who previously led the Heritage Foundation.

As expected, Norman performed well in the upstate areas in and around his congressional district. Graham, meanwhile, bested Norman in populous areas along the coast and around the capital city of Columbia.
Trump’s visit to South Carolina and Fry’s endorsement seem to have boosted her in Horry County, where the Myrtle Beach rally was held.
In the initial GOP primary two weeks ago, Fry won the county with nearly 14,000 votes. But in the Tuesday runoff, Graham crushed Norman there, winning more than 26,000 votes to his nearly 10,000.

title: Democratic socialists notch another win in the Oklahoma Senate primary runoff
summary: Nurse N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas has won the Democratic Senate nomination in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, defeating an older, more moderate opponent.
story: Nurse N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas has won the Democratic Senate primary runoff in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, securing another win for the party’s democratic socialist wing.

Thomas, a 31-year-old member of the Chickasaw Nation, defeated attorney and minister Jim Priest, 70, in the contest, despite being drastically outspent. The two advanced to a runoff after neither clinched a majority of the vote in the initial June primary.

Thomas will face GOP Rep. Kevin Hern, who will be heavily favored this fall to win the open seat to replace former Sen. Markwayne Mullin, now the secretary of homeland security. Oklahoma is a solidly Republican state that President Donald Trump won by 34 points in 2024.

Thomas’ primary victory comes as progressive candidates have made inroads across the country this year. Democratic socialists have won a handful of high-profile primaries in recent weeks, including in Florida’s Senate race and a key House battleground in Michigan.

Thomas is “a self-proclaimed democratic socialist,” she told NBC News in an interview Tuesday morning, though she said she is “not yet” a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. She described democratic socialists as “the next generation” that is “looking to change the system.”

Thomas said that she does not support every plank of the DSA platform. A military spouse, Thomas said she does not support defunding the Defense Department. She did voice support for a slew of progressive policies, including Medicare for All, universal childcare and parental leave, and “making sure that everyone pays their fair share.” Thomas said she also favors abolishing the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.
“The system right now doesn’t work for us and it never has,” said Thomas, noting her pitch to voters is focused on healthcare, as rural areas in the state are struggling with access to quality care.

Asked if she considered herself a capitalist or a socialist, Thomas said, “Capitalism is what’s destroying our country right now,” but she later described capitalism as “inevitable,” saying she supports the concept of people owning their own businesses and property.
Thomas said fellow democratic socialists were finding success in some primaries this year as voters are clamoring for change and “people-first” and “family-first” policies.
“I’m just ready for change and I think everyone else is as well,” she said.
Like some other progressive candidates who have prevailed in primaries this year, Thomas was outspent in the primary by a more moderate opponent.

Priest’s campaign has spent $315,000 so far, while Thomas’ campaign has spent $57,000, according to campaign finance reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. She is also starting the general election at a massive financial disadvantage: Thomas had just $456 in her campaign account as of Aug. 5, while Hern’s campaign had $2.6 million on hand as of June 30.

title: Democrat Everton Blair defeats Rep. David Scott’s daughter in the special election for the late congressman’s seat
summary: NBC News projects that Blair has won the runoff to serve the rest of Scott’s term in Georgia’s 13th District.
story: Former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair has won the special election to serve the rest of Rep. David Scott’s term in Georgia’s 13th District, NBC News projects, defeating the late congressman’s daughter.

Blair’s victory is an upset, as he trailed Marcye Scott during the first round of voting last month 46% to 38%. The two advanced from a crowded all-party special primary election in July after no candidate got a majority of the vote.
In Tuesday’s runoff, Blair led 53% to 47% with most of the expected vote tallied.

Blair supported a series of progressive policies, including a tax on households making over $50 million, “Medicare for All,” universal childcare and massive federal investments in clean energy synonymous with the Green New Deal push.
Marcye Scott tried to frame her campaign as an extension of her father’s legacy, saying she would “ensure the work already underway” advocating for the district continues.
David Scott died at age 80 on April 22 after more than two decades in Congress. He was previously the first Black chairman of the House Agriculture Committee.

Blair’s stay in Washington won’t be long. State Rep. Jasmine Clark, who didn’t run in the special election, won the regularly scheduled primary for the seat and is the heavy favorite to win the November election in this deep-blue district in the Atlanta suburbs. Blair ran in that primary election but lost to Clark.

Scott had sought to be the second daughter in recent memory to succeed her late father in Congress. Last year, Arizona Democrat Adelita Grijalva won a special election for the seat that had been held by her father, Rep. Raúl Grijalva. She is running again this fall for a full two-year term.

Once Blair and Democrat Aisha Wahab, who won a special election last week to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell in California last week, are sworn in, Republicans’ House majority will stand at 218-214, with one independent and two vacancies.

title: San Diego Padres minor-league coach released from ICE custody
summary: Oswaldo José Pirela was detained at El Paso International Airport as he was traveling for work for the team, his family and DHS said.
story: SAN DIEGO — San Diego Padres minor-league catching coordinator Oswaldo José Pirela has been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention on bond, the team said Tuesday.

Pirela, a former Texas Rangers minor-league player from Venezuela, was detained Aug. 16 at El Paso International Airport in Texas as he was traveling for work for the Padres, according to the Department of Homeland Security and his family.

“We are pleased that Oswaldo Pirela has been released on bond and reunited with his family,” Padres spokesperson Craig Hughner said in a statement Tuesday. He added that the team would have no further comment for now out of respect for Pirela’s privacy “and the ongoing matter.”
DHS said Pirela entered the country legally in 2014, was granted permission to remain until early 2018 and overstayed.
It said proceedings to remove him from the country remain on track.

“When approached by law enforcement officers, he was not in possession of legal documentation granting him status in the country,” it said. “On August 24, he was released from ICE custody on bond pending his removal proceedings.”
His family said Pirela has an application for asylum pending. The agency said work authorization and a pending application for asylum “do NOT confer legal status in the United States.”

His family has disputed DHS’ version of the facts in his case. In a previous statement, it said Pirela entered legally on a tourist visa, filed an asylum application and obtained work permits “related to that process.”
The family said 2018 was not an end year for Pirela’s permission to be in the U.S.

“The expiration date of a visa stamped in a passport does not, by itself, determine how long a person was authorized to remain in the United States,” it said, “nor does it prove that he was without any immigration proceedings since that date.”
The family said it is asking DHS to prove via documentation that Pirela, who lives outside Phoenix with family members who include two U.S.-born daughters, is in the country illegally.
Pirela has retained an immigration lawyer, it said, to dispute DHS’ version of his stay.
On Tuesday, Kimberly Pirela thanked God for her husband’s release and said the family is now focused on preventing his removal from the country.

“Now it is up to us to continue with this entire process, and we must concentrate on what is really of interest to us,” she said in a statement translated from Spanish, “which is doing everything as well as possible.”

title: Some allowed to return after Hawk Fire destroys homes in Reno area
summary: The blaze has destroyed 47 homes, and containment was at 27% Tuesday, officials said. There have been no deaths, which the fire chief called “incredible” for how fast it moved.
story: Around 9,000 people have been cleared to return to their Reno, Nevada, area homes Tuesday as firefighters made more progress containing a major, human-caused wildfire that destroyed more than 40 homes, officials said.
Around 5,000 people were still evacuated because of the Hawk Fire, which began Saturday and grew quickly, Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said at a news conference.
But by 2 p.m., residents in the areas east of State Route 395 were allowed to return, Balaam said. The west side of the highway was the hardest hit, he said.
The fire has burned 15,067 acres, and it was 27% contained Tuesday afternoon, officials said at a news conference.
No deaths have been reported in the fire, which Richard Edwards, fire chief of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District, said was remarkable.
“I think it’s incredible that we’ve not had a fatality in this fire, given how fast it’s moved,” he said.
The fire moved six miles within 24 hours of its start Saturday, Edwards said.
The cause of the fire, which is believed to have been human-caused, remains under investigation, said Balaam, the sheriff. It was not known Tuesday whether it was intentional or accidental, he said.
“We can say that because of where it occurred,” Balaam said. “It was in the middle of nowhere. There was no lightning strikes. There was nothing else that could have caused this fire.”
While firefighters have made progress, critical fire weather conditions were forecast to begin Wednesday and last through the weekend, Edwards said.
“Please be careful,” he said. “All of these fires, these large fires that we’ve incurred over the last 2½ weeks, which were human-caused, that means they’re preventable.”

title: Tributes Pour in for Dolly Parton After Music Legend’s Death at Age 80
summary: The world is mourning the loss of country music legend Dolly Parton who died at age 82. Read tributes and reactions from Reba McEntire, Lily Tomlin and more.
story: The world is mourning the loss of beloved country music star Dolly Parton, who died Aug. 25 at her home in Nashville, her nephew said in a video message. She was 80.

Her death comes a few weeks after she provided an update on her health in a video on Aug. 16 after she missed an event at Dollywood, telling fans, “Sometimes I get a little dizzy and I get dehydrated.”
The “Jolene” singer, who dealt with kidney stones earlier this year, also promised to keep active.
“All has gone well on the medical end of things, and I continue working away on all of our other projects,” she said.

Parton was a giant not just in country music, but entertainment as a whole, releasing her debut album, “Hello, I’m Dolly,” in 1967 before going on to win multiple Grammys and making the leap to the big screen, appearing in classics like the 1980 comedy “9 to 5” and 1989’s “Steel Magnolias.”
Here’s a look at how some famous friends are mourning her death.
Patti LaBelle
Parton used to famously use her acrylic fingernails to create rhythm for her music, and that includes a time when she and Patti LaBelle did it on her variety show, “Dolly,” in the ‘80s.
In a statement to NBC News, LaBelle remembered Parton’s “artistry” and “extraordinary life.”

“I am deeply saddened by the loss of my dear friend who was loved by all. Dolly’s artistry, brilliance, and extraordinary life inspired so many people, including me. Her light will forever shine! I send my deepest condolences to all of her loved ones and fans all over the world!”
Reba McEntire
Fellow country music legend and close friend Reba McEntire penned a tribute on X.

“Well, I just got the news that my buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side,” she began. “Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart.”
She continued, “There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang.”
McEntire said she knows Parton will be in heaven singing her favorite songs with all her loved ones.
“I’ll never forget the first time I met you and I’ll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart. I will always love you, Reba,” she concluded.
Jenna Bush Hager

Jenna Bush Hager, who spoke with Parton on several occasions in interviews for TODAY, posted photos to Instagram on Aug. 25, along with a heartfelt message. Two of the photos show Jenna with Dolly during a conversation they had in Dollywood in 2019. At the time, Jenna said, her grandmother Jenna Welch had just passed away.

“As I write this, Dolly’s music is being played in the restaurant where I am eating,” Jenna said. “She was a legend. Her voice was unparalleled, but it was her utter originality and purity of spirit that will be sorely missed. We needed all that glitter and goodness. She gave with all that she was. In this picture of us, I had just recieved the news my grandmother, Jenna had passed away. I was already with her in Knoxville so she held me and gave me such grace. I’ll never forget that kindness. May we take just a little of her beauty and pass it on.
Dionne Warwick
Music icon Dionne Warwick uploaded a picture of her and Parton holding hands on stage together as they performed their duet “Peace Like a River.”
“I will certainly miss her laugher, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend. My heart is heavy,” Warwick said.
Dollywood
The leader of Dollywood, the theme park near Knoxville, Tennessee, that attracts Parton’s legions of fans, issued a statement on Aug. 25 to NBC News.

The greatest privilege of my life has been helping Dolly bring her dreams to life at Dollywood,” Eugene Naughton, Dollywood Parks & Resorts President, said. “Dolly’s heart was as vast as the mountains she cherished, and her compassion knew no bounds. She inspired generations to dream boldly and love deeply. While we grieve her loss, we are honored and committed to carry her light forward. Her legacy will continue to shine in every melody sung, every smile shared and every dream kindled within these gates.”
Shirley MacLaine
Shirley MacLaine, who shared the screen with Parton in “Steel Magnolias,” said in a statement to NBC News, “God sent her to us, and she has returned home.”
Kelly Clarkson
Kelly Clarkson reflected on Parton’s legacy and why she was so beloved in her post.

“Dolly Parton had a way of making everyone feel special, and seen, and welcomed, and as if you were old friends,” she explained in her tribute. “I will miss her heart and her voice as I am sure millions will.”
She added, “What an incredible gift and talent she was and still is with an amazing catalogue of art she has left behind for all of us.”
Keith Urban
Keith Urban shared a brief message to his Instagram story that said, “Heartbroken today. Dolly Parton,” and included a broken heart. “Honestly...... I have no words right now.”
Producers of ‘Dolly: A True Original Musical’
The Broadway production inspired by the life and music of Parton said Aug. 25 after her death that the show will still go on.
“As was Dolly’s wish, the Broadway production of DOLLY: A True Original Musical will begin previews December 7 at the St. James Theatre in New York City.”
Keke Palmer
Keke Palmer, who co-starred with Parton in the 2012 musical dramedy “Joyful Noise,” shared a black-and-white photo of the icon on Instagram. She uploaded a picture of them in “Joyful Noise,” as well.
“I’m devastated. Truly,” she said in the caption.
Kacey Musgraves
Kacey Musgraves mourned Parton’s passing in a series of tweets.

“Dolly,” she wrote and included a broken heart emoji. “This one really hurts.” In a follow-up message, Musgraves said, “The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden.” For her final tweet, she added, “So glad she’s with her Carl Dean,” referring to Parton’s late husband who died in 2023. “No one talk to me today.”
Lily Tomlin

Parton’s “9 to 5” co-star Lily Tomlin uploaded Jamie Lee Curtis’ tribute — which said “Thank you, Dolly. For all of it,” beneath a black-and-white snap of Parton and Dean — to her Instagram story. Tomlin added Parton’s version of “I Will Always Love You” to the post.
She then shared a few pictures of Parton on the next slide, including one of them with fellow “9 to 5” star Jane Fonda and their reunion at the 69th Emmy Awards.
She also praised Parton for being a “comedy treasure” in a third slide featuring Parton’s hit “9 to 5.”
Khloé Kardashian
Khloé Kardashian posted a photo to her Instagram story of her with Parton, writing that she was “heartbroken,” along with a longer message about her legacy.

“Some people are so so extraordinary, their existence feels almost impossible. Dolly was one of those people,” she said, in part. “A once-in-a-lifetime soul. A woman whose light, heart, talent and humanity changed this world forever.”
Parton appeared on Kardashian’s podcast, “Khloé In Wonder Land,” last July.
Paris Hilton
Paris Hilton posted a message on X alongside a photo of herself with the country legend.

“Her talent, heart and kindness touched so many lives, and she truly left this world better than she found it,” Hilton wrote. “Sending all my love to her family, friends and everyone who loved her. Rest in peace, Dolly.”
Sarah Jessica Parker
Although she never got the chance to meet her in person, Sarah Jessica Parker still felt a connection to Parton.
In her tribute on Instagram, she wrote, “No!!!!!! I never met @dollyparton but my gosh, did I love her. I don’t think any of us had to know her to love her.”
She called Parton “one of the greatest this country ever produced” and also pointed out her philanthropic efforts.
“What a loss. But aren’t we so lucky,so fortunate for the endless gifts she shared. With the world. Godspeed and RIP. You will be terribly missed,” she said.
Brandi Cyrus

Brandi Cyrus, whose younger sister Miley Cyrus was Parton’s goddaughter, posted three broken hearts on her Instagram story. She also shared a picture of Parton with her horse and added Miley Cyrus’ song “Rainbowland,” which featured Parton.
Grand Ole Opry
The Grand Ole Opry praised Parton for being “a true music icon” in a post on X.

“There is no doubt Dolly’s mark on the world, and on us here at the Grand Ole Opry, will be deeply felt for generations to come. She taught us to always lead with kindness, generosity, and compassion,” the historic music venue said. “May her legacy live on through her songs, the lives she touched, and the countless artists she inspired. There will never, ever be another one like her. We will always love you, Dolly.”

title: Dolly Parton’s Siblings: What to Know About Her 11 Brothers and Sisters
summary: Dolly Parton, who died on Aug. 25, was one of 12 siblings. Her death was announced by her sister Cassie’s son Bryan Seaver. Here’s what to know about Dolly Parton’s siblings.
story: Dolly Parton, country music icon and 10-time Grammy winning singer-songwriter, died “peacefully” on Aug. 25 in Nashville, Tennessee, according to a news release from True Public Relations.
Her death was announced in a video message by her nephew Bryan Seaver, the son of Dolly Parton’s sister Cassie Parton. He did not provide a cause of death.
Dolly Parton is one of 12 children. Raised by Robert and Avie Lee Parton, the kids grew up in the Appalachia region of Tennessee, according to the Country Music Hall of Fame.

Dolly Parton has six living brothers and sisters: Willadeene, Robert Jr., Stella, Cassie, Freida and Rachel. Five of her brothers have died: Larry, in 1955 when he was just a baby; Floyd, in 2018 at age 61; Randy, in 2021 at age 67; David, in 2024 at age 82; and Coy, in July 2026 at age 82, per People.
Read on for everything you need to know about Dolly Parton’s 11 siblings.
Willadeene Parton

Willadeene Parton, born March 24, 1940, is the eldest of Dolly Parton’s siblings. She “tends to act as a second mother to her younger siblings,” according to a post on Dolly Parton’s official website.

Willadeene Parton, now 86, pursued a career as an author. In 1996, she published a memoir about the Parton clan titled “Smoky Mountain Memories: Stories from the Hearts of the Parton Family.” The following year, she released “All-Day Singing & Dinner on the Ground,” a compilation of recipes from the Parton family.
David Parton

David Parton, who worked as a bridge builder superintendent, died Nov. 15, 2024, at age 82 at his home in White Pine, Tennessee, sister Stella Parton announced. A cause of death has not been revealed.
Sharing news of her brother’s death, Stella Parton posted on Threads, saying that her brother “finally got his angel wings. RIP dear soul. Love you forever.”
Before his death, David Parton largely lived his life out of the spotlight, though he had been photographed escorting Dolly Parton to events, according to Woman’s World.
Stella Parton

Stella Parton, an acclaimed musician born May 4, 1949, was 11 when she made her recording debut with sisters Dolly and Cassie Parton, singing on their uncle Bill Owens’ album, per the Smoky Mountain DNA website, which traces Dolly Parton’s family origins.
Since then, Stella Parton has released more than 30 albums, starting with “I Want to Hold You (In My Dreams Tonight),” which came out in 1975.

Stella Parton, now 77, released a memoir in 2011 titled “Tell It Sister, Tell It: Memories, Music and Miracles.” She has explored acting, too, with appearances in the film “Dolly Parton’s Coat of Many Colors” (2015) and “Dolly Parton’s Christmas of Many Colors: Circle of Love” (2016).
While promoting the 2022 Pure Flix original movie “Nothing is Impossible,” Stella Parton revealed to People that she considers herself a “loner in (her) family.”
“Everybody knows that I’m independent,” she said. “But if they need me, if they call me out to help with something, producing, consulting or whatever, I’m always there.”
Cassie Parton
Cassie Parton, born on Feb. 12, 1951, first recorded music at age 10, singing backup vocals with sisters Dolly and Stella Parton, the Smoky Mountain DNA project revealed.
In 1970, she sang with her sisters on “The Porter Wagoner Show,” and she performed as a vocalist in the 2013 Dollywood production “My People: Dolly’s Letter Home,” according to Knox News.
She also appeared in an episode of the TV series “Dolly” and had a role in the 2022 film “Dolly Parton’s Mountain Magic Christmas,” according to IMDb. Nowadays, she leads a fairly private life.
Her son Bryan Seaver served as Dolly Parton’s head of security for two decades.
Randy Parton
Randy Parton, born Dec. 15, 1953, died in 2021 at the age of 67. On Jan. 21, 2021, Dolly shared his death on Facebook, revealing that her brother had died from cancer.

“The family and I are grieving his loss, but we know he is in a better place than we are at this time,” the country icon said in her statement. “We are a family of faith, and we believe that he is with God and that he is joined by members of the family that have gone on before and have welcomed him with joy and open arms.”

Like his older sister, Randy Parton achieved success in music and entertainment. Famous for his headline performances at Dollywood, the singer-songwriter released several hits that graced Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart, including “Hold Me Like You Never Had Me,” “Shot Full of Love,” “Don’t Cry Baby,” “Oh, No” and “A Stranger in Her Bed,” according to the music publication.
Larry Parton
Larry Parton, Robert and Avie Lee Parton’s ninth child and fifth son, died days after his birth in July 1955. Dolly Parton was 9 years old at the time of her brother’s death.
Floyd Parton
Floyd Parton and twin sister Freida Parton were born June 1, 1957. Like many of his siblings, Floyd Parton pursued a career in the music industry, often collaborating with Dolly Parton.
He penned her 1991 duet with Ricky Van Shelton, “Rockin’ Years” and wrote “Nickels and Dimes” for her 1978 album “Heartbreaker.”
Floyd Parton died Dec. 6, 2018, at the age of 61. The Parton family paid tribute to Floyd Parton at a private memorial in Tennessee, reported Billboard.

“Dolly, and the entire Parton family, wish to thank everyone for their kindness,” the family said in a statement to People at the time. “Yesterday, we laid our sweet baby brother to rest. We all sang his lovely song, ‘Rockin’ Years,’ together as a family at the service to say goodbye to him. He lived a short life of love and beautiful songs.”
Freida Parton
Freida Parton, born June 1, 1957, is Floyd Parton’s twin sister. Freida Parton ventured into the realm of music but diverged from her family’s country origins, singing hard rock songs.

Later in life, Freida Parton became an ordained minister. She told Knoxville News Sentinel in an interview in April 2014 that she had opened Parton Family Wedding Chapel & Antiques, a wedding chapel and store, in the family’s native Sevierville, Tennessee. However, the business appears to have closed.
Rachel Parton George

Rachel Parton George was born on Aug. 31, 1959. She’s known for her portrayal of Doralee Rhodes Brooks in the ABC sitcom “9 to 5,” which was based on the 1980 comedy film of the same name that starred Dolly Parton.

In addition to acting, Rachel Parton George released a country album in 1984, per the Smoky Mountain DNA website. According to her author page for Penguin Random House, she also performed in her family’s singing group.
In September 2024, the youngest sibling of the Parton clan released a cookbook with sister Dolly Parton called “Good Lookin’ Cookin’: A Year of Meals.”
Ahead of the release, Dolly Parton shared a picture of her and her sister on social media.

“The best part of creating this cookbook is getting to spend quality time with my sister Rachel,” Dolly Parton captioned the post with a red heart emoji. “We can’t wait to share our recipes with you all, pre-order now at the link in my bio!”
Coy and Robert Lee Parton Jr.
Dolly’s other siblings — her older brother Coy Parton and younger brother Robert Lee Parton Jr. — largely led lives out of the spotlight.
Coy Parton, who worked as a crane operator, died in July 2026, according to an obituary shared by Atchley Funeral Home. A cause of death was not provided.

title: What Dolly Parton Said About Not Having Children with Husband Carl Dean
summary: Dolly Parton, the country music superstar whose career stretched from the Tennessee mountains to Hollywood, has died.
